sources.says: A deliberative assembly is a group of people free to act together, meeting to decide courses of action for the whole group through full and free discussion. It meets in one room or under equivalent conditions where everyone can hear each other, members act on their own judgment, and each member’s opinion carries equal weight. The list says nothing about a minimum size.

q0001.answer: Being smaller than six people is not one of the characteristics. Free participation, full and free discussion, and equal votes all are.

sources.says: To become the act of the body, a proposition must be approved by more than half of the members present and voting on it, at a regular or properly called meeting.
When members are absent, as is usual, the members present at a regular or properly called meeting act for the entire membership, subject to any limits in the organization’s rules.

q0002.answer: Questions are decided by the members present at a regular meeting, not by officers, by mail, or by the entire membership.

sources.says: A deliberative assembly is a group of people who have or assume the freedom to act together, meeting to decide through discussion what action to take in the name of the whole group.

q0003.answer: An assembly is a body of people who come together as a group. A board session, a special meeting, and a series of meetings are all narrower things.

sources.says: A member of an assembly, in the parliamentary sense, is someone entitled to full participation in its proceedings: attending meetings, making motions, speaking in debate, and voting.

q0004.answer: A member is a person with the right to participate fully in the assembly’s proceedings.

sources.says: Membership in the parliamentary sense means the right to attend meetings, make motions, speak in debate, and vote. No member can be individually deprived of these basic rights.

q0005.answer: Members have the right to make motions, take part in debate, and vote. Nobody is required to debate, and calling out “Question!” does not stop debate.

sources.says: An assembly that hasn’t adopted any rules is generally understood to be bound by the rules and customs of general, or common, parliamentary law, to the extent the members agree on what those rules are.

q0006.answer: Without adopted rules, the assembly follows common parliamentary law.

sources.says: Besides parliamentary procedure and the assembly’s own rules, a deliberative body’s actions are also subject to applicable procedural rules in local, state, or national law.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: An organization may adopt whatever rules it wishes, limited only by the rules of any parent body and by national, state, or local law affecting that kind of organization.

q0007.answer: An assembly is bound by its bylaws and other rules and by all applicable local, state, and national laws.

sources.says: The basic principle of decision is that a proposition must be adopted by a majority vote, meaning more than half of the members present and voting approve it at a regular or properly called meeting.

q0008.answer: The basic principle is that propositions are adopted by a majority vote.

sources.says: Adoption by majority vote means direct approval registered by more than half of the members present and voting on the particular matter.

q0009.answer: A majority vote means more than half of the members present and voting.

sources.says: When a decision needs more than a majority, the most common requirement is a two-thirds vote of those present and voting. In some cases there may also be a requirement of previous notice, meaning the proposal must be announced at the previous meeting or included in the call of the meeting.

q0010.answer: The common requirements are a two-thirds vote, sometimes with previous notice.

sources.says: The call of a meeting is a written notice of the meeting’s time and place, sent to all members of the organization a reasonable time in advance.

q0011.answer: The call is written notice of the time and place, sent to all members in advance.

sources.says: The principal types of deliberative assembly are the mass meeting, the assembly of an organized society, the convention, the legislative body, and the board.

q0012.answer: A committee is not one of the principal types. Legislative bodies, conventions, and boards are.

sources.says: A mass meeting is a meeting of an unorganized group, announced as open to everyone (or everyone in a certain category) interested in a particular problem or purpose set by its sponsors, and called to decide on and take action.

q0013.answer: An unorganized group meeting on a specific problem, open to anyone interested, is a mass meeting.

sources.says: The people invited to a mass meeting might be a category such as supporters of a party or homeowners in a city, and admittance may be limited to that invited category if desired.

q0014.answer: Admittance may be limited to the invited category, but it doesn’t have to be.

sources.says: In an organized society, membership in the assembly is limited to people recorded on the society’s rolls as voting members who are in good standing.

q0015.answer: Membership is limited to people listed on the rolls as voting members in good standing, not whoever attends, whoever the president picks, or charter members.

sources.says: A local society’s bylaws usually provide for regular meetings at stated intervals, such as weekly, monthly, quarterly, or even annually, and usually also provide a way to call special meetings when needed.

q0016.answer: The bylaws usually provide for regular meetings at stated intervals.

sources.says: An organized local society usually holds regular meetings at stated intervals, and each of these meetings normally makes up a separate session.
Each regular meeting normally completes a separate session.

q0017.answer: In organized local societies, each meeting is normally its own session. A convention or legislative session spans many meetings.

sources.says: A convention is an assembly of delegates, normally chosen for one session only, who represent the units or subdivisions of a much larger body in whose name the convention acts.

q0018.answer: An assembly of delegates chosen for one session is a convention.

sources.says: A convention’s voting members are people holding proper credentials as delegates (or otherwise entitled to membership), and their credentials must be certified and reported by the Credentials Committee.
A convention is sometimes called to form an association or federation.

q0019.answer: The voting membership of a convention usually consists of delegates. Conventions can be called to form an association, and the Credentials Committee certifies voting members, not non-delegates.

sources.says: The end of the convention session normally dissolves the assembly. When the next convention meets a year or two later, it is a new assembly.

q0020.answer: When a convention ends, the assembly is normally dissolved.

sources.says: A legislative body is a constitutionally established public lawmaking body of representatives elected for a fixed term, such as Congress or a state legislature.

q0021.answer: Lawmaking groups such as Congress are legislative bodies.

sources.says: A board is an administrative, managerial, or quasi-judicial body made up of elected or appointed people.

q0022.answer: A board’s members may be elected or appointed.

sources.says: A board of any size is a form of assembly. Committees, by contrast, are subordinate instruments of an assembly or accountable to a higher authority in a way that isn’t typical of an assembly.

q0023.answer: A board has the character of a deliberative assembly, which is what sets it apart from a committee.

sources.says: One way a board differs from other kinds of assembly is that boards are often smaller than most other assemblies. No minimum size is given.

q0024.answer: Boards have no minimum size and are usually smaller than other assemblies.

sources.says: A board’s operation is determined by responsibilities and powers delegated to it or conferred on it by an authority outside itself.

A board may be assigned a particular function on behalf of a government, such as a board of education. A board within an organized society is an instrument of the society’s full assembly and is subordinate to it.

q0025.answer: All three statements are true, so the answer is all of the above.

sources.says: Large boards generally follow parliamentary procedure the same way as any other assembly. Small boards and committees apply most rules but are commonly allowed some informality.

q0026.answer: Large boards follow parliamentary procedure the same way as any assembly.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: An organized society needs certain rules to establish its basic structure and how it operates. Adopted rules of procedure are also needed because members may disagree about what parliamentary law is on points that could affect outcomes.

q0027.answer: A society needs rules to establish its basic structure and manner of operation.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: The corporate charter (also called articles or certificate of incorporation) is a legal instrument that states the society’s name and object, plus whatever else the law requires to incorporate it.

q0028.answer: That legal document is the corporate charter.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: A corporate charter sets out the society’s name and object, along with whatever other information is needed to incorporate under the laws of the particular state.

q0029.answer: The charter contains the name, the object, and whatever the state requires, so all of the above.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Incorporation may be necessary or advisable if a society needs to hold property, inherit, make binding contracts, hire employees, sue or be sued, or protect its officers and members from personal liability.

q0030.answer: Incorporation protects officers and members from personal liability for the organization’s obligations.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: A corporate charter should be drafted by an attorney and then processed through the legal procedure for incorporation in the state (or under federal law, where that applies).

q0031.answer: A corporate charter should be drafted by an attorney.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: In an incorporated organization, the corporate charter supersedes all of its other rules, and none of them may legally conflict with it.

q0032.answer: In an incorporated organization, the corporate charter supersedes everything else.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: The constitution or bylaws (or both) are the documents that hold a society’s own basic rules about itself as an organization, as opposed to rules about the parliamentary procedure it follows. The recommended practice today is to combine them into one document, usually called the bylaws.

q0033.answer: The society’s rules about itself as an organization are in its constitution or bylaws.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: The typical articles in an unincorporated society’s bylaws are, in order: the name of the organization, its object, members, officers, meetings, executive board (if needed), committees, parliamentary authority, and amendment.

q0034.answer: The first two articles are the name of the organization and its object.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: The typical bylaws articles cover the name, object, members, officers, meetings, executive board, committees, parliamentary authority, and amendment.

q0035.answer: A list of every member’s legal name and address is not a bylaws article. Committees, parliamentary authority, and officers are.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: An incorporated society generally should not have a constitution separate from its bylaws, because the constitution would duplicate much of the corporate charter.

q0036.answer: An incorporated society should not have a constitution separate from its bylaws.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Apart from the corporate charter of an incorporated society, the bylaws are the highest body of rules in societies today, superseding all of the society’s other rules.

q0037.answer: After the corporate charter, the bylaws are the highest body of rules.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Rules of order are written rules of parliamentary procedure formally adopted by an assembly or organization, dealing with the orderly conduct of business at meetings and the officers’ duties in doing so.

q0038.answer: Formally adopted written rules of parliamentary procedure are called rules of order.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: The term rules of order means the written rules of parliamentary procedure an assembly or organization has formally adopted.

q0039.answer: Rules of order are rules of parliamentary procedure.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: The usual and preferred way for a society to get suitable rules of order is a bylaws provision naming the current edition of a generally accepted parliamentary manual as the organization’s parliamentary authority.

q0040.answer: The manual named in the bylaws is the organization’s parliamentary authority.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: After naming a parliamentary authority in its bylaws, a society adopts any special rules of order it needs to supplement or modify the rules in that manual.

q0041.answer: Rules that supplement or modify the parliamentary authority are special rules of order.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: In a mass meeting or a meeting of a body not yet organized, a parliamentary authority (or individual rules of order) may be adopted at the beginning of the meeting.

q0042.answer: A parliamentary authority may be adopted at the beginning of the meeting.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: The rules in an adopted parliamentary manual are binding in every case where they don’t conflict with the bylaws, any special rules of order, or applicable law.

q0043.answer: The special rule wins, since the parliamentary authority applies only where it doesn’t conflict with special rules of order.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Once a society adopts a particular manual as its parliamentary authority, its rules are binding (except where they conflict with the bylaws, special rules, or law). What another manual says in conflict with the adopted one carries no authority.

q0044.answer: The adopted parliamentary authority, Robert’s Rules of Order Newly Revised, is binding.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Special rules of order are adopted separately from the bylaws. It’s advisable to print them in the same booklet as the bylaws, under a separate heading.

q0045.answer: Special rules of order should be adopted separately from the bylaws.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Rules of order, whether they come from the parliamentary authority or were adopted as special rules of order, can be suspended by a two-thirds vote, with some exceptions.

q0046.answer: Suspending rules of order takes a two-thirds vote of those present and voting.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Adopting or amending special rules of order that are separate from the bylaws requires either previous notice and a two-thirds vote, or a vote of a majority of the entire membership.

q0047.answer: It takes two-thirds with previous notice, or a majority of the entire membership.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Standing rules deal with the details of a society’s administration rather than parliamentary procedure, and can be adopted or changed on the same terms as any ordinary act of the society. They generally aren’t adopted when the society is organized, but one at a time as needs arise.

q0048.answer: Standing rules deal with the details of administration rather than parliamentary procedure.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Examples of standing rules include a rule setting the hour at which meetings begin or one about keeping a guest register.

q0049.answer: A standing rule would typically set the hour meetings begin.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Examples of standing rules include a rule about the hour meetings begin or about keeping a guest register.

q0050.answer: Keeping a guest register is a standing rule. The parliamentary authority, the quorum, and committee chairs’ duties belong in the bylaws.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: A standing rule can be adopted by a majority vote without previous notice, as long as it doesn’t conflict with or amend an existing rule or act of the society.

q0051.answer: A standing rule needs only a majority vote, with no previous notice.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: A standing rule stays in effect until it is rescinded or amended.

q0052.answer: A standing rule remains in effect until rescinded or amended.

sources.says: Ordinary standing rules, which don’t deal with parliamentary procedure as such, can be suspended by a majority vote.

q0053.answer: Standing rules can be suspended at a meeting without notice. The bylaws and charter can’t be suspended this way.

sources.says: The quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present at a meeting for business to be validly transacted. It protects against unrepresentative action by an unduly small group.

q0054.answer: The quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present to transact business.

sources.says: Most voluntary societies should set a quorum in their bylaws. Where they don’t, an assembly with an enrolled membership has a quorum of a majority of all its members.

q0055.answer: Without a bylaws provision, the quorum is a majority of the entire membership.

sources.says: The minimum essential officers for conducting business are a presiding officer, who runs the meeting and sees that the rules are followed, and a secretary or clerk, who keeps a written record of what is done.

q0056.answer: The minimum officers are a presiding officer and a secretary or clerk.

sources.says: The presiding officer’s official station is called “the chair,” and whoever is presiding is also referred to as “the chair.”

q0057.answer: “The chair” means both the person presiding and the station from which they preside.

sources.says: The president or chief officer of an organized society who normally presides is addressed as “Mr. President” or “Madam President,” or by whatever the official title is.

q0058.answer: The president is addressed as “Mr. President” or “Madam President.”

sources.says: A vice-president who is presiding is addressed as “Mr. President” or “Madam President,” unless that would be confusing, such as when the president is also on the platform. Then “Mr. Vice-President” or “Madam Vice-President” may be used.

q0059.answer: With the president not on the platform, a presiding vice-president is addressed as “Mr. President” or “Madam President.”

sources.says: With a very limited number of exceptions, and except in committees and small boards, a member never speaks while seated. With a few more exceptions, a member doesn’t speak without first obtaining the floor.

q0060.answer: With very few exceptions, a member never speaks while seated.

sources.says: The presiding officer never uses “I.” In parliamentary proceedings, they always refer to themselves as “the chair,” as in “The chair rules that…”

q0061.answer: The presiding officer refers to themself as “the chair.”

sources.says: At the meeting time, once a quorum is confirmed, the presiding officer takes the chair, waits or signals for quiet, and while standing announces clearly, “The meeting will come to order.”

q0062.answer: The proper phrase is “The meeting will come to order.”

sources.says: Meetings of permanently organized bodies usually follow an established order of business, which sets the sequence in which general types or classes of business are brought up or allowed to be introduced.

q0063.answer: That sequence is the order of business.

sources.says: A society may follow the order of business in the manual its bylaws name as parliamentary authority, or it may adopt its own particular order of business.

q0064.answer: The society may adopt its own particular order of business.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: The standard order of business runs: reading and approval of minutes; reports of officers, boards, and standing committees; reports of special committees; special orders; unfinished business and general orders; and new business.

q0065.answer: Reading and approval of the minutes comes first after the call to order.

sources.says: At any meeting where officers’ reports are made, they come immediately after the reading and approval of the minutes.

q0066.answer: Officers’ reports come immediately after approval of the minutes.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: In the standard order of business, special orders are followed by unfinished business and general orders, and then new business.

q0067.answer: Unfinished business and general orders follow special orders.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: New business is the last of the standard headings, coming after unfinished business and general orders.

q0068.answer: New business is taken up after unfinished business and general orders.

sources.says: A mass meeting usually needs no order of business, because there is nothing but new business to bring up, unless the meeting is one of a series.

q0069.answer: Only new business can come up at a mass meeting, so no order of business is needed.

sources.says: Calling a meeting to order is separate from the order of business and is not part of it. A meeting is called to order even when it has no order of business, so it’s improper to list “call to order” as the first item of an agenda.

q0070.answer: Calling a meeting to order is not part of the order of business.

sources.says: A convention commonly adopts its own order of business, which often sets exact hours for important questions. It is called the program or the agenda.

q0071.answer: A convention commonly adopts its own order of business.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: A motion is a member’s formal proposal, made in a meeting, that the assembly take certain action. A subject must be put before the assembly as a motion before it can be considered.

q0072.answer: Business is brought before the assembly by a motion.

sources.says: A communication is normally addressed to the president or secretary and read aloud by the secretary, unless its importance or source means the presiding officer should read it.

q0073.answer: The secretary normally reads communications aloud.

sources.says: Reading a communication does not by itself formally bring a question before the assembly. A member may then move appropriate action, and if no one thinks anything needs doing, the matter is dropped without a motion.

q0074.answer: Reading a communication doesn’t put a motion before the assembly.

sources.says: Debate is the parliamentary name for any form of discussion of the merits of a motion.

q0075.answer: Discussion of a motion’s merits is called debate.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: The chair must recognize any member who seeks the floor while entitled to it.

q0076.answer: The chair must recognize any member who seeks the floor while entitled to it. Officers and board members get no preference.

sources.says: To claim the floor, a member rises at their place (or goes to a microphone in a large hall), faces the chair, and addresses the chair by its proper title, such as “Mr. President.”
In small boards and committees, members generally don’t need to rise to get the floor.

q0077.answer: In a large assembly a member must rise and address the chair.

sources.says: Before making a motion or speaking in debate, a member must obtain the floor, meaning the chair recognizes them as having the exclusive right to be heard at that time.
To claim the floor, a member rises, addresses the chair by title, and, if entitled to the floor, is recognized by the chair. Only then does the member have the floor.

q0078.answer: Obtaining the floor means rising, addressing the chair, and waiting to be recognized.

sources.says: Obtaining the floor means being recognized by the chair as having the exclusive right to be heard at that time.

q0079.answer: Having the floor means the member has been recognized by the chair.

sources.says: “Privileges of the floor,” a phrase sometimes used in legislatures or conventions, has nothing to do with having the floor. It only means a person may enter the part of the hall otherwise restricted to members and necessary staff, and it carries no right to speak.

q0080.answer: It means permission to enter the restricted area of the floor, not any right to speak or be recognized.

sources.says: When members’ names aren’t generally known, a member claiming the floor gives their name and any needed identification (such as “Edward Wells, Delegate, Crescent County”) as soon as the chair turns toward them.

q0081.answer: The member states their name and identifying information.

sources.says: When a member finishes speaking, they yield the floor by sitting back down.

q0082.answer: Sitting down means the member has finished speaking.

sources.says: If two or more members rise at about the same time, then all else being equal, the one who rose and addressed the chair first after the floor was yielded is entitled to recognition. Rising before the floor is yielded gives no prior claim.

q0083.answer: The chair recognizes whoever rose and addressed the chair first after the floor was yielded.

sources.says: If the maker of a motion claims the floor and hasn’t yet spoken on it, they’re recognized ahead of others. No one gets the floor a second time on the same motion the same day while someone who hasn’t spoken wants it.

q0084.answer: Call on the member who made the motion and hasn’t debated yet.

sources.says: If the chair mistakenly gives the floor to the wrong person, a member can call attention to it by raising a Point of Order, and the chair must immediately correct the error.

q0085.answer: The mistake is corrected by raising a Point of Order.

sources.says: A motion is normally brought before the assembly in three steps: a member makes the motion, another member seconds it, and the chair states the question on it.

q0086.answer: The motion is made, seconded, and stated by the chair.

sources.says: Once the chair has stated the question, the motion is pending, or “on the floor,” and is open to debate if it is debatable.

q0087.answer: Once stated by the chair, the motion is pending.

sources.says: If the assembly decides to do what a motion proposes, it adopts the motion, or the motion is carried.
If the assembly expressly decides against what a motion proposes, the motion is lost, or rejected.
In simple cases, a member makes a main motion by saying “I move that…” followed by the proposal, worded as it should appear in the assembly’s official record.

q0090.answer: A main motion begins “I move that…”

sources.says: For more important or complex questions, or when more formality is wanted, the motion is presented as a resolution, as in “I move the adoption of the following resolution: ‘Resolved, That…’”

q0091.answer: Complex motions are presented as resolutions.

sources.says: After making a motion, a member sits down. They have the right to speak first in debate, if they wish, once the chair states the question.

q0092.answer: The maker has the right to speak first, not first and last.

sources.says: As soon as a member has made a motion, they sit back down, and may speak first in debate after the chair states the question.

q0093.answer: After making a motion, members resume their seats.

sources.says: Strictly speaking, discussion is allowed only on a pending motion. When necessary, a member may preface a motion with a few words of explanation, but these must not become a speech.

q0094.answer: A member may give a few words of explanation, not a speech.

sources.says: Before making any motion, a member may give a few words of explanation, ask for information, or briefly describe what they want to propose and ask the chair to help word an appropriate motion.

q0095.answer: A member unsure of the wording may ask the chair for help.

sources.says: After a motion is made, another member who wants it considered says “I second the motion,” “I second it,” or even “Second!”, without getting the floor. In small assemblies they don’t even rise.
The second tells the chair whether to state the question and put the motion before the assembly.

q0096.answer: The second comes before the motion is considered. The seconder needn’t be recognized, may vote against it, and needs no one’s approval.

sources.says: A member seconds a motion without obtaining the floor, and in small assemblies without rising. In large assemblies the seconder stands and gives their name without waiting to be recognized.

q0097.answer: The seconder doesn’t need to obtain the floor.

sources.says: A member who wants the motion considered says “I second the motion,” “I second it,” or even just “Second!”, without obtaining the floor.
In small boards (about a dozen members or fewer) the rules are relaxed in several ways, one of which is that motions need not be seconded.
The relaxed small-board procedures apply in the meetings of all standing and special committees, unless the committee has been instructed otherwise.

q0099.answer: Motions in small boards and committees need not be seconded.

sources.says: If no one seconds, the chair asks for a second. If there is still none, the chair says “The motion is not seconded,” or “Since there is no second, the motion is not before this meeting,” and moves to the next item of business.

q0100.answer: The chair says, “Since there is no second, the motion is not before this meeting.”

sources.says: A second only implies that the seconder agrees the motion should come before the meeting, not that they necessarily favor it.

q0101.answer: Seconding means agreeing the motion should come before the assembly.

sources.says: A second doesn’t mean the seconder favors the motion. A member may second a motion because they want the assembly to go on record rejecting it, if they think a vote would have that result.

q0102.answer: Yes. A member opposed to a motion may still second it.

sources.says: The requirement of a second guides the chair in deciding whether to state the question on the motion and so place it before the assembly.

q0103.answer: A second is for the chair’s guidance in stating the question.

sources.says: The purpose of requiring a second is to avoid spending the assembly’s time on a motion that only one person wants introduced.

q0104.answer: A second keeps the assembly from spending time on a motion only one member wants.

sources.says: If the chair is certain a motion has wide approval but members are slow to second it, the chair can state the question without waiting for a second. Until debate begins (or voting starts), though, a member can still raise a point of order that it wasn’t seconded.

q0105.answer: When the motion clearly has wide approval, the chair can state the question without a second.

sources.says: Once debate has begun, or someone has voted, the lack of a second no longer matters and it’s too late to object. A motion considered and adopted without a second is still validly adopted.

q0106.answer: A motion adopted without a second is still adopted.

sources.says: Once a motion is made and seconded, the chair places it before the assembly by stating the question: repeating the exact motion and indicating that it is open to debate.

q0107.answer: Stating the question means repeating the exact motion and opening it to debate.

sources.says: Neither making nor seconding a motion places it before the assembly. Only the chair can, by stating the question, after which the motion is pending and open to debate if debatable.

q0108.answer: The motion is open for debate once the chair states it.

sources.says: After stating the question, the chair turns to the maker to see if they want the floor. If no one claims it, the chair may ask “Are you ready for the question?” or, less formally, “Is there any debate?”

q0109.answer: “Are you ready for the question?” invites debate on the pending question.

sources.says: In stating the question, the chair says “It is moved and seconded that…” and repeats the motion.

q0110.answer: The chair says, “It is moved and seconded that…”

sources.says: For a motion that can be neither debated nor amended, the chair skips questions like “Are you ready for the question?” and puts the motion to a vote immediately after stating it.

q0111.answer: The chair puts it to a vote right after stating it.

sources.says: When a motion isn’t in order, the chair says “The chair rules that the motion is not in order [or is out of order] because…” with a brief reason. The chair must not say “You are out of order” or “Your motion is out of order,” since saying a member is out of order implies a breach of decorum.

q0112.answer: The chair says, “The chair rules that the motion is out of order because…”

sources.says: The chair, on their own initiative or at the secretary’s request, can require any main motion, amendment, or instructions to a committee to be put in writing before stating the question.

q0113.answer: The chair can require a main motion to be in writing.

sources.says: Until the chair states the question, the maker may modify or withdraw the motion freely. After that it belongs to the assembly, and the maker needs the assembly’s consent to do either.

q0114.answer: The maker can modify or withdraw it until the chair states the question.

sources.says: If the maker modifies a motion before the question is stated, the seconder has the right to withdraw their second.

q0115.answer: A seconder may withdraw the second if the maker modifies the motion before the chair states it.

sources.says: In the ordinary case a motion is considered in three steps: members debate it (if anyone wants to), the chair puts the question to a vote, and the chair announces the result.

q0116.answer: Debate, then the chair puts the question, then the chair announces the result.

sources.says: Right after stating the question, the chair turns to the maker to see if they want the floor first in debate. The maker has that right if they claim it before anyone else is recognized, even if others rose first.

q0117.answer: The chair looks to see whether the maker wants the floor to debate.

sources.says: The maker of a motion has the right to be assigned the floor first in debate if they claim it before anyone else is recognized.
The maker doesn’t have to speak at all, and may vote against their own motion, but may not speak against it.

q0118.answer: The maker has the right to speak first. It isn’t required, it isn’t a right to speak last, and it can’t be handed to someone else.

sources.says: Each member may speak twice on the same question on the same day, but can’t make a second speech while any member who hasn’t spoken on it wants the floor.

q0119.answer: A member may speak twice on the same motion on the same day.

sources.says: Without the assembly’s permission, no one may speak longer than the body’s rules allow. In a nonlegislative assembly with no rule of its own on speech length, the limit is ten minutes.

q0120.answer: The default limit is ten minutes per speech.

sources.says: Debate must be confined to the merits of the pending question. Speakers address the chair, stay courteous, avoid personal remarks, and never attack or allude to other members’ motives.

q0121.answer: Debate is confined to the merits of the immediately pending question.

sources.says: The presiding officer can’t interrupt a speaker who has the floor as long as the speaker isn’t breaking the assembly’s rules and no disorder arises. Except in committees and small boards, the presiding officer doesn’t join in debate on the merits.

q0122.answer: The false statement is that the chair can interrupt a speaker for any reason.

sources.says: The exact wording the chair uses in putting the question is definitive (unless corrected on a point of order before anyone votes), and the minutes must use the same wording.

q0123.answer: The motion is recorded as the chair stated it when putting it to a vote.

sources.says: To put the question is to put the motion to a vote, after once more making clear exactly what the assembly is deciding.

q0124.answer: Putting the question means taking the vote on the pending motion.

sources.says: The vote on a motion is normally taken by voice (viva voce), unless in certain situations it is taken by rising or, in committees, small boards, or very small assemblies, by show of hands.
When putting the question, the chair calls first for the affirmative vote and then for the negative.

q0126.answer: The affirmative vote is always taken first.

sources.says: The chair must always call for the negative vote, however unanimous the affirmative seems. This is commonly relaxed for noncontroversial complimentary or courtesy motions, but even then the chair must call for the negative if any member objects.

q0127.answer: For a noncontroversial complimentary motion, the chair need not call for the negative vote, unless a member objects.

sources.says: The chair doesn’t call for abstentions when taking a vote, because the number who respond is meaningless. To abstain means not to vote at all.
In a voice vote the chair says “Those in favor of the motion, say aye,” then “Those opposed, say no.” Alternative forms such as “All those in favor, say aye” are also acceptable.
The simple, uncounted rising vote is used mainly when a voice vote was inconclusive, and as the normal method on motions requiring a two-thirds vote.

q0130.answer: The uncounted rising vote is the usual method for motions that need two-thirds.

sources.says: Either the chair on their own initiative or the assembly by majority vote can order a vote to be counted.

q0131.answer: A count can be ordered by the chair or by the assembly.

sources.says: If a rising vote is still inconclusive, the chair or the assembly can order the vote to be counted.
If after retaking a vote as an uncounted rising vote the chair still can’t tell the result, the chair must take it a third time as a counted rising vote.

q0132.answer: The chair retakes it as a counted rising vote.

sources.says: A show of hands can be the basic voting method in small boards or committees and is used that way in some assemblies. In assemblies it should generally be limited to very small meetings where every member can clearly see every other member.

q0133.answer: A show of hands is for small groups.

sources.says: A member may change their vote up to the time the result is announced. After that, a change needs the assembly’s unanimous permission.

q0134.answer: Members can change their vote until the result is announced.

sources.says: A complete announcement of a vote includes which side “has it” (or whether two-thirds were in favor), a declaration that the motion is adopted or lost, and a statement of the effect of the vote, or an order to carry it out, where appropriate.

q0135.answer: The announcement also states the effect of the vote.

sources.says: For a voice vote, the chair announces “The ayes have it and the motion is adopted” (or “agreed to” or “carried”), or “The noes have it and the motion is lost.”

q0136.answer: The chair says, “The ayes have it, and the motion is adopted.”

sources.says: For a two-thirds motion, the chair announces “There are two thirds in the affirmative and the motion is adopted,” or “There are less than two thirds in the affirmative and the motion is lost.”

q0137.answer: The chair says, “There are less than two-thirds in the affirmative, and the motion is lost.”

sources.says: A tie rejects a motion that needs a majority. When there’s a tie without the chair’s vote, the chair can vote in the affirmative to adopt the motion. If the chair abstains, the motion is lost.

q0138.answer: At 26 to 26, the chair must vote in the affirmative for the motion to pass.

sources.says: When there is one more vote in the affirmative than the negative without the chair’s vote, the chair can vote in the negative to create a tie, and the motion is lost, since a tie is not a majority.

q0139.answer: The chair’s vote makes it 24 to 24, a tie, so the motion is lost.

sources.says: If the chair still can’t determine the result after retaking a vote as an uncounted rising vote, the chair must take it a third time as a counted rising vote.

q0140.answer: The chair takes a counted rising vote.

sources.says: A member may demand a division from the moment the negative votes are cast until the result has been announced, or immediately afterward.

q0141.answer: A division may be demanded until the result is announced, or immediately after.

sources.says: To demand a division, a member calls out, without getting the floor, “Division!”, “I call for [or demand] a division,” or “I doubt the result of the vote.” The chair must then immediately take a rising vote.

If the chair doesn’t order a count and a member wants one, the member moves that the vote be counted. If seconded, the assembly votes on whether to order the count, and without a special rule a majority vote is required.

q0143.answer: The motion to count the vote needs a majority vote.

sources.says: If a division is doubtfully close and the chair doesn’t order a count, a member may, as soon as the result is announced, rise and address the chair, and is entitled to preference in recognition to move that the vote be counted. If seconded, the chair puts that motion to a vote.

q0144.answer: The member rises, is recognized, and moves that the vote be counted. Calling “Division” only gets an uncounted rising vote.

sources.says: In very small assemblies where everyone can clearly see everyone else, an inconclusive voice vote may sometimes be verified by a show of hands, if no member objects.

q0145.answer: In a very small assembly it may be verified by a show of hands.

sources.says: In very small assemblies where everyone can clearly see everyone else, an inconclusive voice vote may be verified by a show of hands if no member objects. A show of hands is not a division, though.

q0146.answer: The chair may verify by a show of hands. It isn’t a division, and it can’t be used over a member’s objection or where members can’t all be seen.

sources.says: The presiding officer, if a member, has the same voting right as anyone else. Except in small boards and committees, or on a ballot vote, the chair protects their impartiality by voting only when it would affect the outcome, and may then either vote or abstain.

q0147.answer: The chair votes when it would affect the outcome, or may abstain.

sources.says: A tie rejects a motion that needs a majority. If there’s a tie without the chair’s vote and the chair abstains, the motion is lost.

q0148.answer: On a tie with no chair vote, the motion is lost.

sources.says: When there seems to be no opposition, time can be saved by unanimous consent, which was formerly also called general consent.

q0149.answer: Unanimous consent was formerly called general consent.

sources.says: Unanimous consent follows from the principle that rules exist to protect the minority, so they generally needn’t be strictly enforced when there is no minority to protect.

q0150.answer: Rules are designed to protect the minority.

sources.says: Unanimous consent can be used to adopt a motion without stating the question and putting it to a formal vote, or to take action without even a formal motion.

q0151.answer: That is adoption by unanimous (general) consent.

sources.says: Correcting the minutes is an example of business normally handled by unanimous consent.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: The chair asks for corrections to the minutes. Corrections are usually handled by unanimous consent, but if a member objects, the usual rules for amendments apply.

q0152.answer: Correcting and approving the minutes is normally handled by unanimous consent.

sources.says: The main motion is the basic form of motion, and the only one whose introduction brings business before the assembly.

q0153.answer: Business is introduced by a main motion.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: Motions are classified as main motions, subsidiary motions, privileged motions, incidental motions, and motions that bring a question again before the assembly. Only the subsidiary, privileged, and incidental motions together are called secondary motions.

q0154.answer: None of those are secondary motions: original and incidental main motions are main motions, and the bring-back motions are their own class.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: Once a secondary motion is made and admitted by the chair as in order, it must be acted on or disposed of before direct consideration of the main question can continue.

q0155.answer: The secondary motion must be disposed of before the main motion can be considered further.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: When more than one secondary motion is pending along with the main motion, the one most recently stated by the chair (among those not yet voted on) is the immediately pending question.

q0156.answer: The motion most recently stated by the chair is immediately pending.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: The main motion, the seven subsidiary motions, and the five privileged motions have a definite order of precedence. The main motion, which takes precedence over nothing, ranks lowest.

q0157.answer: The main motion has the lowest rank.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: A main motion is one whose introduction brings business before the assembly. It can be made only when no other motion is pending, and it ranks lowest in precedence.

q0158.answer: Main motions bring business before the assembly.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Subsidiary motions help the assembly treat or dispose of a main motion, and sometimes other motions.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: If an embarrassing main motion has been brought before the assembly, a member can propose disposing of it without a direct vote by moving to Postpone Indefinitely.

q0160.answer: Postpone Indefinitely is for avoiding an embarrassing matter. Postponing to a later time or the next meeting is Postpone Definitely.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The subsidiary motions, in order, are Postpone Indefinitely, Amend, Commit, Postpone to a Certain Time, Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, Previous Question, and Lay on the Table.

q0161.answer: Postpone Indefinitely is a subsidiary motion. Point of Order, Parliamentary Inquiry, and Division of the Assembly are incidental.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: If a main motion might work better in a different form, a member can move to Amend it, proposing a change in wording to clarify it or, within limits, modify its meaning before it is voted on.

q0162.answer: To change the wording, move to Amend.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: When a matter needs more study or a better-worded proposal than the full assembly can efficiently produce, a member can move to Commit, or Refer, it to a committee.

q0163.answer: Move to refer it to a committee.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: If the assembly might prefer to take up the main motion later in the same meeting or at another meeting, a member can move to Postpone to a Certain Time, also called Postpone Definitely.

q0164.answer: Move to postpone it definitely (to a certain time).

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: To consider a main motion later in the same meeting or at another meeting, a member moves to Postpone to a Certain Time (Postpone Definitely).

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Postpone to a Certain Time is one of the seven subsidiary motions.

q0166.answer: Postpone to a Certain Time is subsidiary, not incidental. The other three are incidental motions.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: The motion can limit debate in forms such as “I move that debate be limited to one speech of five minutes for each member,” or set a time to close debate, as in “I move that after twenty minutes debate on the resolution be closed.”

q0167.answer: Say, “I move to limit debate to twelve more minutes.”

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: The motion can limit debate by reducing the number or length of speeches or by setting when debate will close. It can extend debate by allowing more and longer speeches than the regular rules.

q0168.answer: It can do all of those.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: If the assembly wants to close debate and vote immediately, a member can move the Previous Question.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: To lay the main motion aside temporarily without setting a time to resume, with the ability to take it up again whenever a majority decides, a member moves to Lay on the Table.

q0170.answer: Move to Lay on the Table.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Subsidiary motions are always applied to another motion while it is pending, and they can be applied to any main motion.

q0171.answer: Subsidiary motions can be applied to any main motion.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Every subsidiary motion can be amended except Postpone Indefinitely, the Previous Question, and Lay on the Table.

q0172.answer: Postpone Indefinitely can’t be amended. Amend, Postpone to a Certain Time, and Commit can.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: When a motion to Postpone to a Certain Time is immediately pending, motions to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, the Previous Question, and Lay on the Table are in order. Lower-ranking motions such as Postpone Indefinitely and Commit are not.

q0173.answer: Lay on the Table can be moved. Commit, Postpone Indefinitely, and a new main motion can’t.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Privileged motions don’t relate to the pending business. They deal with matters of immediate and overriding importance that should be allowed to interrupt anything else without debate.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The five privileged motions have an order of precedence and generally take precedence over motions of every other class. As a class they are also known as “privileged questions,” which shouldn’t be confused with questions of privilege.

q0175.answer: Privileged motions are also known as “privileged questions.” They don’t relate to pending business, do have an order of precedence, and are undebatable.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The privileged motions, in ascending order of rank, start with the Call for the Orders of the Day, followed by Raise a Question of Privilege, Recess, Adjourn, and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q0176.answer: Call for the Orders of the Day is the lowest-ranking privileged motion.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day is a privileged motion by which a member can require the assembly to follow its agenda, program, or order of business, or to take up a general or special order that is due, unless two-thirds of those voting want otherwise.

q0177.answer: It’s in order when a member demands that the assembly conform to its agenda.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day needs no second, and it isn’t debatable or amendable. When a single member calls for them, the orders of the day must be enforced, but a two-thirds vote can set them aside.

q0178.answer: One member can require it, and a two-thirds vote can set it aside.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: If a pressing situation affects the rights or privileges of the assembly or a member, such as noise or inadequate ventilation, a member can Raise a Question of Privilege, which lets them interrupt pending business to make an urgent request or motion.

q0179.answer: Poor ventilation calls for Raising a Question of Privilege.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: A member can move to Adjourn, and the assembly can adjourn, even while business is pending, as long as the time for the next meeting is already set by rule or by the assembly.

q0180.answer: Adjourning with business pending is allowed when the time for the next meeting has been established.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: When the assembly wants to set a date and hour for another meeting, in an established society one before the next regular meeting, it uses the motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q0181.answer: Use the motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The privileged motions are listed in ascending order of rank. Each one outranks those before it, ending with Adjourn and then Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q0182.answer: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is the highest-ranking privileged motion.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Incidental motions relate in various ways to the pending business, or to other business at hand. As a class they deal with questions of procedure, most often arising out of another pending motion, and they usually have to be decided right away, before business can go on. Most of them can’t be debated.

q0183.answer: That is the description of incidental motions.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: As a class, incidental motions deal with questions of procedure arising most commonly out of another pending motion, and sometimes out of a motion or item of business about to be introduced or just pending.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Incidental motions have no order of precedence among themselves.

q0184.answer: Incidental motions usually deal with procedural questions arising out of another pending motion.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: With few exceptions, incidental motions are related to the main question in a way that means they must be decided immediately, before business can proceed. Most are undebatable.

q0185.answer: They must be decided immediately before business can proceed.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Most incidental motions are undebatable.

q0186.answer: Most incidental motions are not debatable.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Any member who thinks the chair isn’t enforcing the rules can call attention to the breach when it happens by making a Point of Order, which requires the chair to rule on it.

q0187.answer: A breach of the rules is raised with a Point of Order.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The subsidiary motions are Postpone Indefinitely, Amend, Commit or Refer, Postpone to a Certain Time, Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, Previous Question, and Lay on the Table.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Point of Order is listed among the incidental motions: a member who believes the chair isn’t enforcing the rules can raise one when the breach happens, which requires the chair to rule on it.

q0188.answer: Point of Order is an incidental motion, not a subsidiary one.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Among the incidental motions is the Appeal: any two members, by moving and seconding an appeal right after the chair rules, can require the ruling to be put to a vote of the assembly.

q0189.answer: Appeal is incidental. Recess is privileged, Extend Debate is subsidiary, and postponing an event is a main motion.

sources.says: If any discussion of a particular original main motion might do harm, the proper course is to raise an Objection to the Consideration of the Question before its consideration begins.

q0190.answer: Raise an Objection to the Consideration of the Question.

sources.says: When a motion on a single subject has several parts, each able to stand as a complete proposition on its own, the parts can be separated and voted on as distinct questions by adopting a motion for Division of a Question.

q0191.answer: The member moves a Division of the Question.

sources.says: Whenever a member doubts the result of a voice vote or a show of hands, because it seems close or not enough members voted, they can call for a Division of the Assembly, which requires the vote to be retaken by rising.

q0192.answer: Call for a Division of the Assembly.

sources.says: Any member, by demanding a Division, can require a voice vote or show of hands to be retaken as a rising vote, but no single member can force it to be counted.

sources.section: §30 Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
sources.says: Ballot votes, roll calls, and counted votes are ordered by motions relating to methods of voting, which the assembly must adopt.

q0193.answer: One member can require a standing (rising) vote. Roll call, ballot, and counted votes take an assembly vote.

sources.section: §32 Request to Be Excused from a Duty
sources.says: A Request to Be Excused from a Duty takes precedence over any motion it’s connected with and can also be made when nothing is pending. While pending, it yields to the other incidental motions, among others.

q0194.answer: A Request to Be Excused from a Duty is an incidental motion.

sources.says: A Parliamentary Inquiry is a question to the presiding officer for information on parliamentary law or the organization’s rules as they bear on the business at hand.

q0195.answer: It asks the chair’s opinion on a point of procedure related to the business at hand.

sources.says: A Request for Information (Point of Information) is directed to the chair, or through the chair to another officer or member, for information relevant to the business at hand but not about parliamentary procedure.

q0196.answer: It goes to the chair, or to a member through the chair.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Incidental motions have no rank among themselves. With the exception of a Division of the Assembly, they yield to the privileged motions.

q0197.answer: Incidental motions have no rank among themselves. Not all of them yield to privileged motions, since Division of the Assembly doesn’t.

sources.says: Rescind, also known as Repeal or Annul, cancels a previous action or order. Its effect is to strike out an entire main motion, resolution, order, or rule that was adopted earlier.

q0198.answer: Rescind, Repeal, and Annul are names for the same motion, so any of them.

sources.says: The motion to Discharge a Committee lets the assembly take a matter out of a committee’s hands after referring it and before the committee’s final report, so the assembly can consider it itself.

q0199.answer: It takes the matter out of the committee’s hands.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: If, later in the same session and no later than the same or next business-meeting day, new information or a changed situation suggests a different result would reflect the assembly’s will, a member who voted with the prevailing side can move to Reconsider the vote.

q0200.answer: New information after a vote calls for the motion to Reconsider.

sources.says: Rescind and Amend Something Previously Adopted are two forms of one incidental main motion, governed by identical rules.

q0201.answer: Rescind is an incidental main motion.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Discharge a Committee (applied to a referred motion) and Take from the Table share the feature of proposing that the assembly take up a matter still “within its control” that was temporarily disposed of.

q0202.answer: Both propose taking up a matter still within the assembly’s control.

sources.says: Many of the key rules for individual motions boil down to eight standard descriptive characteristics, which also show how each motion compares with a main motion.
The first standard characteristic covers precedence. The main motion ranks lowest, takes precedence over no other motion, and yields to all subsidiary, privileged, and applicable incidental motions.

q0204.answer: Ranking lowest means the main motion takes precedence over no other motion.

sources.says: The eight standard characteristics of a motion are: what it takes precedence over and yields to; what motions it can be applied to and what motions can be applied to it; whether it’s in order when another has the floor; whether it needs a second; whether it’s debatable; whether it’s amendable; what vote it needs; and whether it can be reconsidered.

q0205.answer: Which other motions apply to the motion is one of the eight. Number of speeches, the secretary’s duties, and when the minority speaks are not.

sources.says: The standard characteristics note for the main motion that it ranks lowest, is not in order when another has the floor, is debatable, and is amendable.
The eight standard characteristics include whether a motion requires a second, whether it’s debatable, whether it’s amendable, and what vote it needs. Which members may debate is not one of them.

q0207.answer: Which members can debate is not a standard characteristic.

sources.says: The seventh standard characteristic is what vote is required to adopt the motion. A main motion needs a majority, with some exceptions.

q0208.answer: It covers what vote is required for adoption.

sources.says: A meeting is a single official gathering of an assembly’s members in one room or area to transact business, with no break in proceedings and members not separating except for a short recess.

q0209.answer: A meeting is a single official gathering of the members.

sources.says: Unless the bylaws define it otherwise, a session is a meeting or a series of connected meetings devoted to a single order of business, program, agenda, or announced purpose.

q0210.answer: A session is a meeting or series of connected meetings.

sources.says: A recess, strictly speaking, is a short intermission within a meeting that doesn’t end the meeting or break its continuity.

q0211.answer: A short intermission that doesn’t end the meeting is a recess.

sources.says: Adjournment sine die is also called adjournment without day.

Adjournment sine die usually means the close of a session of several meetings where the adjournment dissolves the assembly (as in a series of mass meetings or a convention) or where the body won’t meet again for a long time unless called into special session.

q0213.answer: It is the final adjournment that closes the assembly’s session.

sources.says: Adjournment of a mass meeting, or the last meeting of a convention, dissolves the assembly unless provision has been made for it to be reconvened later.

q0214.answer: Adjourning sine die dissolves the assembly.

sources.says: A standing rule adopted by majority vote stays in force until rescinded or amended, but it doesn’t materially limit a later session, because any session can suspend it for its own duration by a majority vote.

q0215.answer: A standing rule can be suspended for a session by a majority vote.

sources.says: Bylaws and special rules of order contain the provisions expected to stay stable from session to session and to represent the judgment of the whole society, so changing them requires previous notice and a two-thirds vote, or a majority of the entire membership.

q0216.answer: They contain the provisions expected to stay stable from session to session.

sources.says: For regular meetings, the day (such as “the first Tuesday of each month”) should be set in the bylaws, and the hour and place fixed by a standing rule.

q0217.answer: The hour should be fixed in the standing rules.

sources.says: If two business sessions are separated by more than a quarterly time interval, business can go over from the earlier session to the later one only by referral to a committee.

q0218.answer: With sessions more than a quarter apart, the only way to carry a motion over is to refer it to a committee.

sources.says: A special (or called) meeting is a separate session held at a time different from any regular meeting, convened only to consider the business specified in the call of the meeting.

If the bylaws don’t authorize special meetings, they aren’t permitted, except when the assembly calls one for a disciplinary trial. The bylaws should say who can call one and how much notice is required.
Only business specified in the call can be transacted at a special meeting. Action on anything else must be ratified at a regular meeting (or another properly called special meeting) to become valid.

q0220.answer: The false statement is that a special meeting is set by a motion at the previous regular meeting. It is called under the bylaws, with notice.

sources.says: If the bylaws don’t authorize special meetings, such meetings aren’t permitted, except when authorized by the assembly itself as part of formal disciplinary procedures.

q0221.answer: Special meetings must be authorized in the bylaws.

sources.says: Notice of a special meeting’s time, place, and purpose, clearly describing the business to be brought up, must be sent to all members a reasonable number of days in advance.

q0222.answer: Notice of the time, place, and purpose must go to members several days in advance.

sources.says: The only business that can be transacted at a special meeting is what was specified in the call of the meeting, though related privileged, subsidiary, and incidental motions may still be considered.

q0223.answer: A special meeting considers the items specified in the call of the meeting.

sources.says: If a special meeting acts on business not mentioned in the call, that action becomes valid only if the organization ratifies it at a regular meeting, or at another special meeting properly called for that purpose.

q0224.answer: It must be ratified by the organization at a regular meeting.

sources.says: An adjourned meeting is a continuation of the session of the immediately preceding regular or special meeting, scheduled when the assembly adjourns to or until a particular time.
If a regular or special meeting can’t finish its work, an adjourned meeting can be scheduled for later that day or another convenient time before the next regular meeting.

q0226.answer: Adjourning until October 21 creates an adjourned meeting.

sources.says: A special meeting is also called a called meeting.

q0227.answer: Another name for a special meeting is a called meeting.

sources.says: An adjourned meeting picks up its work where it was interrupted in the order of business or in the postponed question, except that the minutes of the preceding meeting are read first.

q0228.answer: At an adjourned meeting, the minutes of the preceding meeting are read first.

sources.says: Some societies hold only one business meeting of the general membership a year, leaving management to a board in the meantime. That meeting is the society’s annual meeting.

q0229.answer: That meeting is the annual meeting.

sources.says: Where regular meetings are held throughout the year, the minutes of the annual meeting are read and approved at the next regular meeting, not held a year for the next annual meeting.

q0230.answer: The annual meeting’s minutes are approved at the next regular meeting.

sources.says: In general usage, an executive session is any meeting of a deliberative assembly, or part of one, at which the proceedings are secret.

q0231.answer: Secret proceedings are held in executive session.

sources.says: A motion to go into (or out of) executive session is a question of privilege, and is adopted by a majority vote.
Minutes of an executive session may be read and approved only in executive session, unless their content isn’t secret. Members who reveal what happened there can be subject to discipline.

q0232.answer: A motion to go into executive session is a question of privilege adopted by a majority vote. The proceedings stay secret, and the session isn’t limited to officers.

sources.says: A member who violates the secrecy of an executive session can be punished under disciplinary procedure. Anyone else permitted to be present is honor-bound not to reveal what happened.

q0233.answer: The member may be punished under disciplinary procedure.

sources.says: Minutes of an executive session may be read and approved only in executive session.

q0234.answer: They are read and approved at another executive session.

sources.says: An original main motion introduces a substantive question as a new subject. It is the most common motion and the basic way a matter is put before the assembly.

q0235.answer: An original main motion introduces a substantive question as a new subject.

sources.says: An incidental main motion proposes an action specifically defined under parliamentary law and described by a particular parliamentary term, so there is a definite number of them. Like all main motions, it can be made only when nothing is pending.

q0236.answer: It proposes an action defined under parliamentary law with a particular parliamentary name.

sources.says: An incidental main motion doesn’t mark the start of the assembly’s involvement in a substantive matter, as an original main motion does. It relates to the assembly’s business, or its past or future action.

q0237.answer: Unlike an original main motion, it never introduces a substantive question as a new subject.

sources.says: Examples of incidental main motions include adopting a committee’s recommendations, and procedural motions with no pending business, such as taking a recess or placing a special limit on the length of speeches throughout a meeting.

q0238.answer: All three are incidental main motions.

sources.says: The chief difference in the rules is that an Objection to the Consideration of a Question can be applied to original main motions but not to incidental main motions, because with an incidental main motion the assembly is already involved and it’s too late to object.

q0239.answer: An Objection to the Consideration of a Question can’t be applied to an incidental main motion.

sources.says: The main motion is applicable to no other motion, while all subsidiary motions and certain incidental motions can be applied to it. It ranks lowest, so it takes precedence over nothing.

q0240.answer: A main motion can be applied to no other motion.

sources.says: All subsidiary motions, and certain incidental motions under various conditions, can be applied to a main motion.

q0241.answer: Every subsidiary motion can be applied to an original main motion.

sources.says: A main motion is not in order when another member has the floor. It needs a second, is debatable and amendable, and requires a majority vote with some exceptions.

q0242.answer: Main motions are out of order when another member has the floor.

sources.says: A motion whose only effect is to have the assembly refrain from doing something shouldn’t be offered if offering no motion would get the same result, such as moving “that no response be made” to a request.

q0243.answer: Don’t propose a motion that the assembly refrain from doing something.

sources.says: Avoid motions with negative statements, since members may be confused about the effect of voting for or against them. Instead of going on record as “not in favor of” something, move to “oppose” or “declare its opposition to” it.
It’s incorrect to move “that no response be made” or “that our delegates be given no instructions” when doing nothing would have the same effect.

q0244.answer: “Declare its opposition to the increase” is the best-worded motion. The others are negative or propose doing nothing.

sources.says: Any resolution, and any long or complicated motion, should always be submitted in writing.

q0245.answer: A resolution should always be submitted in writing.

sources.says: When background or reasons should be included, the motion is cast as a resolution with a preamble placed before the resolving clauses. A preamble consists of one or more clauses beginning “Whereas.”
In considering a resolution with a preamble, the preamble is always amended last, because changes to the resolving clauses may require changes to the preamble.

If the Previous Question is ordered on a resolution before its preamble has been reached, the order doesn’t cover debate and amendment of the preamble. The assembly takes up the preamble before voting on the resolution.

q0248.answer: The preamble is still open to debate.

sources.says: The word “Resolved” is underlined or printed in italics, followed by a comma and “That” with a capital T.
Each preamble clause is its own paragraph beginning “Whereas,”, and the preamble never contains a period. Its paragraphs close with semicolons.

q0249.answer: “Resolved” is underlined or in italics. Preamble clauses are separate paragraphs ending in semicolons, never periods or colons.

sources.says: No main motion is in order that presents substantially the same question as one finally disposed of earlier in the same session by being rejected, postponed indefinitely, or blocked by a sustained objection to consideration. It can be renewed at a later session.

q0250.answer: The false statement is that a main motion may repeat a question already rejected in the same session.

sources.says: A main motion is out of order if it conflicts with the charter, constitution, bylaws, or procedural rules set by law; if it proposes action outside the organization’s object, unless two-thirds authorize it; or if it conflicts with or presents the same question as one temporarily disposed of and still within the assembly’s control.

q0251.answer: All three make a main motion out of order.

sources.says: After a main motion is made and before the chair states it, any member can quickly rise and informally suggest modifications, which the maker may accept or reject.

q0252.answer: Any member can informally suggest changes to the maker.

sources.says: Once the chair has stated the question, the motion belongs to the assembly, and the maker can modify or withdraw it only with the assembly’s consent.
A pending motion can be changed only by vote or unanimous consent of the assembly, even if the maker says they “accept” the change.

q0253.answer: The maker must ask for unanimous consent (or the assembly must vote).

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: If properly amending a main motion would take a lot of time, or more information is needed, the motion can be turned over to a committee for study or redrafting by moving to Commit (Refer).

When several motions are pending, they are voted on in reverse order of their making, starting with the highest-ranking one. So a motion to refer the main question and its amendment to a committee is voted on before the amendment or the main motion.

q0255.answer: The motion to refer is voted on first.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely takes precedence over nothing but the main question it is applied to. It is the lowest-ranking subsidiary motion.

q0256.answer: Postpone Indefinitely is voted on before the main motion.

sources.says: A main motion normally can be moved only when nothing is pending. But some questions can come up as main motions after interrupting other business, if brought up by a Call for the Orders of the Day or by Raising a Question of Privilege.

q0257.answer: A Call for the Orders of the Day can bring up a main motion while another is pending.

sources.says: When debate seems to have ended, the chair makes sure no one else wants to speak by asking “Are you ready for the question?” or “Is there any further debate?”, then puts the motion to a vote.

q0258.answer: The chair asks, “Are you ready for the question?” or “Is there any further debate?”

sources.says: Previous notice means an announcement that a motion will be introduced, indicating its content, must be included in the call of the meeting, or given at the preceding meeting if no more than a quarterly interval separates them.

Motions that change something the assembly already did, such as Rescind, Amend Something Previously Adopted, Discharge a Committee, or postponing a scheduled event, require previous notice if they are to be adopted by only a majority vote.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Adopting or amending special rules of order separate from the bylaws requires either previous notice and a two-thirds vote, or a vote of a majority of the entire membership.

q0261.answer: The usual requirement is previous notice and a two-thirds vote. A majority of the entire membership is the alternative.

sources.says: When no question is pending, a member who wants to give notice is entitled to preference in recognition, and if necessary the notice can even interrupt pending business.

q0262.answer: Any member present at the meeting may give notice. Nonmembers can’t, and it isn’t limited to board or charter members.

sources.says: When no question is pending, a member wishing to give notice is entitled to preference in recognition. It interrupts pending business or comes after an adjournment vote only if the member couldn’t get the floor otherwise, and never after the chair declares the meeting adjourned.
