q0263.answer: The normal time is when no question is pending.

sources.says: Previous notice can be included in the call of the meeting sent to members, or given at the preceding meeting.
Oral notice at a meeting can, if necessary, interrupt pending business, and is in order when someone has been assigned the floor but hasn’t started speaking.

q0264.answer: All of those are allowable ways to give notice.

sources.says: The motion to ratify (also called approve or confirm) is an incidental main motion used to confirm or make valid an action already taken that can’t become valid until the assembly approves it.

q0265.answer: Ratify is an incidental main motion.

sources.says: The motion to ratify is also called approve or confirm. It is used to confirm or validate action already taken.

Ratify is an incidental main motion used to make valid an action already taken, such as action at a meeting without a quorum, business outside a special meeting’s call, or action by officers or committees beyond their authority.

q0267.answer: Adopting a motion to ratify makes valid an action already taken.

sources.says: An assembly can ratify only what it could have authorized in advance. It can’t validate a voice-vote election when the bylaws require a ballot, or anything done in violation of law or its own bylaws, though it may ratify action taken without a quorum.

q0268.answer: Ratify can’t be used to confirm a voice-vote election when a ballot is required.

sources.says: Because the motion to ratify is a main motion, it is debatable and opens the entire question to debate.

q0269.answer: A motion to ratify opens the question to debate again.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely is a motion that the assembly decline to take a position on the main question. Adopting it kills the main motion for the session and avoids a direct vote.

q0270.answer: The assembly uses it to show it doesn’t want to take a position on the main motion.

sources.says: Adopting Postpone Indefinitely kills the main motion for the duration of the session and avoids a direct vote on it.
Adopting Postpone Indefinitely kills the main motion for the duration of the session.

q0272.answer: The main motion is killed for the rest of the session.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely avoids a direct vote on the question. It is useful for disposing of a badly chosen motion that couldn’t be adopted or expressly rejected without possibly undesirable consequences.

q0273.answer: It is used to avoid a direct vote on the question.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely takes precedence over nothing except the main question it is applied to. It is the lowest-ranking subsidiary motion and yields to all other subsidiary, privileged, and applicable incidental motions.

q0274.answer: It takes precedence over nothing but the main question.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely can be applied only to the main question, so it can be made only while a main question is immediately pending. It can’t be committed, or postponed or laid on the table by itself.

q0275.answer: It can be applied only to the main question.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely can be made only while a main question is immediately pending, and it yields to all other subsidiary motions.

q0276.answer: With an amendment pending, Postpone Indefinitely is out of order. Point of Order, Limit Debate, and Adjourn are in order.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely can be made only while a main question is immediately pending. It can’t be committed or laid on the table alone.

q0277.answer: It can be moved only when the main motion is immediately pending.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely can’t be laid on the table alone, but if the main question is laid on the table while it is pending, it goes to the table too.
If the main motion is referred to a committee while Postpone Indefinitely is pending, Postpone Indefinitely is dropped and doesn’t go to the committee.

q0278.answer: It stays with the main motion when the main motion is laid on the table, but not when it is referred.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, and is debatable. Unlike any other subsidiary motion, debate on it can go fully into the merits of the main question.

q0279.answer: It is debatable, and debate can go fully into the merits of the main question.

sources.says: An affirmative vote on Postpone Indefinitely can be reconsidered. A negative vote on it cannot.

q0280.answer: Only an affirmative vote can be reconsidered.

sources.says: Postponing a question indefinitely suppresses it for the current session. In a convention of several meetings, the suppression lasts through the entire series of meetings.

q0281.answer: The suppression lasts through the entire series of meetings.

sources.says: Strategists sometimes use Postpone Indefinitely to test their strength on a motion they oppose. Members who have used up their debate on the main question can speak again, because debate on this motion goes into the main question.

q0282.answer: It allows more debate on the main question.

sources.says: Adopting Postpone Indefinitely kills the main motion for the session without a direct vote on it.
Like other subsidiary motions, it requires obtaining the floor and a second.

q0283.answer: Obtain the floor and move to postpone the motion indefinitely. A point of order doesn’t address merits, and moving to lay on the table from your seat is improper.

sources.says: The subsidiary motion to Amend modifies the wording, and within limits the meaning, of a pending motion before that motion is acted on.

q0284.answer: Amend is used to modify the wording of a pending motion.

sources.says: Adopting an amendment doesn’t adopt the motion it amends. That motion remains pending in its modified form.
Rejecting a motion to Amend leaves the pending motion worded as it was before the amendment was voted on.

q0286.answer: The pending motion stays worded as it was.

sources.says: A member’s vote on an amendment doesn’t obligate them to vote any particular way on the motion it applies to. They may vote as they please on the main motion, amended or not.

q0287.answer: The member is free to vote either way on the main motion.

sources.says: An amendment must be germane to be in order, meaning it must in some way involve the same question raised by the motion it is applied to.

q0288.answer: An amendment must always be germane.

sources.says: Amend can be applied to any main motion, and in limited ways to any other motion with a legitimately variable factor, such as the length of a recess or the hour to which a question is postponed. It can’t have Commit, Postpone Definitely, or Lay on the Table applied to it alone.

q0289.answer: Amend can be applied to any main motion or any motion with a variable factor.

sources.says: Amend can be applied to any motion with a legitimately variable factor, and can be applied to itself to create a secondary amendment. It requires a majority vote.

q0290.answer: The false statement is that an amendment can’t be applied to a motion with a variable.

sources.says: An amendment is debatable whenever the motion it applies to is debatable, and undebatable whenever that motion is undebatable.

q0291.answer: A primary amendment is debatable whenever the motion it applies to is debatable.

sources.says: Debate on an amendment must be confined to whether the amendment is desirable, and must not extend to the merits of the motion being amended, except as needed to decide whether the amendment is advisable.

q0292.answer: While an amendment is pending, the merits of the motion being amended aren’t discussed.

sources.says: An amendment of the third degree is not permitted. Instead, a member can announce that if the pending secondary amendment is voted down, they will offer a different secondary amendment.

q0293.answer: The chair rules the motion to amend the secondary amendment out of order.

sources.says: Amend is generally amendable, which creates two degrees of amendment, primary and secondary, but a secondary amendment cannot be amended.

q0294.answer: An amendment to an amendment may not be amended.

sources.says: The first process of amendment is to insert words, or, when they go at the end of the sentence or passage, to add words.

q0295.answer: Placing words at the end is adding.

sources.says: To substitute is, in effect, to strike out a paragraph, or the whole text of a resolution or main motion, and insert another in its place. Strike out and insert applies to words.

q0296.answer: Replacing a whole paragraph is substitution.

sources.says: The three processes of amendment are inserting or adding, striking out, and the combination of the two: striking out and inserting (for words) or substituting (for paragraphs).

q0297.answer: Filling a blank isn’t one of the forms of amendment. Striking out, inserting, and adding words are.

sources.says: A primary amendment applies directly to the pending motion. A secondary amendment applies to a pending primary amendment.

q0298.answer: An amendment to a primary amendment is a secondary amendment.

sources.says: To be germane, an amendment must in some way involve the same question raised by the motion it is applied to.

q0299.answer: Germane means the amendment involves the same question as the motion it amends.

sources.says: In a motion to commend an officer, an amendment to strike out “commend” and insert “censure” is germane and in order, even though it opposes the original intent, because both deal with the body’s opinion of the officer’s action.

q0300.answer: The amendment is germane and in order, so the chair accepts it and asks for a second.

sources.says: In borderline cases where the chair can’t judge germaneness, the chair should admit the amendment or, in important cases, ask the assembly to decide whether it is germane.

q0301.answer: Refer the question of germaneness to the assembly for a vote.

sources.says: Improper amendments include one that isn’t germane, one that would make the amended question out of order, and one that strikes out the word “Resolved” or other enacting words.

q0302.answer: All three are always out of order.

sources.says: A motion to insert words must name the exact place: the word before or after which, or the words between which, the insertion goes.
Words placed at the end of the sentence or passage are said to be added rather than inserted.

q0303.answer: Inserted words go within the text, while words at the end are added. Of the choices, “between other words” fits best.
q0303.conflict: RONR also lets you insert words before a named word, including at the very start of a sentence, so “always between” is stricter than the book. The real distinction is that the end of a passage takes “add,” not “insert.”

sources.says: A motion to insert words must specify the exact place by naming the word before or after which, or the words between which, the insertion is made.

q0304.answer: “Inserting the word ‘three’ before the word ‘basketballs’” names the exact place, as required.

sources.says: Words placed at the end of the sentence or passage being amended are added rather than inserted.
Example: with a main motion pending, a member obtains the floor and says “I move to add the words ‘and convert it into a parking lot.’”

q0305.answer: Obtain the floor and move to add the words “from 9 p.m. to 11:30 p.m.” at the end.

sources.says: Adopting an amendment doesn’t adopt the motion it amends. That motion remains pending in its modified form.

q0306.answer: Debate continues on the main motion as amended.

sources.says: Some amendments are so simple or acceptable that they can be adopted by unanimous consent. The chair says “If there is no objection…” and, with no objection, declares the amendment adopted.
Commit, Postpone Definitely, and Lay on the Table can’t be applied to an amendment alone.

q0307.answer: An amendment can be adopted by unanimous consent. It can’t be postponed, referred, or tabled by itself.

sources.says: The best way to strike out separated words is to move to strike out the entire clause or sentence containing them and insert a new clause or sentence.

q0308.answer: Strike out the whole clause containing the separated words and insert a new clause.

sources.says: A substitute offered for a main motion or resolution, or for a paragraph within one, is a primary amendment, so it can be moved only when no other amendment is pending.

q0309.answer: A substitute is a primary amendment.

sources.says: After a paragraph or version has been substituted, it can’t be amended during the same session except by adding something that doesn’t change its existing content, just as with any inserted paragraph.

q0310.answer: A substituted section can be amended only by adding words.

sources.says: Cases suited to filling blanks include main motions or primary amendments containing names of persons or places, dates, numbers, or amounts.

q0311.answer: Blanks work for names of persons, places, and amounts, so all of the above.

sources.says: The motion to create a blank is actually an incidental motion. It requires a second but is neither debatable nor amendable.

q0312.answer: The motion to create a blank requires a second.

sources.says: A blank can be created three ways: a member offers a motion or amendment containing a blank, a member moves to create a blank, or the chair suggests creating one.

q0313.answer: All three ways create a blank.

sources.says: The chair can suggest creating a blank, saying for example “The chair suggests creating a blank by striking out…,” and if no one objects, the blank is created.

q0314.answer: The chair suggests creating a blank and asks for unanimous consent.

sources.says: Filling a blank with one name works much like nominations. The chair repeats each name as proposed, then votes on each in order until one receives a majority.
Suggestions to fill a blank don’t need a second.

q0315.answer: A name fills the blank when it gets a majority vote. Suggestions need no second, and the chair repeats each name.

sources.says: Commit or Refer generally sends a pending question to a small group of selected people, a committee, so it can be carefully investigated and put into better shape for the assembly to consider.

q0316.answer: The purpose is careful investigation, putting the question in better condition for the assembly.

sources.says: Committees allow greater freedom of debate, meaning there is no limit on the number of times a member can speak. Three variations of Commit give the full assembly that same freedom.

q0317.answer: Members can speak as many times as they wish.

sources.says: The three variations of the motion to Commit are to go into a committee of the whole, to go into a quasi committee of the whole (consider as if in committee of the whole), and to consider informally.

q0318.answer: All three are variations of Commit.

sources.says: “Recommit” is a motion to refer a question a second time, either to the same committee that considered it before or to a different one.

q0319.answer: Recommit means referring a question a second time.

sources.says: Commit takes precedence over the main motion, Postpone Indefinitely, and Amend. It yields to Postpone Definitely, Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, the Previous Question, Lay on the Table, and all privileged motions.

q0320.answer: Commit takes precedence over Amend. It yields to Lay on the Table, Recess, and Limit Debate.

sources.says: Commit can be applied to main motions, along with any pending amendments or motions to divide or consider by paragraph. It can reach an adhering appeal or point of order only together with the main question.

q0321.answer: The motion to Refer applies to main motions.

sources.says: Commit can be applied to main motions together with any amendments that are pending. It is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, and is debatable.

q0322.answer: It can be applied to a main motion along with its pending amendments.

sources.says: Commit is debatable, but debate can extend only to whether to commit the main question and to the details of the motion to Commit. It must be seconded and is out of order when another has the floor.

q0323.answer: Debate is limited to the desirability of committing the main question.

sources.says: If the question goes to a special committee, the motion should specify the number of members and how they are selected (unless the rules prescribe the method), or may name the members.

q0324.answer: The motion may specify the number, the method of selection, and the names, so all of the above.

sources.says: Instructions in a motion to Commit are binding on the committee. They may cover when it meets, how it considers the question, whether it hires an expert consultant, and when it reports.

q0325.answer: All of those can be binding instructions.

sources.says: A committee can be given “full power” to act for the society in a specific case.

q0326.answer: A committee appointed with power can act for the society in the specific case referred.

sources.says: A committee given “full power” to act for the society in a specific case can also be authorized to spend money or even add to its own membership.

The chair must rule out of order, as dilatory, any motion to Commit that is obviously absurd or unreasonable, such as one that because of the time involved would defeat the purpose of the main question.

q0328.answer: The chair rules the motion to refer dilatory, since reporting next month would defeat a matter that needs action tomorrow.

sources.says: When a motion to Commit merely lacks details, the chair shouldn’t rule it out of order. Members can offer suggestions or amendments to complete it (or the chair can call for them), or the chair can put it to a vote at once and fill in the details afterward.

q0329.answer: All of those approaches are allowed.

sources.says: When different ways of selecting a committee are proposed, they are voted on in this order: election by ballot; open nominations with viva voce election; nominations by the chair; and appointment by the chair.

q0330.answer: Election by ballot is voted on first.

sources.says: The power to appoint a committee carries with it the power to appoint its chairman and to fill any vacancy on the committee.

q0331.answer: The chairman who appointed the committee also names its chairman.

sources.says: If a main motion is referred to a committee while Postpone Indefinitely is pending, Postpone Indefinitely is ignored and doesn’t go to the committee, because adopting Commit shows the assembly doesn’t favor indefinite postponement.

q0332.answer: The chair declares that Postpone Indefinitely can no longer be considered.

sources.says: Commit or Refer sends a pending question to a committee so it can be carefully investigated and put into better condition for the assembly.
Example: a member obtains the floor and says “I move that the resolution be referred to a committee to be appointed by the chair,” and the motion is seconded.

q0333.answer: Obtain the floor and move to refer the main motion to a committee appointed by the chair.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Postpone to a Certain Time puts off action on a pending question to a definite session, day, meeting, or hour, or until after an event, and can be moved regardless of how much debate there has been.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Neither the motion nor any amendment to it is in order if its effect would be the same as Postpone Indefinitely, that is, if it would kill the measure.

q0334.answer: The false statement is that it has the same effect as Postpone Indefinitely. It delays a question, while Postpone Indefinitely kills it.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Postpone to a Certain Time takes precedence over the main motion and over Postpone Indefinitely, Amend, and Commit, so it can be made while an amendment is pending. It yields to Lay on the Table and is out of order when another has the floor.

q0335.answer: It can be made while a main motion with an amendment is pending.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Postpone to a Certain Time takes precedence over the main motion and over Postpone Indefinitely, Amend, and Commit.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Postpone to a Certain Time yields to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, the Previous Question, Lay on the Table, and all privileged motions.

q0337.answer: It yields to Lay on the Table.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Postpone to a Certain Time is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, is debatable only as to postponement (not the merits of the main question), and normally needs a majority vote.

q0338.answer: It is out of order when another member has the floor.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Postpone to a Certain Time is debatable, though debate must not go into the merits of the main question more than needed to decide whether and to when it should be postponed.

q0339.answer: Postpone to a Certain Time is debatable. Lay on the Table, the Previous Question, and Limit Debate are not.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: The subsidiary motion to Postpone is debatable, amendable as to the time and as to making it a special order, and an affirmative vote on it can be reconsidered. In its usual form it makes the question a general order, not a special order.

q0340.answer: It is debatable, amendable, and can be reconsidered.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Where more than a quarterly time interval will pass between meetings, as in an annual convention or a society that meets only annually, a question can’t be postponed beyond the end of the present session.

q0341.answer: It can’t be postponed beyond the end of the present session.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Where no more than a quarterly interval passes between sessions, a question can be postponed until, but not beyond, the next regular business session. A society meeting weekly can’t postpone a question for longer than a week.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Where no more than a quarterly time interval will elapse between sessions, a question can be postponed until, but not beyond, the next regular business session.

q0343.answer: It can’t be postponed beyond the end of the next session.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: A postponed question becomes an order of the day for the session, day, meeting, or hour to which it is postponed.

q0344.answer: Postpone Definitely makes the question an order of the day.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: When a main motion is postponed, any adhering motions pending with it, such as amendments, are postponed along with it, and business resumes in the same condition when the question comes up again.

q0345.answer: The pending amendment is postponed with the main motion.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: When a question is taken up on a different day from the one on which it was postponed, members’ right to debate starts over, as if the question had not been debated before, except for any unexhausted order limiting or closing debate.

q0346.answer: Each member can again speak twice.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: To postpone a question to the next meeting, a member says “I move to postpone the motion to the next meeting.”

q0347.answer: Obtain the floor and move to postpone the main motion to the next regular meeting.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate can limit debate by reducing the number or length of speeches, or by closing debate at a certain hour or after a set length of time. It can also extend debate by allowing more and longer speeches.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate takes precedence over all debatable motions. It is out of order when another has the floor and requires a two-thirds vote.

q0349.answer: It takes precedence over all debatable motions.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate can be applied to any immediately pending debatable motion, a series of pending debatable motions, or a consecutive part of such a series. It can’t be laid on the table alone.

q0350.answer: It can be applied to any immediately pending debatable motion.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate can’t be laid on the table alone, but if the main question is laid on the table while it is pending, it goes to the table too. It must be seconded, is undebatable, and needs two-thirds.

q0351.answer: It can be laid on the table along with the main motion.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate is not debatable, but it is amendable, and any amendment to it is also undebatable.

q0352.answer: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate is undebatable but amendable.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: The motion requires a two-thirds vote because it suspends the rules, and because limiting debate takes away every member’s basic right to full discussion and may restrict the minority’s ability to present its case.

q0353.answer: It takes away members’ rights to full and free discussion.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: While a motion to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate is pending, its precedence prevents lower-ranking subsidiary motions, including Postpone Indefinitely, Amend, Commit, and Postpone to a Certain Time.

q0354.answer: An amendment to the main motion is out of order while Limit Debate is pending.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: After an order that sets a time for closing debate on the main question, motions to Commit or Postpone to a Certain Time are no longer in order, since the order implies the question will be voted on at that time.

q0355.answer: Referring the matter to a committee is no longer in order.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: To reduce the number or length of speeches, a member moves, for example, “that debate be limited to one speech of five minutes for each member.”

q0356.answer: Obtain the floor and move that debate be limited to one speech for each member.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Unless Limit or Extend Limits of Debate is adopted by unanimous consent, the chair puts it to a rising vote.

q0357.answer: The chair takes a rising vote.

sources.says: Ordering the Previous Question immediately closes debate and stops amendment on the pending question(s), and prevents the making of any other subsidiary motions except the higher-ranking Lay on the Table.

q0358.answer: Lay on the Table can still be made.

sources.says: Ordering the Previous Question immediately closes debate on, and stops amendment of, the immediately pending question (and any others it specifies), so the assembly proceeds to vote.

Ordering the Previous Question closes debate and stops amendment on the pending question(s), and prevents other subsidiary motions except Lay on the Table. It doesn’t prevent privileged or incidental motions.

q0360.answer: It stops debate and amendment on the pending question.

sources.says: The Previous Question is not allowed in committees.
An order for the Previous Question doesn’t prevent privileged or incidental motions, as applicable.
The Previous Question is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, and is not debatable.

q0362.answer: It doesn’t prevent privileged or incidental motions. It needs a second, isn’t debated, and needs the floor.

sources.says: In practice the motion is usually made unqualified, “I move the previous question,” and then applies only to the immediately pending question. In qualified form it can cover a consecutive series of pending questions.

q0363.answer: The unqualified form applies only to the immediately pending question.

sources.says: The unqualified “I move the previous question” applies only to the immediately pending question, and the motion requires a two-thirds vote.

q0364.answer: None of those is right. It needs two-thirds, applies only to the immediately pending question, and has nothing to do with asking questions.

sources.says: The Previous Question requires a two-thirds vote. If it fails to get two-thirds, debate continues as if the motion had not been made.

q0365.answer: Debate continues as if the motion hadn’t been made.

sources.says: A motion or “call for the question” may lead to unanimous consent to end debate. If anyone objects or seeks the floor, the chair must ask for a second, and if seconded, take a vote on ordering the Previous Question. It always needs a second and a two-thirds vote to cut off debate against anyone’s will.

q0366.answer: The chair asks for a second, then votes on it.

sources.says: When the Previous Question is ordered on a series of pending motions, they are voted on in order of rank starting with the immediately pending one, which is the reverse of the order in which they were made.

q0367.answer: They are voted on in reverse of the order they were made.

sources.says: The Previous Question is exhausted when all the motions on which it was ordered have been finally disposed of, or when any remaining ones are no longer affected by the order.

q0368.answer: It is exhausted when all the motions it was ordered on are finally disposed of.

sources.says: A vote ordering the Previous Question can be reconsidered before, but not after, any of the motions affected by the order have been voted on.

q0369.answer: It can be reconsidered before any affected motion is voted on.

sources.says: The motion is made in forms like “I move the previous question.” Calls of “Question!” from members’ seats are not motions for the Previous Question and are disorderly if someone is speaking or seeking recognition.
Example: a member obtains the floor and says “I move the previous question,” and it is seconded.

q0370.answer: Obtain the floor and say, “I move the previous question.”

sources.says: Ordering the Previous Question immediately closes debate on, and stops amendment of, the immediately pending question.
When the result is affirmative, the chair at once states the question on the motion that is then immediately pending.

q0371.answer: The chair takes the vote on the amendment right away.

sources.says: Lay on the Table lets the assembly set the pending question aside temporarily when something of immediate urgency has come up, with no set time to resume but with the ability to take it up again by majority vote.

q0372.answer: It lays a question aside temporarily when something more urgent arises.

sources.says: Lay on the Table sets the pending question aside temporarily. There is no set time for taking it up again, but it can be resumed whenever a majority wishes, within time limits.
Lay on the Table is not debatable and not amendable.

q0373.answer: It sets the question aside temporarily with no set time to resume. It isn’t debatable or amendable, and it doesn’t kill the motion.

sources.says: Lay on the Table is commonly misused in ordinary assemblies in place of Postpone Indefinitely, Postpone to a Certain Time, or other motions. In those misuses it is often called a motion “to table.”

q0374.answer: It is commonly misused in place of Postpone to a Certain Time.

sources.says: If a time for resuming consideration is specified when moving to Lay on the Table, the motion can be admitted only as a motion to Postpone, which is debatable.

q0375.answer: Treat it as a motion to Postpone, suggesting the maker offer it that way.

sources.says: Lay on the Table takes precedence over the main motion, all other subsidiary motions, and any incidental motions pending when it is made. It yields to all privileged motions.

q0376.answer: It takes precedence over all other subsidiary motions.

sources.says: Ordering the Previous Question prevents any other subsidiary motion except the higher-ranking Lay on the Table.
No subsidiary motion can be applied to Lay on the Table, and it can’t be applied to a subsidiary motion alone, only in connection with the main question.

q0377.answer: Lay on the Table can still be made after the Previous Question. It isn’t debatable or amendable and can’t be applied to an amendment alone.

sources.says: Laying a question on the table carries with it everything adhering to it. If a resolution with a pending amendment is laid on the table, the amendment goes too, and they all come back together if taken from the table.

q0378.answer: The amendment adheres to the main motion and goes to the table with it.

sources.says: No subsidiary motion can be applied to the motion to Lay on the Table.

q0379.answer: No subsidiary motion can be applied to it.

sources.says: Lay on the Table is out of order when another has the floor. It takes precedence over all other subsidiary motions, so it can be made while they are pending.

q0380.answer: It is out of order when another member has the floor.

sources.says: Lay on the Table must be seconded and isn’t debatable, but it is proper for the maker to state the reason first, and the chair can ask them to, such as “Our speaker must catch an early flight.” It isn’t amendable.

q0381.answer: The maker may state the reason before moving it.

sources.says: An affirmative vote on Lay on the Table can’t be reconsidered, because it’s simpler to take the question from the table. A negative vote can be reconsidered only in limited circumstances.

q0382.answer: Lay on the Table is the motion where only a negative vote can sometimes be reconsidered.

sources.says: A question laid on the table can be taken from the table by a majority vote once the interrupting business is disposed of, or later within time limits, when no question is pending.

q0383.answer: Take from the Table requires a majority vote.

sources.says: A tabled question can be taken from the table during the same session, or, if the next regular session is within a quarterly time interval, until the end of that next session. After that it dies.

q0384.answer: It stays on the table until the end of the next regular session.

sources.says: It is not in order to move to lay a pending question on the table if there is evidently no other matter requiring immediate attention.

q0385.answer: It is out of order when there’s evidently no urgent matter needing attention.

sources.says: Lay on the Table is for setting the pending question aside temporarily when something else of immediate urgency has arisen.
A member can’t move to lay a question on the table until a stated time or event. That’s a motion to Postpone.

q0386.answer: Obtain the floor and move to lay the question on the table, without naming a time.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day is a privileged motion by which a member can require the assembly to conform to its agenda, program, or order of business, or to take up a general or special order that is due, unless two-thirds wish otherwise.

q0387.answer: It requires the meeting to conform to its agenda.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day doesn’t require a second. When a single member calls for them, the orders of the day must be enforced, unless a two-thirds vote sets them aside.

q0388.answer: Any single member can call for the orders of the day, with no second.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day doesn’t require a second, isn’t debatable (though the caller may remind the chair what is due), and isn’t amendable.

q0389.answer: It isn’t seconded, debated, or amended.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: The orders of the day must be enforced on a single member’s call, except that a two-thirds vote can set them aside, either by voting down the chair’s question on proceeding to them or by a member’s motion to extend time or suspend the rules.

q0390.answer: The orders of the day can be set aside by a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: If the chair senses the assembly would rather continue with the pending question, the chair can, instead of announcing the orders of the day, put the question on whether the assembly will proceed to them. It takes two-thirds in the negative to refuse.

q0391.answer: The chair can put to a vote whether the assembly wishes to proceed to the orders of the day.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: Once the assembly has refused to proceed to the orders of the day, they can’t be called for again until the pending business is disposed of.

q0392.answer: Not until the pending business is disposed of.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: To call for the orders of the day, a member rises and, addressing the chair without waiting for recognition, says “Mr. President, I call for the orders of the day,” or “I demand the regular order.”

q0393.answer: Rise and, without obtaining the floor, say “Madam President, I call for the orders of the day.”

sources.says: Raise a Question of Privilege is a device that lets an urgent request or main motion about the rights and privileges of the assembly or a member come up for immediate consideration while business is pending, when it otherwise would not be in order.
It needs no second and isn’t debatable, it yields to applicable incidental motions, and the chair’s ruling on admitting it cannot be reconsidered.

q0394.answer: It may permit action that otherwise wouldn’t be in order. The other statements contradict its characteristics.

sources.says: To raise a question of privilege, a member stands, addresses the chair without waiting to be recognized, and announces that they rise to a question of privilege affecting the assembly, or to a question of personal privilege.

The chair, even if someone else has been assigned the floor, then directs the member to state the question of privilege. The member either describes the problem and asks that it be fixed, or makes a motion if formal action is needed. Unless it can be settled quickly, the chair rules on whether it really is a question of privilege and whether it is urgent enough to interrupt.

It is in order when someone else has the floor if the situation is urgent, but only after the floor has been assigned and before that person begins speaking. It can’t interrupt a member who is actually speaking unless waiting would defeat its purpose, and it can never interrupt voting.

q0395.answer: Dunbar keys the choice that the member states the request once the chair directs them to. It can be raised while an amendment is pending, and the chair rules on it instead of a two-thirds vote.
q0395.conflict: Under 19:6, the statement that it usually can’t interrupt a member speaking is also true in the 12th edition. Expect Dunbar’s keyed choice on a Dunbar-based test, but know the interruption rule too.

sources.says: Raise a Question of Privilege takes precedence over all other motions except the three higher-ranking privileged motions: Recess, Adjourn, and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q0396.answer: It takes precedence over everything listed except Recess.

sources.says: Raising a question of privilege is in order when another has the floor if the situation is urgent enough. It can’t interrupt someone actually speaking unless the purpose would otherwise be defeated.

q0397.answer: A member with the floor may be interrupted to raise a question of privilege. Amendments, limiting debate, and the Previous Question need the floor.

sources.says: Raising a question of privilege doesn’t require a second (unless it is stated as a motion), isn’t debatable, and isn’t amendable. A main motion admitted as a question of privilege can then be debated and amended.

q0398.answer: The device of raising a question of privilege isn’t amendable, debatable, or seconded.

sources.says: Raising a question of privilege is ruled on by the chair. No vote on admissibility is taken unless the ruling is appealed.

q0399.answer: The chair makes the initial ruling.

sources.says: Questions of the privileges of the assembly include those about the comfort of members, such as heating, ventilation, lighting, and noise.
Example: when jackhammers start outside during a speech, a member rises and says “I rise to a question of privilege affecting the assembly,” then asks that the windows be closed.

q0400.answer: It could be used to request that windows be opened to improve ventilation.

sources.says: Questions of the privileges of the assembly concern its organization, members’ comfort, the conduct of officers, and similar matters, and a motion to go into executive session is one. Charges circulated against a member’s character are a question of personal privilege.

q0401.answer: Charges against a member’s character are a matter of personal privilege, not the assembly’s privilege.

sources.says: If a question of privilege is made as a motion and seconded, and the chair admits it and decides it should be taken up immediately, the chair states the question and proceeds as with any other main motion.
Once admitted, a question of privilege made as a motion is treated as a main motion, which is debatable and amendable.

q0402.answer: Treat it as a main motion: open it to debate, then vote.

sources.says: Example: when jackhammers start outside during a speech, a member rises, interrupts, and says “Mr. President, I rise to a question of privilege affecting the assembly,” then describes the noise so it can be dealt with.

q0403.answer: Rise without obtaining the floor and say, “Mr. President, I rise to a question of privilege affecting the assembly.”

sources.says: A motion to go into executive session, closing the meeting to nonmembers, is a question of the privileges of the assembly.
A question of privilege made as a motion must be seconded, and once admitted for immediate consideration it is handled like any other main motion, including debate.

q0404.answer: Ask for a second and open the new motion to debate.

sources.says: A recess is a short intermission that doesn’t close the meeting. It may be taken, for example, to count ballots, get information, or allow informal consultation.
The privileged motion to Recess is a motion that a recess begin immediately, made while another question is pending.

q0406.answer: Made while another motion is pending, Recess is a privileged motion.

sources.says: The privileged motion to Recess proposes that a recess begin immediately.
A motion to recess made when no question is pending, whether the recess starts now or later, is a main motion.

q0408.answer: With nothing pending, a motion to recess is a main motion.

sources.says: A motion to recess is privileged only when another question is pending, and a motion for a recess at a future time is in order only when no question is pending.
The privileged motion to Recess can’t be reconsidered.

q0409.answer: It is privileged only when made while another question is pending.

sources.says: A motion to take a recess at a future time is in order only when no question is pending. Only a recess beginning immediately is privileged.

q0410.answer: A recess “after the vote” is a future-time recess, so the chair declares it out of order while a main motion is pending.

sources.says: A motion to take a recess at a future time is in order only when no question is pending.

q0411.answer: Only when no question is pending.

sources.says: Recess takes precedence over the main motion, all subsidiary and incidental motions, and all privileged motions except Adjourn and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q0412.answer: Recess outranks Refer to a Committee, but not Adjourn or Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.says: The privileged motion to Recess must be seconded, isn’t debatable, is amendable as to the length of the recess, and requires a majority vote.

q0413.answer: It is amendable as to the length of the recess.

sources.says: Recess is amendable as to the length of the recess, and any such amendment is undebatable. It requires a majority vote.

q0414.answer: An amendment to Recess is not debatable.

sources.says: If an adopted agenda provides for a recess, the chair, with no further action by the assembly, declares the recess when the time arrives. If the chair doesn’t, a member can call for the orders of the day.

q0415.answer: The chair declares the recess at the scheduled time.

sources.says: If the chair doesn’t announce a recess provided in the adopted agenda at the scheduled time, a member can call for the orders of the day, demanding that the recess be declared.

q0416.answer: The member should call for the orders of the day.

sources.says: If the assembly doesn’t want to recess when the scheduled time arrives, the time for the recess can be postponed by a two-thirds vote.

q0417.answer: A scheduled recess can be postponed by a two-thirds vote.

sources.says: Forms of the motion include “I move to recess for ten minutes” and “I move that the meeting recess until 2 P.M.”
The privileged motion to Recess is out of order when another has the floor and must be seconded.

q0418.answer: Obtain the floor and say, “I move to recess for ten minutes.”

sources.says: When a recess is adopted, the chair announces that the meeting stands recessed, rapping once with the gavel if desired.
An adjournment may be signaled by a single rap of the gavel, if desired.

q0419.answer: Of the choices, recess, adjournment, and breach of order is the one Dunbar’s key accepts.
q0419.conflict: RONR 12th ed. mentions the gavel for a recess and an adjournment, but doesn’t list rapping for a breach of order. In fact 61:9 says the chair should never try to drown out a disorderly member with the gavel. That part of the answer comes from Dunbar, not the 12th edition.

sources.says: “I move to adjourn” or “I move that the meeting now adjourn” may be used for either a privileged or a main motion. Forms that set a time to meet again or adjourn sine die are main motions only.
The privileged motion to Adjourn is out of order when another has the floor.

q0420.answer: Obtain the floor and say, “I move to adjourn.”

sources.says: The privileged motion to Adjourn is always moved in an unqualified form, with no mention of a time. It proposes closing the meeting immediately, where another meeting is provided for and no time for adjourning has already been set.

q0421.answer: All three describe the privileged motion to Adjourn.

sources.says: In ordinary societies whose bylaws provide for several regular meetings a year and that have no fixed hour for adjournment, an unqualified motion “to adjourn” is always privileged.

q0422.answer: It is privileged when it is unqualified and no time for adjournment has been set.

sources.says: A motion to adjourn is not privileged when it is qualified in any way, as in adjourning at or to a future time. It is then treated like any other incidental main motion.

q0423.answer: A qualified motion to adjourn is a main motion.

sources.says: Because a qualified motion to adjourn is a main motion, a motion to adjourn at or to a future time is always out of order while business is pending.

q0424.answer: It is always out of order while business is pending.

sources.says: A motion to adjourn is always privileged except when it is qualified, when a time for adjourning is already set, or when adjourning would dissolve the assembly.
The privileged motion to Adjourn is not applied to other motions, is out of order when another has the floor, and is not amendable.

q0425.answer: An unqualified motion to adjourn is a privileged motion.

sources.says: The privileged motion to Adjourn takes precedence over all motions except the privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q0426.answer: Only Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn outranks it.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: The privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn takes precedence over all other motions, and is in order even after the assembly has voted to adjourn, as long as the chair hasn’t yet declared it adjourned.

q0427.answer: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is in order while Adjourn is pending.

sources.says: The privileged motion to Adjourn is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, and is neither debatable nor amendable. It requires a majority vote and can’t be reconsidered.
The privileged motion to Adjourn cannot be reconsidered. If it fails, it can be renewed after progress in business.

q0429.answer: Nobody can move to reconsider a defeated motion to adjourn.

sources.says: In societies meeting at least quarterly, the full order of business is followed at the next regular session, and a question pending at adjournment is taken up as the first item under unfinished business (or under special orders, if it was one).

q0430.answer: It is taken up first under unfinished business at the next meeting.

sources.says: A motion to close a session in an assembly that will be dissolved, or won’t meet again for a long time, is often called a motion to “adjourn sine die,” meaning “adjourn without day.”

While the privileged motion to Adjourn is pending, members may still point out business needing attention, make important announcements, make (but not take up) a motion to reconsider, move to Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes, and give notice of a motion for the next meeting.

q0432.answer: A main motion is not in order. Announcements, notice, and Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes are.

sources.says: A motion to Adjourn or to Recess can be renewed after material progress in business or in debate, such as an important decision or speech.

q0433.answer: It can be renewed after further progress, such as additional debate.

sources.says: Because Adjourn can be renewed after any progress, it is sometimes abused. The chair should refuse to entertain a motion to adjourn obviously made for obstructive purposes, such as one moved again right after being voted down with nothing having happened since.

q0434.answer: The chair should refuse to entertain it.

sources.says: When there seems to be no further business in an ordinary society’s meeting, the chair can ask “Is there any further business?” and, with no response, say “Since there is no further business, the meeting is adjourned.”

q0435.answer: The chair asks for further business and, hearing none, declares the meeting adjourned.

sources.says: “I move to adjourn” and “I move that the meeting adjourn” may be privileged or main motions. Forms such as “I move that the club now adjourn to meet at 8 P.M. on April 10” are in order only as a main motion.

q0436.answer: “I move that we now adjourn to meet at 6 p.m. on May 5” is the main-motion form.

sources.says: The privileged motion to Adjourn is out of order when another has the floor and must be seconded.
Example: a member obtains the floor and moves to adjourn, it is seconded, and the chair immediately puts the undebatable question.

q0437.answer: Obtain the floor and say, “I move to adjourn.”

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Whether privileged or main, the motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn establishes an adjourned meeting, which continues the session at which it is adopted.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn sets the time, and sometimes the place, for another meeting to continue the session’s business, without affecting when the present meeting adjourns.

q0439.answer: That is Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: A motion to fix the time to which to adjourn is privileged only when it is made while a question is pending.

q0440.answer: It is privileged only when made while a motion is pending.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The motions to Recess, Adjourn, and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn each have a corresponding incidental main motion of the same name.

q0441.answer: It may be a privileged motion or an incidental main motion.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: A motion to fix the time to which to adjourn made when no question is pending is in order, debatable, and subject to all the other rules for main motions.

q0442.answer: It follows all the rules for a main motion.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: The motion sets a time for another meeting to continue the session’s business, with no effect on when the present meeting will adjourn.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Amend can be applied to it, and it is out of order when another has the floor.

q0443.answer: The false statement is that it affects when the present meeting adjourns.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: The privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn isn’t applied to any motion, must be seconded, isn’t debatable, and can be amended.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Forms of the motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn include “I move that when this meeting adjourns, it adjourn to meet at 2:00 P.M. tomorrow.”

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Its effect is to establish an adjourned meeting, a continuation of the current session.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: The effect of the motion is to establish an adjourned meeting, another meeting that continues the session at which the motion is adopted.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Adopting it doesn’t adjourn the present meeting or set a time for its adjournment.

q0446.answer: It establishes a continuation of the present meeting.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Example: late at an annual meeting with a controversial item pending, a member obtains the floor and moves “that when this meeting adjourns, it adjourn to meet at the same time tomorrow evening.”

q0447.answer: Obtain the floor and move that when this meeting adjourns, it adjourn to meet at 9:00 a.m. tomorrow.

sources.says: When a member thinks the assembly’s rules are being violated, they can make a Point of Order, calling on the chair for a ruling and enforcement of the rules.

q0448.answer: A Point of Order calls on the chair to enforce the rules.

sources.says: A Point of Order takes precedence over any pending question out of which it arises. It yields to all privileged motions, and, if it adheres to pending questions, to a motion to lay the main question on the table.

q0449.answer: A Point of Order yields to all privileged motions.

sources.says: A Point of Order takes precedence over any pending question out of which it arises. While it is pending, no subsidiary motion can be made until it is disposed of.

q0450.answer: The point of order is disposed of first.

sources.says: The presiding officer may do brief research or consult the parliamentarian before ruling, and may let the assembly stand at ease meanwhile. Once the chair rules, any two members can appeal.

q0451.answer: The chair should try to rule on it.

sources.says: A Point of Order calls on the chair for a ruling.
The presiding officer rules on it, possibly after consulting the parliamentarian, and any two members may appeal the ruling.

q0452.answer: The chair normally rules on it.

sources.says: Every member who notices a breach of the rules has the right to insist on their enforcement. If the chair doesn’t correct it, any member can make a Point of Order.

q0453.answer: The grounds for a Point of Order are a breach of the rules.

sources.says: If the chair states the question on a motion that hasn’t been seconded, the time to raise a point of order is when the chair states the motion.
A point of order about an unseconded motion must be raised when the chair states the motion. Once debate has begun, it is too late.
Raising points of order on minor technical irregularities is undesirable in ordinary meetings when no one’s rights are harmed.

q0455.answer: Once an unseconded motion has been debated and adopted, a point of order is too late.

sources.says: If a member is unsure of their point, or wants to hear what the maker has to say before pressing it, they may, with the chair’s sufferance, “reserve a point of order.” After the maker has spoken, they must insist on the point or withdraw it.

q0456.answer: The member can reserve a point of order.

sources.says: Debate on an amendment must be confined to the amendment and must not extend to the merits of the motion being amended, except as needed.
A member who notices a breach that may do harm rises and, without waiting for recognition, says “I rise to a point of order,” or “Point of order!”

q0457.answer: Rise without obtaining the floor and say, “I rise to a point of order.”

sources.says: When the chair is in doubt how to rule on an important point, the chair can submit it to the assembly for decision, stating the point and asking the assembly to decide it.

q0458.answer: Submit it to a vote of the assembly.

sources.says: The assembly gives its presiding officer the duty to rule on questions of parliamentary law, but any two members have the right to Appeal from a ruling, one making the appeal and one seconding it, which takes the decision from the chair and puts it to the assembly.
Members have no right to criticize a ruling of the chair unless they appeal from it.

q0459.answer: An appeal expresses disagreement with the chair’s ruling.

sources.says: Any two members, one making and one seconding the appeal, can take a ruling from the chair to the assembly.
An Appeal yields to all privileged motions, and, when debatable, also yields to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate and the Previous Question.

q0460.answer: All three are characteristics of an Appeal.

sources.says: By appealing, two members transfer the chair’s ruling on a question of parliamentary law to the assembly for its decision.

q0461.answer: An Appeal puts the chair’s ruling to a vote of the assembly.

sources.says: An appeal must be made at the time of the chair’s ruling. If any debate or business has intervened, it is too late.

q0462.answer: It must be made at the time of the ruling.

sources.says: An Appeal is in order when another has the floor and must be seconded. It is debatable except in certain cases, and it isn’t amendable.

An Appeal is debatable unless it relates to indecorum or a transgression of the rules of speaking, relates to the priority of business, or is made while an undebatable question is immediately pending or involved.

q0464.answer: All three make an appeal undebatable.

sources.says: When an appeal is debatable, no member may speak more than once except the presiding officer, who may speak twice (first and at the close of debate) and need not leave the chair, but should stand.

q0465.answer: Only the presiding officer may speak twice.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: On an appeal, a tie vote sustains the chair’s decision, even if the chair’s own vote made the tie, since the chair’s decision can be reversed only by a majority.

q0466.answer: A tie sustains the decision of the chair.

sources.says: No appeal can be made from the chair’s response to a parliamentary inquiry or other query, since that is an opinion, not a ruling.
The chair’s judgment about which side is larger in a vote is also not a ruling and can’t be appealed. A member who doubts the result should call for a Division.

q0467.answer: None of those can be appealed.

sources.says: The chair’s judgment about which side won a vote, or whether there was a two-thirds majority, isn’t a ruling, so it can’t be appealed. A member who doubts an announced result should instead call for a Division or move that the vote be counted.

q0468.answer: Suggest that the member call for a Division, since there is nothing to appeal.

sources.says: A member who wants to appeal rises and, without waiting to be recognized, says “I appeal from the decision of the chair.” After a second, the chair says “The decision of the chair is appealed from.”

q0469.answer: Rise and say, “I appeal from the decision of the chair.”

sources.says: The vote on an appeal is taken so the affirmative favors sustaining the decision: “Those in favor of sustaining the chair’s decision, say aye… Those opposed to sustaining this decision, say no.”
The question isn’t on “sustaining the chair,” because it is the decision, not the presiding officer, that is in question.

q0470.answer: “Those in favor of sustaining the chair’s decision, say ‘aye.’”

sources.says: When an assembly wants to do something at a meeting that would violate its regular rules, it can adopt a motion to Suspend the Rules that interfere, as long as the action doesn’t conflict with the bylaws, applicable law, or a fundamental principle of parliamentary law.

q0471.answer: The assembly can suspend the rules.

sources.says: Suspend the Rules is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, isn’t debatable or amendable, and usually requires a two-thirds vote.

The object of Suspend the Rules is to suspend one or more rules that interfere with a proposed action at a meeting, such as rules in the parliamentary authority, special rules of order, or standing rules.

q0473.answer: It can suspend rules in all of those.

sources.says: The motion to Suspend the Rules doesn’t name the particular rules, but it must state its specific purpose, and adopting it permits nothing else to be done under the suspension.

q0474.answer: It must state its specific purpose.

sources.says: Rules protecting absentees can’t be suspended, even unanimously, such as the quorum requirement or previous notice of a bylaw amendment.
Rules protecting a basic right of the individual member can’t be suspended.
Suspend the Rules can be applied to any rule except the bylaws (or constitution or charter).

q0475.answer: All three generally can’t be suspended.

sources.says: Adopting by two-thirds a motion “to dispense with the regular order of business and proceed to” a subject is, in effect, suspending the rules to skip over the intervening items.

q0476.answer: It is done by suspending the rules.

sources.says: The rules of order in the manual adopted as parliamentary authority, or in special rules of order, are rules of parliamentary procedure, and suspending them requires a two-thirds vote.
Rules of order, whether in the parliamentary authority or adopted by the society, require a two-thirds vote to suspend.
The rule requiring previous notice of a proposed bylaw amendment protects absentees and can’t be suspended at all.
Skipping the established order of business requires a two-thirds vote.

q0478.answer: Dunbar’s key says “none of the above.”
q0478.conflict: Under RONR 12th ed., none of the three can be suspended by a majority vote: rules of order and the order of business need two-thirds, and the bylaw notice rule can’t be suspended at all. “None of the above” only makes sense if the question is read as “which can be suspended by a majority.” Treat this key as suspect.

sources.says: Ordinary standing rules, which don’t deal with parliamentary procedure, can be suspended by a majority vote.

q0479.answer: A majority vote, with no notice required.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: An Objection to the Consideration of a Question lets the assembly avoid a particular original main motion altogether when it would be strongly undesirable for it even to come before the assembly.

q0480.answer: Raise an Objection to the Consideration of the Question.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: The objection can be raised only before any debate, or before any subsidiary motion other than Lay on the Table has been stated. After that, consideration has begun and it is too late.

q0481.answer: Before any debate or any subsidiary motion has been stated.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: An Objection to the Consideration can be applied to original main motions and to petitions and communications not from a superior body. It can’t be applied to incidental main motions.

q0482.answer: It applies to original main motions.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: The objection doesn’t require a second and isn’t debatable or amendable. A two-thirds vote against consideration is required to sustain it.

q0483.answer: Sustaining the objection takes a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: The presiding officer can, on their own initiative, submit an objection to consideration to a vote, just as they can raise a question of order.

q0484.answer: The chair can make an Objection to the Consideration.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: If the objection is sustained, the main motion is dismissed for that session and can’t be renewed then except by unanimous consent or by reconsidering the vote on the objection. It can be introduced at a later session.

q0485.answer: The main motion is dismissed for that session.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: A member rises, even if another has been assigned the floor, and without waiting to be recognized says “Mr. President, I object to the consideration of the question.”

q0486.answer: “Mr. President, I object to the consideration of the motion” is the right wording.
q0486.conflict: RONR 12th ed. says the objection is made without waiting for recognition, so obtaining the floor isn’t required. Dunbar’s key still picks this option because the other three use the wrong motion.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: When a member objects, the chair responds “The consideration of the question is objected to. Shall the question be considered?” and takes a rising vote for and against considering it.

q0487.answer: “The consideration of the question is objected to. Shall the question be considered?”

sources.says: When a motion on a single subject has several parts that could each stand as a complete proposition, Division of a Question lets those parts be considered and voted on as separate questions.

q0488.answer: It separates distinct parts of a motion to be debated and voted on separately.

sources.says: Parts of a motion that could each stand alone can be separated and voted on as distinct questions by adopting a motion for Division of a Question.
Division of the Assembly is different: it retakes a doubtful vote by rising.

q0489.answer: Use Division of the Question. Division of the Assembly only retakes a vote.

sources.says: Division of a Question takes precedence over the main motion and Postpone Indefinitely, but a motion to divide the main question can’t be made while an amendment to the main question is pending.

q0490.answer: It can’t be made on the main question while an amendment is pending.

sources.says: A question can be divided only when it contains several parts, each capable of standing as a complete proposition if the others are removed.

q0491.answer: Buying a computer and buying a printer are two parts that each stand alone, so that motion is the one to divide.

sources.says: When a question is indivisible and a member opposes part of it, they can seek the result they want by moving to strike out that part.

q0492.answer: Move to strike out the objectionable part.

sources.says: When independent resolutions on different subjects are offered in one motion, any single member can demand that one or more of them get separate consideration and vote, without a motion to divide.

q0493.answer: A single member can demand separate consideration of each.

sources.says: Example: a member obtains the floor and says “I move to divide the resolution so as to consider separately the question of purchasing the books,” and it is seconded.

q0494.answer: Obtain the floor and move to divide the motion so the two parts are considered separately.

sources.says: A long motion or report with several paragraphs or sections that aren’t fully separate questions can have its parts opened to debate and amendment one at a time, without dividing it, by a motion to Consider by Paragraph (or Seriatim).

q0495.answer: It is called Consideration by Paragraph or Seriatim.

sources.says: Consideration by Paragraph is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, isn’t debatable, is amendable, requires a majority vote, and can’t be reconsidered.
When a document is considered seriatim, each member can speak twice on each paragraph, section, or unit taken up separately.
If the chair suggests considering a document by paragraph and a member thinks time would be saved by acting on it as a whole, the member can move “that it be considered as a whole.”

q0498.answer: Obtain the floor and move that it be considered as a whole.

sources.says: When the chair doesn’t start seriatim consideration on their own, a member obtains the floor and says “I move that the resolution be considered by paragraph [or seriatim].”

q0499.answer: Obtain the floor and move that the resolution be considered seriatim.

sources.says: A member who doubts the result of a voice vote or show of hands can call for a Division of the Assembly, requiring the vote to be retaken by rising.

q0500.answer: The vote is retaken by rising.

sources.says: Any member, without a second, has the right to require that a voice vote or show of hands be retaken as a rising vote (a Division of the Assembly), unless the demand is plainly dilatory.

q0501.answer: A Division of the Assembly must be taken on the demand of one member.

sources.says: A Division of the Assembly may be called for from the moment the negative votes have been cast until the announcement of the result is complete, or immediately thereafter.

q0502.answer: Until the announcement is complete, or immediately after.

sources.says: A Division of the Assembly is in order when another has the floor, doesn’t require a second, isn’t debatable or amendable, and doesn’t require a vote.
When there has clearly been a full vote and no reasonable doubt about which side is in the majority, a call for a Division is dilatory, and the chair should not allow the member’s right to be abused.

q0504.answer: The chair declares the call for a Division dilatory.

sources.says: While or right after the chair announces a result, a member can call from their seat, without the floor, “Division!”, “I call for a division,” or “I doubt the result of the vote.”

sources.section: §30 Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
sources.says: Motions relating to methods of voting obtain a vote in a form other than voice, show of hands, or rising, such as by ballot, by roll call, by counted standing vote, or by some unusual method.

q0506.answer: Ballot, roll call, and standing votes are all legitimate methods.

sources.section: §30 Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
sources.says: Motions relating to methods of voting can be applied to any motion on which the assembly votes, other than another motion on voting method or on closing or reopening the polls.

q0507.answer: They can be applied to any motion the assembly votes on.

sources.section: §30 Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
sources.says: When different methods of voting are suggested, they’re usually treated as filling blanks, with the vote taken first on the method that takes the most time.

q0508.answer: The method that takes the most time is voted on first.

sources.says: While an election is pending, members may offer motions to set the method of making nominations (if the bylaws don’t), and motions to close or reopen nominations.

q0509.answer: All three are motions relating to nominations.

sources.says: Incidental motions relating to nominations yield to privileged motions, can have Amend applied, are out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, and are not debatable.
A motion to close nominations is generally unnecessary. When nominations have been made, the chair asks for any further nominations and, with no response, declares nominations closed.

q0511.answer: The chair usually declares nominations closed.

sources.section: §32 Request to Be Excused from a Duty
sources.says: A member can’t decline a duty imposed by the bylaws as a matter of right, but, except as the bylaws provide otherwise, the assembly can grant a request to be excused, by unanimous consent or by a motion.

q0512.answer: The assembly can grant the request by unanimous consent or a motion, unless the bylaws prevent it.

sources.section: §32 Request to Be Excused from a Duty
sources.says: A motion on a request to be excused yields to all subsidiary motions except Postpone Indefinitely.

q0513.answer: Postpone Indefinitely can’t be applied to it.

sources.section: §32 Request to Be Excused from a Duty
sources.says: A motion on a request to be excused yields to all subsidiary motions except Postpone Indefinitely, to all privileged motions, and to other incidental motions.

q0514.answer: It yields to all of those.

sources.section: §32 Request to Be Excused from a Duty
sources.says: A motion to grant another member’s request to be excused doesn’t need a second, since two members already want it considered. The motion is debatable, amendable, and needs a majority vote.

q0515.answer: It sometimes needs no second, when the motion grants another member’s request.

sources.section: §32 Request to Be Excused from a Duty
sources.says: A member can’t, as a matter of right, refuse a duty such as a committee assignment or demand to be excused from it, but the assembly can grant the member’s request to be excused. The request can be granted by unanimous consent, or someone can move to grant it, and that motion is debatable and amendable.

sources.section: §32 Request to Be Excused from a Duty
sources.says: Its standard characteristics include that it requires a majority vote, but it is often settled by unanimous consent.

q0516.answer: It is often settled by unanimous consent. No three-fourths vote is involved, and the president’s permission isn’t required.

sources.section: §32 Request to Be Excused from a Duty
sources.says: A member who can’t perform an office or duty should submit a resignation, in writing to the secretary or appointing power, or at a meeting orally or in writing. The chair can then assume a motion “that the resignation be accepted.”

q0517.answer: Submit a written resignation, and the chair puts the question of accepting it.

sources.says: Members may make these requests and inquiries: Parliamentary Inquiry, Request for Information, Request for Permission to Withdraw or Modify a Motion, Request to Read Papers, and Request for Any Other Privilege.

q0518.answer: All three are requests and inquiries.

sources.says: Requests and inquiries generally need no second. No vote is taken on a Parliamentary Inquiry or a Request for Information, and neither can be reconsidered.

q0519.answer: They are not seconded, voted on, or reconsidered.

sources.says: A Parliamentary Inquiry is a question to the presiding officer for information on parliamentary law or the organization’s rules as they bear on the business at hand.

The chair should answer a parliamentary inquiry when it helps a member make a proper motion, raise a point of order, or understand the situation or a motion’s effect. The chair isn’t obliged to answer hypothetical questions.

q0521.answer: The chair need not answer hypothetical questions.

sources.says: To make an inquiry, a member rises and, without obtaining the floor, says “Madam President, I rise to a parliamentary inquiry.” The chair asks them to state it, and the member asks, for example, whether a motion is in order.

q0522.answer: Rise without obtaining the floor and say, “I rise to a parliamentary inquiry.”

sources.says: The chair’s reply to a parliamentary inquiry can’t be appealed, since it is an opinion, not a ruling. A member may act contrary to it and appeal any resulting ruling.

q0523.answer: The reply is an opinion, not a ruling.

sources.says: A Request for Information, also called a Point of Information, is directed to the chair, or through the chair to another officer or member, and asks for information relevant to the business at hand that isn’t about parliamentary procedure.

q0524.answer: It is directed through the presiding officer.

sources.says: A Request for Information (Point of Information) is directed to the chair, or through the chair to another officer or member, for information relevant to the business at hand but not about parliamentary procedure.

q0525.answer: It seeks information relevant to the business at hand, not about procedure.

sources.says: A member rises and says “Mr. President, I have a request for information” or “A point of information, please,” and the chair has them state the question.
The request may be directed through the chair to another member.

q0526.answer: Rise without obtaining the floor and say, “Mr. Chairman, point of information, please.”

sources.says: If a speaker yields to another member for a question, the time the question takes is charged to the speaker.
Because the time is taken out of the speaker’s allowed time, the chair asks whether the speaker is willing to be interrupted.

q0527.answer: The time for the question comes out of the speaker’s allowed time.

sources.says: Before the chair states a motion, it belongs to its maker, who can withdraw or modify it without anyone’s consent.

q0528.answer: Before it is stated by the chair, the maker can withdraw a motion without anyone’s consent.

sources.says: In the interval between making a motion and the chair stating it, the maker can withdraw it by saying “Madam President, I withdraw the motion.”

q0529.answer: Rise without obtaining the floor and say, “I withdraw the motion.”

sources.says: Once the chair has stated a motion, it belongs to the meeting, and the maker must ask the assembly’s permission to withdraw or modify it.
After the chair has stated a motion, it belongs to the meeting as a whole, and the maker must request the assembly’s permission to withdraw or modify it.

q0531.answer: The maker must ask the assembly’s permission to withdraw it.

sources.says: A request for permission to withdraw a motion can be made any time before voting on it has begun, even if the motion has been amended and even if subsidiary or incidental motions are pending.
Requests take precedence over any motion with whose purpose they are connected.
