A request to withdraw a motion can be made even while subsidiary or incidental motions are pending, and if the main motion is withdrawn, those adhering motions go with it.

q0533.answer: The request to withdraw the main motion is immediately pending.

sources.says: After a motion has been withdrawn, it is as though it had never been made, so the same motion can be made again at the same meeting.

q0534.answer: It can be made again at the same meeting.

sources.says: A pending motion can be amended only by vote or unanimous consent of the assembly, even if the maker says they “accept” the amendment.
Whether or not the maker “accepts” a so-called friendly amendment, it must be opened to debate and voted on formally, unless adopted by unanimous consent.

q0535.answer: The maker’s acceptance doesn’t adopt it. It must go through the assembly as a formal amendment.

sources.says: If a member objects to another reading a paper in debate, the chair can put the question on granting permission, or any member can move “that permission to read a paper in debate be granted.”

q0536.answer: The chair puts the question on granting permission.

sources.says: The object of Take from the Table is to make pending again a motion, or series of adhering motions, that was previously laid on the table.

q0537.answer: It makes pending again a motion that was laid on the table.

sources.says: Take from the Table, one of the motions that bring a question again before the assembly, makes pending again a motion that was laid on the table.

q0538.answer: Take from the Table brings a question again before the assembly.

sources.says: Take from the Table takes precedence over no pending motion, so it can’t be moved while any other question is pending.

q0539.answer: It can be moved only when no motion is pending.

sources.says: Take from the Table must be moved while business of the same class, or unfinished business, general orders, or new business, is in order.
A tabled question can be taken from the table during the same session, or until the end of the next regular session if within a quarterly interval.

Take from the Table can’t be moved until some business has been transacted since the question was laid on the table, and if voted down, it can’t be renewed until more business has been transacted. It is out of order when another has the floor.

q0541.answer: It is in order once some other business has been transacted.

sources.says: Take from the Table must be seconded, isn’t debatable or amendable, requires a majority vote, and can’t be reconsidered.
Take from the Table requires a majority vote.
If the motion to Take from the Table is adopted, the question can be laid on the table again should a legitimate need arise.

q0544.answer: It can be laid on the table again.

sources.says: A tabled question can be taken from the table during the same session, or until the end of the next regular session only if that session comes within a quarterly time interval. Otherwise it dies, though it can be reintroduced later as a new question.

q0545.answer: In a group meeting once a year, the tabled motion dies at the end of the session. None of those motions can revive it; it must be introduced again as a new motion.

sources.says: A tabled question can be taken from the table by majority vote as soon as the interrupting business is disposed of, or later within the time limits.
Even after a new motion is made but before the chair states it, a member who quickly rises to move to take a question from the table is entitled to the floor.
It can also be taken from the table at the next regular session if that is within a quarterly time interval.
If a question isn’t taken from the table within the time limits, it dies, although it can be reintroduced later as a new question.
If a tabled question is taken up on a different day, all members have their right to debate renewed under the regular limits, which is two speeches per member.

q0548.answer: Each member may debate twice again.

sources.says: Take from the Table is out of order when another has the floor and must be seconded, so a member obtains the floor to make it.
Its object is to make pending again a motion that was laid on the table.

q0549.answer: Obtain the floor and move to take from the table the motion about the car wash.

sources.says: Rescind and Amend Something Previously Adopted are two forms of one incidental main motion.

q0550.answer: Amend Something Previously Adopted is an incidental main motion.

sources.says: Rescind, also known as Repeal or Annul, is the motion by which a previous action or order can be canceled or countermanded.

q0551.answer: Annul, Repeal, and Rescind are all names for it.

sources.says: Amend Something Previously Adopted is the motion used to change only part of the text, or to substitute a different version.

q0552.answer: That motion is Amend Something Previously Adopted.

sources.says: Rescind and Amend Something Previously Adopted are out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, and are debatable, with debate going into the merits of the question to be rescinded or amended.

q0553.answer: Both are debatable, and debate can go into the merits of what they would change.

sources.says: Rescind takes precedence over nothing, so it can be moved only when no other motion is pending. It can be applied to anything adopted by main motion that still has force, and it is amendable.

Rescind is not in order when something done as a result of the vote can’t be undone (such as a contract the other party has been informed of), or when a resignation has been acted on and the person notified.
Rescind can be applied to anything adopted by a main motion that still has continuing force and effect.

q0555.answer: It can be applied to an adopted main motion, but not to a communicated contract or an accepted resignation.

sources.says: Rescind requires either a two-thirds vote, a majority vote with previous notice, or a majority of the entire membership. Any one of these suffices.

q0556.answer: Any of those votes is enough.

sources.says: Unlike Reconsider, there is no time limit on moving to Rescind, and any member may make it, regardless of how they voted on the original motion.

q0557.answer: Unlike Reconsider, Rescind can be made by any member.

sources.says: Without prior notice, a member obtains the floor and says “I move to rescind the motion relating to… adopted at the May meeting.” It then needs two-thirds or a majority of the entire membership.

q0558.answer: Obtain the floor and move to rescind the motion adopted at last month’s meeting.

sources.says: Rescind and Expunge from the Minutes, used rarely to express the strongest disapproval, requires a majority of the entire membership. Even a unanimous vote at a meeting isn’t enough if it isn’t a majority of the entire membership.

q0559.answer: It needs a majority of the entire membership.

sources.says: If the motion is adopted, the secretary, before the assembly, draws a single line through or around the words in the minutes and writes “Rescinded and Ordered Expunged” with the date and signature. The words aren’t blotted out, but they are omitted from any published record.
Discharge a Committee lets the assembly take a referred matter out of a committee’s hands before the committee makes its final report, so the assembly can consider it itself.

q0561.answer: It takes a matter out of a committee’s hands before its final report.

sources.says: Discharge a Committee is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, and is debatable, with debate going into the merits of the question in the committee’s hands. It can be applied to any referred main motion.
Because it changes action already taken, Discharge a Committee requires a two-thirds vote, a majority vote with previous notice, or a majority of the entire membership.

q0563.answer: A unanimous vote is never required.

sources.says: Discharging a committee is generally advisable only when it has failed to report promptly, or when the assembly urgently wants to proceed without the committee’s help, or wants to drop the matter.

When a committee is discharged from considering a matter, whether by a motion to discharge it or by its final report, a standing committee continues to exist, but a special committee that was appointed for that matter goes out of existence. Either way, the committee chairman returns the papers on the matter to the secretary.

q0565.answer: A standing committee continues its existence.

sources.says: For a standing committee, a member obtains the floor and moves, for example, “that the Finance Committee be discharged from further consideration of the resolution relating to…”

q0566.answer: Obtain the floor and move that the Membership Committee be discharged from further consideration of recruiting.

sources.says: Reconsider enables a majority, within a limited time and without notice, to bring back for further consideration a motion that has already been voted on, to correct hasty or mistaken action or account for new information.

q0567.answer: That is the motion to Reconsider.

sources.says: The motion to Reconsider can be made only by a member who voted with the prevailing side: aye if the motion was adopted, no if it was lost. Committees are an exception.

q0568.answer: Only a member who voted with the prevailing side can make it.

sources.says: The motion to Reconsider needs only a majority vote, whatever vote the motion being reconsidered originally required.

Only a member who voted with the prevailing side may move to reconsider: someone who voted aye if the motion was adopted, or no if it was lost. There are time limits. In a one-day session, such as an ordinary club meeting, it can be moved only on the same day as the vote; in a session lasting more than one day, only on that day or the next day of the session on which a business meeting is held.

q0569.answer: Requiring two-thirds or notice is not a characteristic, because Reconsider never requires either. The other choices all describe the motion.

sources.says: In a session of one day, such as an ordinary club meeting, the motion to Reconsider can be made only on the same day the vote was taken.

q0570.answer: It must be made on the same day as the vote.

sources.says: Making the motion to Reconsider takes precedence over any other motion and yields to nothing, so it is in order when any question is pending. It must be made by someone on the prevailing side, but any member may second it, and it is debatable when the motion reconsidered is.

q0571.answer: The false statement is that the seconder must have voted on the prevailing side.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: After a member has been assigned the floor but before they begin speaking, another member may rise, if there may be no other opportunity, to make a motion to Reconsider.

q0572.answer: It can be made after another member is assigned the floor but before they start speaking.

sources.says: When taken up, the motion to Reconsider is debatable if the motion proposed to be reconsidered is debatable, and debate can go into the merits of that question.

q0573.answer: It is debatable when the motion to be reconsidered is debatable.

sources.says: The motion to Reconsider requires only a majority vote, regardless of the vote needed to adopt the motion being reconsidered.

The right to debate the motion to Reconsider is separate from the original consideration. Even a member who used up their debate on the original motion may speak the regular number of times, twice, on the motion to Reconsider.

q0575.answer: A member may debate it two more times.

sources.says: Although any member can call up a motion to Reconsider, usually no one but the mover calls it up on the day it is made, so the mover can pick the time.

q0576.answer: Usually the member who made the motion to Reconsider.

sources.says: To reconsider the vote on an amendment after the main question it adhered to has been finally disposed of, the vote on the main question must also be reconsidered.

q0577.answer: The vote on the main question must also be reconsidered.

sources.says: In committees, Reconsider can be moved regardless of time elapsed and any number of times, by any member who didn’t vote on the losing side (including one who didn’t vote or was absent). It needs a two-thirds vote unless everyone who voted on the prevailing side is present or was notified.

q0578.answer: The false statement is that it always needs only a majority. In committees it can require two-thirds.

sources.says: The motion is made in a form like “I move to reconsider the vote on the resolution relating to the annual banquet. I voted for [or against] the resolution.”

q0579.answer: You must also state how you voted.

sources.says: Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes, moved on the same day as the vote, can’t be called up until another day. That protects against a temporary majority acting at an unrepresentative meeting.

q0580.answer: It can’t be called up on the day it is made.

sources.says: Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes can be moved only on the same day as the vote, takes precedence over the regular motion to Reconsider, and can’t be applied to votes on motions whose purpose would be defeated by a day’s delay.

No motion can be renewed during the same session in which it was already before the assembly, except where a specific rule allows it, and such a rule always implies the motion has in some way become a different question.

q0582.answer: Only if the question has in some respect become different.

sources.says: A motion to Postpone Indefinitely can’t be renewed as to the same main question during the same session, even if the main motion has been materially amended since the earlier vote.

q0583.answer: It can’t be renewed as to the same main motion during the session.

sources.says: When the chair rules adversely on a Point of Order or Question of Privilege, it can’t be raised again at the same session unless an appeal is made and the chair’s decision is reversed.

q0584.answer: Only if an appeal reverses the chair’s decision.

sources.says: A motion to Adjourn or to Recess can be renewed after material progress in business or debate, such as an important decision or speech.

q0585.answer: Adjourn can be renewed after material progress.

sources.says: A motion is dilatory if it seeks to obstruct or thwart the will of the assembly as clearly shown by the parliamentary situation.

Dilatory tactics include constantly raising points of order and appealing, demanding a division when the result is clear, laying on the table the matter a special meeting was called for, and repeatedly moving to adjourn.
Amending a primary amendment with a secondary amendment is a normal, permitted degree of amendment.

q0587.answer: Moving to amend a primary amendment is legitimate, not dilatory.

sources.says: The chair must prevent members from misusing motions merely to obstruct business. When convinced a member is doing so, the chair can simply not recognize them, or rule the motion out of order.
A call for a Division when the result is clear is dilatory.

q0588.answer: The chair can decline to recognize them or rule the call out of order.

sources.says: Motions that conflict with a society’s charter, constitution, or bylaws, or with procedural rules set by national, state, or local law, are not in order, and if adopted they are null and void.

q0589.answer: An improper motion conflicts with any of those.

sources.says: No motion outside the society’s object as defined in its charter, constitution, or bylaws can be introduced unless the assembly agrees by a two-thirds vote to consider it.

q0590.answer: Only if the assembly agrees by a two-thirds vote.

sources.says: A quorum is the number of members who must be present for business to be validly transacted. It counts members present, not the number voting on a question.

q0591.answer: The quorum is the number of members who must be present.

sources.says: In a mass meeting, the quorum is simply the number of people present, since they make up the entire membership at that time.

q0592.answer: It is the number of persons present at the time.

sources.says: In a body of delegates such as a convention, the quorum is a majority of those registered as attending, even if some have left. This may differ greatly from the number elected.

q0593.answer: A majority of the delegates registered as attending.

sources.says: In an assembly with an enrolled membership whose bylaws don’t set a quorum, the quorum is a majority of all the members.

q0594.answer: A majority of all the members.

sources.says: Voluntary societies with an enrolled membership generally need a bylaws provision setting a relatively small quorum, considerably less than a majority, since a majority rarely attends.

q0595.answer: A relatively small quorum, well under a majority.

sources.says: If a bylaws quorum provision is struck out first, the quorum instantly becomes a majority of the membership. The proper method is to strike out and insert the new provision in one vote.

q0596.answer: It would become a majority of the membership.

sources.says: In boards and in committees (other than a committee of the whole), the quorum is a majority of the members unless a different quorum is provided for.
Business transacted in the absence of a quorum, other than certain procedural actions, is null and void.

Even without a quorum, the assembly may fix the time to which to adjourn, adjourn, recess, or take measures to obtain a quorum. Other motions may also be considered if they relate to those actions or to running the meeting while it lacks a quorum.

q0599.answer: All three choices are permitted, so the answer is All of the above.

sources.says: Without a quorum, the assembly may still fix the time to which to adjourn, adjourn, recess, or take measures to obtain a quorum.

The rule against doing business without a quorum can’t be waived, even by unanimous consent. If important business can’t wait until the next regular meeting, the assembly should set the time for an adjourned meeting and then adjourn.

q0600.answer: Setting a time for an adjourned meeting. Approving the minutes, or going into a committee of the whole or a quasi committee of the whole, would be transacting business.

sources.says: Motions to obtain a quorum, as main or privileged motions, must be seconded, are debatable except when privileged, are amendable, require a majority vote, and can be reconsidered.

q0601.answer: They are adopted by a majority vote.

sources.says: Before calling a meeting to order, the presiding officer has the duty to determine, though not necessarily announce, that a quorum is present.
Even without a quorum, the assembly may fix the time to which to adjourn, adjourn, recess, or take steps to obtain a quorum. Other business is not in order.

q0603.answer: A motion to adjourn can be voted on without a quorum.

sources.says: A member who notices that a quorum is no longer present can make a point of order to that effect at any time, as long as they don’t interrupt someone speaking.

q0604.answer: Make a point of order that a quorum isn’t present.

sources.says: In legislative bodies or assemblies with legal power to compel attendance, a Call of the House is a motion that unexcused absent members be brought to the meeting under arrest, to obtain a quorum. It doesn’t apply in voluntary societies.

q0605.answer: It compels the attendance of members.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Order of business, orders of the day, agenda, and program are closely related terms for the order in which business is taken up in a session and the scheduling of particular business.

q0606.answer: All three deal with the order of business.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: An order of business is any established sequence in which business is to be taken up at a session of an assembly.

q0607.answer: That is an order of business.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: The standard order of business consists of reading and approval of minutes; reports of officers, boards, and standing committees; reports of special committees; special orders; unfinished business and general orders; and new business.

q0608.answer: Roll call is not one of the standard headings. It is optional and placed with opening ceremonies.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: In the standard order of business, unfinished business and general orders come just before new business.

q0609.answer: Unfinished business comes before new business.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Where copies of the minutes are sent to all members in advance, the chair announces this, and reading them aloud is omitted unless a member asks for them to be read.

q0610.answer: When they were sent to all members in advance and no one asks to hear them.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: A formal motion to approve the minutes isn’t necessary. The chair asks for corrections, which are usually handled by unanimous consent.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When there are no further corrections, the chair declares the minutes approved.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: The secretary’s draft, whether or not circulated in advance, doesn’t become the minutes, the official record, unless it is approved.

q0612.answer: They become official only when approved.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: In most societies it is customary to hear reports from all officers, boards, and standing committees only at annual meetings. At other meetings the chair calls only on those who have reports.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: A motion arising out of an officer’s, board’s, or committee’s report is taken up immediately, since the order of business gives priority to classes of business in their listed order.

q0614.answer: It is taken up immediately after the report.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Special committees that are to report are called on in the order in which they were appointed.

q0615.answer: In the order they were appointed.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When the designated hour for a special order arrives, it automatically interrupts pending business (with a few exceptions), and the chair simply announces it.

q0616.answer: The chair announces the special order and takes it up.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Unfinished business includes, first, the question that was pending when the previous meeting adjourned, if it wasn’t a special order.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Unfinished business means questions carried over from the previous meeting, other than special orders, because that meeting adjourned without completing its order of business and without setting an adjourned meeting.

q0618.answer: That is unfinished business and general orders.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: The chair should not announce the heading of Unfinished Business and General Orders unless the minutes show there is business to come up under it, and shouldn’t ask “Is there any unfinished business?” but state the first item due.

q0619.answer: Only if the minutes show there is some.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: An informal understanding during a meeting that a subject should be “brought up at the next meeting” doesn’t make it unfinished business. It has to be introduced at the next meeting as new business.

q0620.answer: It must be introduced as new business.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: After unfinished business and general orders have been disposed of, the chair asks “Is there any new business?”

q0621.answer: After unfinished business and general orders.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Under new business, members can introduce new items or move to take from the table any matter lying on it.
A main motion rejected at an earlier session can be renewed, introduced again as if new, at any later session.

q0622.answer: Members can do any of those.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Opening ceremonies right after the call to order may include an invocation (always first), the national anthem, the Pledge of Allegiance, a ritual recalling the organization’s ideals, or the like.

q0623.answer: The Pledge of Allegiance is an opening ceremony.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Besides the standard order of business, regular meetings sometimes include optional headings such as opening ceremonies, roll call, a consent calendar, good of the order, announcements, and a program.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Legislatures and city, town, or county councils with many routine or noncontroversial matters may find a consent calendar useful for disposing of them.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: A program of a cultural, educational, or civic nature is usually presented before the meeting is adjourned, since it may prompt the assembly to act, though it can be moved by special rule or by suspending the rules.

q0626.answer: Just before the meeting is adjourned.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: If, as a courtesy to a guest speaker, the chair wants the talk at an unscheduled point in the meeting, the chair can usually get unanimous consent to suspend the rules simply by announcing it.

q0627.answer: Ask the assembly for unanimous consent to hear the guest early.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Any item of business can be taken up out of its proper order by adopting a motion to Suspend the Rules by a two-thirds vote, though this is usually done by unanimous consent.

q0628.answer: Adopt a motion to suspend the rules.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Taking an item up out of its proper order requires suspending the rules by a two-thirds vote, or unanimous consent.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: An order of the day is a particular item of business set in advance to be taken up during a given session, day, or meeting, or at a given hour, if nothing with precedence interferes.

q0630.answer: It is set in advance to be taken up at a given session.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Orders of the day are divided into general orders and special orders.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When the hour for a special order arrives, it automatically interrupts pending business, except motions about adjournment or recess, questions of privilege, earlier special orders, or the special order for the meeting.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: A general order cannot interrupt pending business, even when its time has arrived.

q0632.answer: Special orders can interrupt pending business at their set time.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: A postponed question becomes an order of the day for the session, day, meeting, or hour to which it is postponed.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: A pending question is made an order of the day for a future time by means of the motion to Postpone.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: In the standard order of business, orders of the day not set for particular hours are taken up under the headings Special Orders and Unfinished Business and General Orders.

q0634.answer: They come up under those headings, so any of the above.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: A general order set for a particular hour can’t be considered before that hour unless the rules are suspended by a two-thirds vote, or the vote that made it can still be reconsidered.

q0635.answer: Only if the rules are suspended by a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: If several general orders were made for the same time, they are taken up in the order in which they were made (or, if made in one motion, the order listed).

q0636.answer: In the order in which they were made.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When the hour set for a special order arrives, it automatically interrupts pending business, with only a few exceptions.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When special orders conflict, the one made first takes precedence over those made afterward.

q0637.answer: Dunbar’s key picks the special order set for a particular time, since it interrupts other business when its hour arrives.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When its hour arrives, a special order automatically interrupts pending business except a motion relating to adjournment or recess, a question of privilege, an earlier-made special order, or the special order for the meeting.

q0638.answer: It doesn’t interrupt any of those.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Among conflicting special orders, the one made first takes precedence over all made afterward, even if the later ones were set for earlier hours.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Example: if a 2 P.M. special order made later is still pending at 3 P.M., the earlier-made 3 P.M. special order is taken up immediately, interrupting it.

q0639.answer: The 2 p.m. order, made first, interrupts the pending 1 p.m. order.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When the hour for a scheduled recess or adjournment arrives, the chair announces it and declares the assembly in recess or adjourned, even if a special order is pending.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: For an order of business specially adopted for a given session, “program” is often used instead of “agenda.” An agenda strictly covers items of business, while a program can also include times for speakers, meals, and other nonbusiness matters.

q0641.conflict: RONR 12th ed. uses both “agenda” and “program” for an order of business adopted for a session (41:58–64), so “agenda” is also defensible. The book prefers “program” when the schedule includes nonbusiness items.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: Before making a motion or speaking in debate, a member must claim the floor by rising and addressing the chair, and must be recognized by the chair.

q0642.answer: They must then be recognized by the chair.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: The chair normally recognizes a member by announcing their name or title, or the place or unit they represent.
In a small meeting where only one person seeks the floor and all can see one another, the chair can recognize the member by nodding.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: A member assigned the floor may use it for any proper purpose or combination, for example debating a pending motion and concluding by moving any secondary motion in order at the time.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: If two or more rise at about the same time, the member who rose and addressed the chair first after the floor was yielded is entitled to recognition. Rising before the floor is yielded gives no claim.

q0645.answer: The one who rose and addressed the chair first after the floor was yielded.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: The maker of the pending motion who hasn’t spoken is entitled to preference, and, for a motion implementing a committee recommendation, the reporting member has that preference.
A member seeking to move to take a question from the table is entitled to the floor in preference to a new main motion.

q0646.answer: All three have preference in recognition.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: When the chair knows those seeking the floor have opposite opinions, and preference isn’t otherwise settled, the chair lets the floor alternate as far as possible between those favoring and opposing the measure. No one gets a second turn while someone who hasn’t spoken wants the floor.

q0647.answer: The chair should alternate between those for and against.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: When a question has been laid on the table to take up a more urgent matter, the member who moved to lay it on the table is entitled to preference in recognition to introduce the urgent business.

q0648.answer: The member who moved to lay it on the table, in order to introduce the urgent business, has preference.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: If the chair is in doubt about who is entitled to the floor, the chair can let the assembly decide by a vote, and the member receiving the largest vote gets the floor.

q0649.answer: The assembly can decide by a vote.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: If the chair mistakenly assigns the floor to the wrong person, a Point of Order can be raised, and (except in a mass meeting) the chair’s decision can be appealed by two members.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: A member who has begun speaking can be interrupted only for urgent purposes such as a Call for the Orders of the Day, raising a question of privilege, or a Point of Order.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: When an interruption occurs, the member with the floor doesn’t lose it, but sits while the interrupting matter is handled, and the chair then directs them to proceed.

q0652.answer: The member sits while the interruption is dealt with.

sources.says: Every member has the right to speak on every debatable motion before it is finally acted on, and, apart from general limits set by parliamentary law or rules, this right can’t be interfered with except by a two-thirds vote.
A matter can’t be debated until it is before the assembly as a motion: made by a member with the floor, seconded (unless from a board or committee), and stated by the chair.

q0654.answer: It must be made, seconded, and stated by the chair.

sources.says: A member may speak in debate and conclude by offering a secondary motion, such as an amendment, since a member recognized for any legitimate purpose has the floor for all legitimate purposes.

q0655.answer: Ask for a second and process the amendment.

sources.says: When debate seems to be over, the chair may ask “Are you ready for the question?” or “Is there any further debate?” If no one rises after a reasonable pause, the chair may put the question.

q0656.answer: The chair is checking whether debate has concluded.

sources.says: In a nonlegislative body with no special rule on speech length, a member can speak no longer than ten minutes without the assembly’s consent.
Permission to speak longer than ten minutes can be given by unanimous consent or by a motion to Extend Limits of Debate, which needs two-thirds without debate.

q0658.answer: Move to Extend Limits of Debate.

sources.says: Rights in debate aren’t transferable. A member can’t yield unused time to another member or save it for later. Time used by a question the speaker yields to is charged to the speaker.
A committee chairman presenting or reading the committee’s report is not considered to be debating.

q0659.answer: The false statement is that unused time can be transferred to another member.

sources.says: Unless there is a special rule, a member can’t yield any unexpired part of their time to another member. Yielding the floor early waives the rest.

q0660.answer: Tell the member unexpired time can’t be transferred.

sources.says: Unless a special rule says otherwise, no member can speak more than twice on the same question on the same day, except that on an Appeal only the presiding officer may speak twice.
On an Appeal, only the presiding officer can speak twice (the second time at the close of debate). All other members are limited to one speech.
If two-thirds of those voting wish to close debate immediately, they can do so by adopting the motion for the Previous Question.

q0663.answer: By two-thirds voting for the Previous Question.

sources.says: To prevent any discussion of a subject, even by the motion’s maker, the only way is to raise an Objection to the Consideration of the Question before debate begins.

q0664.answer: Raise an Objection to the Consideration of the Question.

sources.says: To keep the length of speeches but remove limits on how many times members can speak, the assembly can go into a committee of the whole (or its alternate forms), and those speeches don’t count against members’ debate in the assembly.

q0665.answer: There’s no limit on how many times members may speak.

sources.says: A member’s remarks in debate must be germane to the question, meaning they must bear on whether the immediately pending motion should be adopted.
Members can’t address one another directly, but must address all remarks through the chair.

q0667.answer: Address all remarks through the chair.

sources.says: A speaker may choose whether to allow another member’s question, but if they do, the time it takes comes out of the speaker’s time.

q0668.answer: It is taken out of the member’s debating time.

sources.says: Members’ names should be avoided in debate. It is better to say “the member who spoke last” or “the delegate from Mason County,” and officers should be referred to by title.

q0669.answer: Calling a member by first name, “John,” should be avoided.

sources.says: The maker of a motion may vote against it but may not speak against it. They need not speak, but if they do, they must take a favorable position.

q0670.answer: The maker can’t speak in opposition to it.

sources.says: When the presiding officer rises to rule, give information, or otherwise speak within their privilege, any member speaking should be seated until the chair finishes.
During debate, the chair’s remarks, and voting, no member should disturb the assembly by whispering, walking across the floor, or in any other way.

A presiding officer who is a member has the same right to debate as anyone else, but can’t use it while presiding and normally should say nothing on the merits. In the rare case where they feel they must speak, they have to give up the chair, normally to the highest-ranking vice-president present who hasn’t spoken on the question, and they may not return to the chair until the pending main question has been disposed of.

q0673.answer: Turn the chair over to the vice-president.

sources.says: A presiding officer who leaves the chair to debate may not return to it until the pending main question has been disposed of, since they have shown partisanship on it.

q0674.answer: When the main motion has been disposed of.

sources.says: In general, for a member to speak when no question is pending, without promptly leading to a motion, requires permission of the assembly.
Amend is debatable whenever the motion it applies to is debatable, and undebatable whenever that motion is undebatable.
Postpone Indefinitely, Commit, and Postpone to a Certain Time are debatable, to differing degrees.
The privileged motions are all undebatable, because their high privilege would let debate interfere with business.

q0677.answer: None of the privileged motions are debatable.

sources.says: Except for an Appeal (in most cases) and the incidental motion to create a proviso (when its motion is debatable), the incidental motions are undebatable, because of their high privilege to interrupt.

q0678.answer: The rest of the incidental motions are undebatable.

sources.says: An Appeal relating to indecorum, the rules of debate, or the priority of business is undebatable, as is one made while an undebatable question is pending. At all other times it is fully debatable.

q0679.answer: All three make an appeal undebatable.

sources.says: Reconsider is debatable only to the extent the motion to be reconsidered is debatable. Rescind and Amend Something Previously Adopted are fully debatable, and Take from the Table is always undebatable.

q0680.answer: Reconsider is undebatable when applied to an undebatable motion.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: The word majority means “more than half.”

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: An unqualified majority vote means more than half the votes cast by persons entitled to vote, excluding blanks or abstentions, at a regular or properly called meeting.

q0682.answer: More than half the votes cast, excluding blanks and abstentions.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A majority means more than half of the votes cast.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A majority means more than half of the votes cast.

q0684.answer: Half of 51 is 25.5, so at least 26 are needed.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A majority means more than half of the votes cast by persons entitled to vote.

q0685.answer: With 30 votes cast, more than half is 16.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A majority means more than half of the votes cast.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: On a tie vote, a motion requiring a majority is lost, since a tie is not a majority.

q0686.answer: 25 to 24 is more than half of the votes cast, so it adopts the motion.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A majority means more than half of the votes cast, not of the members present or of the membership.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: The book’s worked example distinguishes a majority of votes cast from a majority of members present and of the entire membership.

q0687.answer: With 120 votes cast, more than half is 61.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A majority means more than half of the votes cast, excluding abstentions.

q0688.answer: 40 present minus 10 abstaining leaves 30 votes cast, so 16 are needed.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A majority of the entire membership is a majority of the total number of members of the voting body at the time of the vote.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: The word majority means more than half, when the term is used without qualification.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: An unqualified two-thirds vote means at least two-thirds of the votes cast by persons entitled to vote, excluding blanks or abstentions. For example, with 30 votes cast, two-thirds is 20.
The Previous Question requires a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: Two-thirds means at least two-thirds of the votes cast.

q0691.answer: With 60 votes cast, the Previous Question needs 40.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A two-thirds vote means at least two-thirds of the votes cast, which is the same as the affirmative being at least twice the negative.

q0692.answer: 24 to 12 is exactly twice as many in favor, so it meets two-thirds. The others don’t.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: An unqualified two-thirds vote means at least two-thirds of the votes cast by persons entitled to vote, excluding blanks or abstentions.

q0693.answer: Votes cast by persons entitled to vote.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: As a compromise between individual and assembly rights, a two-thirds vote is required for any motion that suspends or modifies an adopted rule of order, prevents a question from being introduced, closes or limits or extends debate, limits nominating or voting, or takes away membership.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: To determine whether a question has two-thirds of the votes cast, the chair takes a rising vote (or a show of hands in a very small assembly if no one objects), and counts it when in doubt.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: Two-thirds means at least two-thirds of the votes cast.
The Previous Question requires a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: Voting requirements based on members present are generally undesirable, since an abstention then has the same effect as a negative vote, denying members a neutral position.

q0697.answer: An abstention becomes, in effect, a negative vote.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A plurality is the largest number of votes given any candidate or proposition when three or more choices are possible. A plurality that isn’t a majority never decides anything unless a special rule provides for it.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: The candidate receiving the largest number of votes when there are three or more choices has a plurality.

q0699.answer: John has a plurality with 50, though not a majority of the 147 votes.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: The presiding officer, if a member, can, but is not obliged to, vote whenever the vote will affect the result: to break or cause a tie, or to reach or block two-thirds.

q0700.answer: The chair is never required to vote.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: On a tie vote, a motion requiring a majority is lost, since a tie is not a majority. The chair may vote to break the tie, but need not.
If the chair abstains when there is a tie, the motion is lost.

q0701.answer: The chair simply announces the motion is lost, with no need to vote.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: If there is a tie without the chair’s vote, the presiding officer can vote in the affirmative, causing the motion to be adopted.

q0702.answer: At 20 to 20, the chair’s affirmative vote would adopt it.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: If there is one more in the affirmative than the negative, such as 72 to 71, the chair can vote no to create a tie and defeat the motion. The chair’s vote matters only when it changes the result.

q0703.answer: At 25 to 24, the chair can create a tie and defeat it. In the other cases a single vote can’t change the outcome.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: If there is one more vote in the affirmative than the negative without the chair’s vote, the chair can vote no to create a tie, and a tie defeats a motion needing a majority.

q0704.answer: The chair’s vote makes it 30 to 30, a tie, so the motion is lost.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: Where two-thirds is required, the chair can vote to cause or block reaching two-thirds, such as voting yes when the affirmative is one less than twice the negative.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: Two-thirds means at least two-thirds of the votes cast.

q0705.answer: At 59 to 30, two-thirds isn’t reached. The chair’s yes vote makes it 60 to 30, exactly two-thirds, so the motion passes.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: The chair can vote to break or cause a tie, or to reach or block two-thirds, or abstain. The chair cannot vote twice, once as a member and again as presiding officer.

q0706.answer: The false statement is that the chair can vote twice.

sources.says: A member behind in dues who hasn’t been formally dropped from the rolls and isn’t under disciplinary suspension keeps full voting rights, unless the bylaws provide otherwise.

q0707.answer: They may vote, unless suspended or the bylaws say otherwise.

sources.says: No member should vote on a question in which they have a direct personal or monetary interest not common to other members, such as a contract with a firm they profit from. They should abstain.
The rule about abstaining on questions of personal interest doesn’t mean a member shouldn’t vote for themself for an office members are generally eligible for.

q0709.answer: Make no ruling. She may vote for herself.

sources.says: Except on a secret vote, a member has a right to change their vote up to the time the result is announced. Afterward it takes unanimous consent.

q0710.answer: Up to the time the result is announced.

sources.says: Voting by rising is used to verify an inconclusive voice vote and on motions requiring a two-thirds vote.

q0711.answer: On motions requiring a two-thirds vote.

sources.says: A show of hands can replace a rising vote in very small assemblies if no one objects, and some small groups use it instead of a voice vote. In large assemblies, two-thirds motions are voted on by rising.
Show of hands should generally be limited to very small meetings where everyone can see everyone.

q0712.answer: The false statement is that it is always used in large assemblies for two-thirds votes.

sources.says: When putting the question, the chair calls first for the affirmative vote, then for the negative.
If after retaking a vote as an uncounted rising vote the chair still can’t determine the result, the chair must take it a third time as a counted rising vote.

q0714.answer: The chair takes a counted rising vote.

sources.says: In counting a rising vote, those in the affirmative are always counted first. In a large assembly the chair should appoint tellers to count.

q0715.answer: The affirmative is always counted first.

sources.says: Other methods of voting, including ballot, roll call, and absentee voting, are used only when expressly ordered by the assembly or prescribed by its rules.
Voice, rising, and show of hands are the regular methods.
Voting by ballot, or secret ballot, is used when secrecy of members’ votes is desired.

q0717.answer: When members’ votes should be kept secret.

sources.says: When the bylaws require a ballot vote, that requirement can’t be suspended, even by a unanimous vote, to take the vote by a nonsecret method.

q0718.answer: It can’t be suspended even by a unanimous vote.

sources.says: Unless another method is specified, a ballot vote is taken on slips of paper on which voters mark their votes.

q0719.answer: Members mark their votes on slips of paper.

sources.says: In balloting at a meeting, the chair appoints tellers to distribute, collect, and count the ballots, and to report the vote.
The presiding officer, if a member, can always vote on a ballot at the same time as other members. If they fail to vote before the polls close, they need the assembly’s permission.

q0721.answer: The chair can always vote by ballot with the other members.

sources.says: Tellers ignore blank ballots and others that show no preference, treating them as abstentions.
If two or more filled-out ballots are found folded together, each set is recorded as one illegal vote and not credited. A blank ballot folded with a filled one is simply ignored.

q0723.answer: They are recorded as an illegal vote.

sources.says: Unintelligible ballots, or ballots for an unidentifiable or ineligible candidate, are treated as illegal votes: counted as votes cast but not credited to anyone.
Illegal votes cast by persons entitled to vote are counted as votes cast in computing the majority, but aren’t credited to any candidate or choice.

q0725.answer: They count only toward the number of votes cast for computing the majority.

sources.says: Each section of a multi-office ballot is treated as a separate ballot. If a member leaves sections blank, that doesn’t affect the validity of the sections they filled.

q0726.answer: The filled-in choices still count as legal votes.

sources.says: The tellers’ report gives the number of votes cast, the number needed for election, the votes each candidate received, and the illegal votes with their reasons.

q0727.answer: The tellers’ names aren’t part of the report.

sources.says: The reporting teller never declares the result of a ballot vote. The result is always declared by the chair, who also reads the tellers’ report.
A recount of a ballot vote may be ordered by the voting body by a majority vote, at the same session or within the allowed time.
A roll-call vote (yeas and nays) places on the record how each member votes, the opposite of a ballot vote. It is usually confined to representative bodies whose proceedings are published.

q0730.answer: It puts on record how each member voted.

sources.says: The roll is called in alphabetical order, except that the presiding officer’s name is called last, and only when their vote will affect the result.

q0731.answer: Alphabetically, with the chair’s name called last.

sources.says: On a roll call, a member who doesn’t wish to vote answers “present” (or abstain). A member not ready to vote who wants to be called again after the roll is complete answers “pass.”
A vote by mail, when authorized in the bylaws, is generally reserved for important issues, such as bylaw amendments or officer elections, where a full membership vote is desired.

Preferential voting is more complicated than common methods and no substitute for repeated balloting, but it is especially useful and fair in an election by mail when taking more than one ballot is impractical. It can’t be used unless the bylaws authorize it.

q0734.answer: It is especially useful and fair in an election by mail.

sources.says: A proxy is a power of attorney given by one person to another to vote in their place. The term also means the person holding it.

Proxy voting is incompatible with a deliberative assembly, where membership is personal and nontransferable, and isn’t permitted unless state law or the bylaws provide for it. In nonstock corporations it is generally inadvisable, since proxies can let a few people control elections without attending.

q0736.answer: Proxies can control elections without attendance. The other statements contradict the book.

sources.says: A nomination is, in effect, a proposal to fill the blank in an assumed motion “that ___ be elected” to the position.

q0737.answer: A nomination is a proposal to fill a blank.

sources.says: Methods of nomination are by the chair, from the floor, by a committee, by ballot, by mail, and by petition.

q0738.answer: Telephone isn’t a recognized method of nominating.

sources.says: Nominations from the floor are sometimes called “open nominations.”

When nominations are taken from the floor, a member doesn’t need to be recognized by the chair to nominate someone, unless they also want to debate the nomination at the same time. In a large meeting or convention the member should stand to nominate, though in small groups people often nominate from their seats. A nomination needs no second, although members sometimes second one to show support. No one may ever nominate more people than there are positions to fill.

q0740.answer: A member need not be recognized to nominate. A second isn’t required, members in large assemblies should rise, and no one can nominate three people for a single office.

sources.says: The nominating committee should be elected by the organization or its board where possible. In an organized society the president should not appoint it or be a member of it.
Members of the nominating committee are not barred from becoming nominees themselves.

q0741.answer: The false statement is that the chair should appoint the nominating committee in an organized society.

sources.says: A nominating committee is automatically discharged when its report is formally presented, though it revives if a nominee withdraws before the election.

q0742.answer: When its report is formally presented.

sources.says: After the nominating committee reports and before voting takes place, the chair must call for further nominations from the floor.

q0743.answer: The chair must call for further nominations from the floor.

sources.says: When no one else wants to nominate, the chair asks again for further nominations and, with no response, normally declares nominations closed without waiting for a motion.
Where there is no rule, a motion to fix the method of voting in an election is an incidental main motion if made before the election is pending, or an incidental motion if made while it is pending.
When all offices are voted on by a single ballot, elections should take place early in the meeting, to allow time for additional balloting for any office where no one gets a majority.

q0746.answer: Early in the meeting, so there’s time for more ballots if needed.

sources.says: Trying to limit the candidates for an office to two, by whatever method, is an unfortunate practice that should be discouraged.
Balloting for an unfilled office is repeated as many times as needed to get a majority for one candidate, and no one is dropped unless they withdraw voluntarily.

q0747.answer: All candidates stay on the ballot, and voting continues until one gets a majority.

sources.says: When repeated balloting is needed, candidates are never removed from the next ballot unless they voluntarily withdraw. The one in last place may become a “dark horse” compromise.

q0748.answer: All the names stay on the ballot.

sources.says: If more candidates receive a majority than there are positions to fill, the chair declares them elected in order of their vote totals, starting with the highest, until every position is filled.

q0749.answer: Those with the largest vote totals fill the places.

sources.says: Viva voce election is used mainly in mass meetings, or when an election isn’t strongly contested and the bylaws don’t require a ballot.
In a viva voce election with more than one nominee, candidates are voted on in the order in which they were nominated, until one receives a majority.

q0751.answer: In the order they were nominated.

sources.says: If only one person is nominated and the bylaws don’t require a ballot, the chair, after making sure no one wants to nominate anyone else, simply declares the nominee elected by unanimous consent, or “acclamation.”

q0752.answer: The chair can declare the nominees elected without a vote.

sources.says: In a roll-call vote, the secretary repeats each member’s name and answer aloud as it is given and records the answers in separate columns.

q0753.answer: The secretary records each vote and repeats it aloud.

sources.says: Every society should specify in its bylaws what officers it requires, how they are elected or appointed, their term of office, and any qualifications or duties different from those in the parliamentary authority.

q0754.answer: All three belong in the bylaws.

sources.says: Officer duties that differ from or add to those in the parliamentary authority should be specified in the bylaws.
For term-limit purposes, an officer who has served more than half a term in an office is considered to have served a full term.

q0756.answer: More than half a term counts as a full term.

sources.says: An officer’s term begins as soon as they are elected, unless the bylaws set a different time.

q0757.answer: As soon as the officer is elected.

sources.says: The presiding officer is ordinarily called the chairman when no special title has been assigned, or in a body not permanently organized, like a mass meeting.
In a body not permanently organized, such as a mass meeting, the presiding officer is called the chairman.
The presiding officer, especially of a large assembly, should be chosen mainly for the ability to preside, and should know parliamentary law and the organization’s rules well.

The presiding officer’s duties include protecting the assembly from obviously dilatory motions, enforcing the rules of debate and decorum, and expediting business in every way compatible with members’ rights.

At each meeting the presiding officer should have a copy of the bylaws and other rules, a copy of the parliamentary authority, a list of all standing and special committees and their members, and a memorandum of the order of business.

Except in a small board or committee, the presiding officer should stand when calling the meeting to order or adjourning it, when putting a question to vote, and when explaining the reasons for a ruling at any length.
While a member is speaking in debate, the presiding officer should remain seated, or step back slightly if their view would be blocked.

The chair should turn the chair over during a motion referring only to themself, such as censure or commendation, but should not hesitate to put the question on electing officers or appointing delegates or a committee even if included.

q0765.answer: A motion electing officers, even if the chair is included.

sources.says: If the president vacates the chair during a meeting and no vice-president is available, the president can, subject to the assembly’s approval, appoint a chairman pro tem.
If neither the president nor any vice-president is present, the secretary, or in the secretary’s absence another member, calls the meeting to order, and the assembly elects a chairman pro tem.
If neither the president nor any vice-president is present, the assembly immediately elects a chairman pro tem to preside during that session.

q0768.answer: A chairman pro tem should be elected.

sources.says: A presiding officer should make every effort to know more parliamentary procedure than other members.
The presiding officer must not let members press on so fast that parliamentary steps are skipped.
The president should never be technical or more strict than necessary for the good of the meeting.

q0769.answer: All three describe an effective presiding officer.

sources.says: As an ex-officio committee member, the president has the same rights as other members, but isn’t obligated to attend and isn’t counted toward the quorum.

q0770.answer: The president has the same rights as other members.

sources.says: When an organization elects its president a full term in advance, the person chosen is called the president-elect during the term after the election. The office exists only if the bylaws provide for it.
In the absence of the president, the vice-president serves in the president’s place, so the vice-president should be competent to perform the president’s duties.
A presiding vice-president is addressed as “Mr. President” or “Madam President,” unless the president is also on the platform, when “Vice-President” may be used.
The secretary is the recording officer and custodian of records. This officer is sometimes called the clerk, recording secretary, recorder, or scribe.

q0774.answer: All of those names are used.

sources.says: The secretary is the recording officer of the assembly and the custodian of its records, except those assigned to others, such as the treasurer’s books.

q0775.answer: Serving as recording officer and custodian of the records.

sources.says: The secretary’s duties include keeping the minutes, filing committee reports, keeping the membership roll, and furnishing delegates with credentials. In the absence of the president and vice-president, the secretary calls the meeting to order and presides only until a chairman pro tem is elected.

q0776.answer: Presiding over a whole meeting is not a secretary’s duty. The secretary presides only until a chairman pro tem is elected.

sources.says: In the secretary’s absence, a secretary pro tem must be elected. A corresponding, financial, or executive secretary isn’t an automatic replacement.

q0777.answer: A secretary pro tem should be elected.

sources.says: Official correspondence to be read under reports of officers is normally read by the recording secretary, not the corresponding secretary.
Any member has the right to examine the reports and minutes, including executive session minutes, at a reasonable time and place, without abusing the privilege.
In larger societies, issuing notices of meetings and conducting general correspondence are often assigned to a separate officer, the corresponding secretary.
The treasurer is the officer entrusted with the custody of the organization’s funds and should be bonded.
The treasurer’s specific duties vary depending on the size and complexity of the society, but the treasurer can’t disburse funds without authority.

q0782.answer: They vary with the size and complexity of the organization.

sources.says: Some organizations also have a financial secretary, who bills members for dues, receives payment, keeps a ledger of each member’s account, and turns the money over to the treasurer.
Other officers a society may have include a curator, who serves as custodian of any objects of value belonging to the society, other than library holdings.
A sergeant-at-arms (or warden, or warrant officer) assists in preserving order on the floor as the chair directs.

Like an honorary degree, an honorary office or membership is perpetual unless rescinded or limited by the bylaws. It carries the right to attend and speak, but not to make motions or vote unless also a regular member.

q0786.answer: It is perpetual unless rescinded or limited by the bylaws.

sources.says: Honorary officers and members must be authorized by the bylaws. They may attend meetings and speak, but may not make motions or vote unless they are also regular members or the bylaws give full rights.

q0787.answer: The false statement is that they can make motions and vote.

sources.says: The executive secretary runs the central office and acts under the immediate direction of the board and the executive committee, if there is one.

The executive secretary recommends plans of work and conducts the day-to-day business of the organization. Hiring, firing, and setting staff salaries are usually done with the approval of the board or executive committee.

q0789.answer: Conducting day-to-day business needs no board approval. Hiring, firing, and salaries do.

sources.says: The parliamentarian is a consultant, commonly a professional, who advises the president, other officers, committees, and members on parliamentary procedure.

During a meeting, the parliamentarian’s work should be limited to advising the chair and, when asked, other members, and inconspicuously pointing out to the chair any error that could harm members’ rights.
Only the chair has the power to rule on questions of order.

q0791.answer: Giving advice to the chair and members as a consultant.

sources.says: The parliamentarian should be seated next to the chair, convenient for quiet consultation, though the chair shouldn’t check with the parliamentarian too often or too obviously.
A member serving as parliamentarian must stay impartial, so doesn’t make motions, debate, or vote, except on a ballot vote.
In an ordinary society, the minutes should record mainly what was done at the meeting, not what members said, and must never reflect the secretary’s opinion.

q0794.answer: What was done at the meeting.

sources.says: The maker of a main motion is named in the minutes, but the seconder’s name is not entered unless the assembly orders it.
The minutes include the kind of meeting, whether the regular chairman and secretary were present, and all points of order and appeals with the chair’s reasons.

q0795.answer: The seconder’s name generally isn’t included.

sources.says: The minutes should show each main motion in the exact wording in which it was adopted or otherwise disposed of, with any amendments incorporated.

q0796.answer: Use the exact wording of the motions acted on.

sources.says: The minutes show all main motions made or taken up, except, normally, any that were withdrawn.

q0797.answer: A withdrawn motion normally doesn’t appear in the minutes.

sources.says: The last paragraph of the minutes should state the hour of adjournment.
When a count has been ordered, the number of votes on each side is entered in the minutes. When the vote is by ballot, the full tellers’ report is entered.

q0799.answer: When a count is ordered or the vote is by ballot.

sources.says: The minutes can give the name and subject of a guest speaker, but no effort should be made to summarize the remarks.

q0800.answer: A summary of the speaker’s remarks shouldn’t be included.

sources.says: Where regular meetings are frequent, the minutes of each meeting are normally read and approved at the beginning of the next regular meeting, right after the call to order and opening ceremonies.

q0801.answer: At the beginning of the next regular meeting, after the call to order and opening ceremonies.

sources.says: An adjourned meeting approves the minutes of the meeting that set it up. Its own minutes are approved at the next adjourned or regular meeting, whichever comes first.

q0802.answer: At the next regular or adjourned meeting, whichever comes first.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: A formal motion to approve the minutes isn’t needed. The chair asks for corrections, which are usually handled by unanimous consent.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When no further corrections are offered, the chair declares the minutes approved, without a formal vote.
The assembly may, by majority vote without debate, dispense with reading the minutes. They can then be taken up later in the meeting, and if not, they are read and approved at the following meeting.

q0804.answer: They must still be read at a later time.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When the draft minutes are sent to all members in advance, they are not read at the meeting unless a member requests it. Correction and approval are handled as usual.

q0805.answer: They aren’t read unless someone asks.

sources.says: When the minutes are approved, the word “Approved,” with the secretary’s initials and the date, is written below them.

q0806.answer: The secretary writes “Approved” below them with the date and initials.

sources.says: If an error in approved minutes is established later, even many years later, it can be corrected by the motion to Amend Something Previously Adopted.
An error or material omission in minutes can be corrected whenever it becomes established after approval, even many years later, by Amend Something Previously Adopted.

q0808.answer: The assembly can correct them whenever a mistake is discovered.

sources.says: At any meeting where officers’ reports are made, they immediately follow the reading and approval of the minutes.
Motions to adopt or implement an officer’s recommendations should be made from the floor by a member other than the reporting officer.

q0810.answer: Any member except the reporting officer.

sources.says: At each meeting the chair may ask for a Treasurer’s report, which may be simply an oral statement of the cash balance on hand, or that balance less obligations.

q0811.answer: It may be just an oral statement of the cash balance.

sources.says: A routine Treasurer’s report requires no action by the assembly.
No acceptance by the assembly is required or proper on the treasurer’s report, unless it is important enough, like an annual report, to be audited.
The treasurer must make a full financial report annually, and that annual report should always be audited.
Ordinary societies can have reports audited by an auditing committee of members, and in some organizations by elected officers known as “trustees.”
Adopting the auditors’ report relieves the treasurer of responsibility for the period it covers, except in case of fraud.

q0815.answer: It relieves the treasurer of responsibility for that period, except for fraud.

sources.says: An officer’s report becomes a permanent official document only if formally adopted. Accounts prepared by the historian don’t become official history until the assembly adopts them.

q0816.answer: It must be formally adopted by the assembly.

sources.says: Except in the smallest societies or those meeting very often, it is advisable for the bylaws to create a board empowered to act for the society between its regular meetings. Such a board is usually called the executive board.

The board empowered to act between meetings is usually called the executive board, or, where there is an executive committee within it, the board of directors, board of managers, or board of trustees.
If a society has an executive board, the bylaws should specify the number of members and how they are determined, define its duties and powers, and provide for its meetings.
In organizations meeting monthly or more often, and sometimes quarterly, the board is not given so much power, since the society can handle much of its own business.

q0820.answer: It is not given so much power.

sources.says: Except in matters the bylaws place exclusively under the board’s control, the society’s assembly can instruct the board and rescind or amend any board action that can still be undone.

q0821.answer: Except matters the bylaws place exclusively under the board’s control.

sources.says: If someone holds an office in a society they aren’t a member of, and the bylaws make that office ex officio a board member, the nonmember is a full-fledged board member.
Ex-officio board members may serve by virtue of an office in the society, in a parent or allied group, or even a public office.

q0822.answer: An ex-officio board member may be a nonmember of the society.

sources.says: An ex-officio board member not under the society’s authority, such as a governor who is ex officio a trustee of a private academy, has all rights including making motions and voting but no obligations, and isn’t counted toward the quorum.

q0823.answer: The governor isn’t counted in determining a quorum.

sources.says: In ordinary societies with executive boards, the president and secretary of the society serve in the same roles within the board, unless the bylaws provide otherwise.

q0824.answer: The society’s president and secretary serve in the same roles on the board.

sources.says: A board can transact business only at a regular or properly called meeting with a quorum. Approval obtained separately by phone, interview, or in writing, even from every member, isn’t the board’s approval.
In small boards, procedure is relaxed: members may speak seated, motions need no second, and informal discussion is allowed while no motion is pending.

As a general principle, a board cannot delegate its authority, meaning it can’t empower a subordinate group to act independently in its name, unless the bylaws allow it. It can appoint committees that work under its supervision.

q0825.answer: Dunbar’s key says a board can meet informally to make decisions.
q0825.conflict: RONR 12th ed. doesn’t support this key. A board can decide things only at a properly called meeting with a quorum (49:16), so it can’t “meet informally to make decisions,” though small boards may use relaxed procedure at such a meeting (49:21). And 49:12 says a board generally cannot delegate its authority, which makes “cannot delegate its authority” the choice the book supports.

sources.says: Where the board is large or members travel far to meet, the bylaws usually create an executive committee of board members with much of the board’s power between meetings, in effect a “board within a board.”
Under general parliamentary law, large boards transact business under the same rules of procedure as other deliberative assemblies.

q0827.answer: The same rules as any other deliberative assembly.

sources.says: A board can transact business only at a regular or properly called meeting, for which every board member was sent any required notice, and at which a quorum is present.
In boards and committees, the quorum is a majority of the members unless a different quorum is provided for.

q0829.answer: A majority, more than half the members.

sources.says: Only members of the board have the right to examine the board’s minute book, unless the board orders otherwise.
The board can order that anyone, including all society members, may view board minutes, by majority vote if they aren’t protected by executive-session secrecy.
The society’s assembly can also grant that permission, or order the minutes read, by a two-thirds vote, a majority of the entire membership, or a majority with previous notice.

In small boards of about a dozen members or fewer, members may speak seated, there is no limit on the number of times a member can speak to a debatable question, and informal discussion is permitted while no motion is pending.

q0832.answer: All three are true in small boards.

sources.says: In small boards, motions need not be seconded, there is no limit on the number of times a member can speak to a debatable question, informal discussion is allowed with no motion pending, and the chair may vote on all questions.

q0833.answer: There’s no limit on how many times a member can speak.

sources.says: In small boards, members may raise a hand instead of standing, motions need no second, and the chairman need not rise while putting questions to a vote.
Motions to close or limit debate are in order in small boards, but not in committees.

q0834.answer: The chairman doesn’t need to rise while putting questions to a vote.

sources.says: In a small board, a chairman who is a member may speak in informal discussion and debate and vote on all questions without leaving the chair.
The chairman may start informal discussion to put forward proposals without a formal motion, though the chairman also has the right to make a motion.
Motions to close or limit debate are in order even in small board meetings.

q0835.answer: Dunbar’s key says the chairman can only make incidental motions.
