q0835.conflict: RONR 12th ed. contradicts this key. 49:21n4 says a small-board chairman has the right to make a motion, and 49:21n3 says motions to close or limit debate are in order in small boards. Under the 12th edition, “propose a motion to close or limit debate” is the better answer.

sources.says: When part of a board’s membership is replaced periodically, it becomes in effect a new board. Matters not finally disposed of fall to the ground, and if the board elects its own officers or appoints standing committees, new ones are chosen.
A committee generally has less authority to act independently for the society than a board is understood to have.

q0837.answer: A board has more authority to act independently.

sources.says: A committee appointed “with power” has power to take all the steps necessary to carry out its instructions.

q0838.answer: It can take all the steps necessary to carry out its instructions.

sources.says: Standing committees are constituted to perform a continuing function and remain in existence permanently or for the life of the assembly.
Ordinary committees are either standing committees, which continue, or special committees, which end when their task is done.
If the bylaws name certain standing committees, no others can be established without amending the bylaws, unless the bylaws authorize creating additional standing committees.
A standing committee of a society reports to the assembly of the society, not to the executive board, unless the bylaws provide otherwise.
A special (select, or ad hoc) committee is appointed to carry out a specified task and automatically ceases to exist when it presents its final report.
A special committee automatically ceases to exist on presenting its final report to the assembly.
Where the bylaws don’t say how committee members are chosen, the method can be decided when the committee is appointed, or, for a special committee, specified in the motion establishing it.

q0844.answer: It is specified in the motion that establishes the committee.

sources.says: A committee member’s resignation goes to the appointing power, which is responsible for filling the vacancy.
The power to appoint a committee includes the power to fill any vacancy in it.
Election by ballot is principally used for important standing committees with extensive powers. Nominees are voted on by ballot, as in electing a board, with a majority needed.
Committees can be appointed by ballot election, by nominations from the floor with viva voce election, by nominations by the chair with confirmation, or by appointment by the chair.
Absent special conditions, appointment of committees by the chair, or regular presiding officer, is usually the best method in large assemblies, if authorized by the bylaws or the assembly.

A bylaw that the president “shall appoint all committees” means the president selects the members of committees the bylaws establish or the assembly orders. It doesn’t let the president create committees, and no vote is taken on the chair’s appointees.

q0849.answer: All three statements are true, so none is false.

sources.says: The first person the chair names is automatically the committee chairman, unless the assembly rejects them or they decline, though it is good practice to name the chairman explicitly.
A committee (other than a committee of the whole) can appoint subcommittees, which are responsible to and report to the committee, not the assembly.

q0851.answer: They report to the standing committee.

sources.says: When a committee is appointed, the secretary makes sure all appointees are notified, gives the chairman a list of members, and provides copies of any papers or motions referred with the assembly’s instructions.
If the chairman fails to call a needed committee meeting, any two members may call one, unless the assembly’s rules require a larger number.
The quorum in a committee is a majority of its membership unless the assembly has prescribed a different one.

q0854.answer: A majority of the committee members.

sources.says: The quorum in a committee is a majority of its membership unless the assembly has prescribed a different quorum.

q0855.answer: A majority, unless the assembly prescribes otherwise.

sources.says: The relaxed small-board procedures apply in all standing and special committees, and the chairman is usually the most active participant in the committee’s discussions.
Under those procedures the chairman may speak in debate and vote without leaving the chair, and need not rise when putting questions.
Committees of organized societies operate under the society’s bylaws, parliamentary authority, and applicable special rules or standing rules, and may not adopt their own rules unless authorized.
When a committee is to make important recommendations, it should let society members appear and present their views at a scheduled time. Such a meeting is usually called a hearing.
When a special committee finishes its assigned business, a motion is made for the committee to “rise,” which is equivalent to adjourning sine die, and for a member to report to the assembly.

q0859.answer: “Rise” means the committee adjourns sine die.

sources.says: Members of an old standing committee continue their duties until their successors are chosen.
Standing committee members usually serve for a term matching the officers’, or until successors are chosen.

q0860.answer: Until their successors are chosen with the new officers.

sources.says: A detailed report with recommendations is best organized as: how the committee undertook its charge; the facts or information obtained; the findings or conclusions; and, last, the recommendations.
For the report of a board whose chairman is also the assembly’s presiding officer, the secretary or another member of the board acts as reporting member.

q0862.answer: Another member, such as the secretary, reports. Dunbar’s key accepts any of those.

sources.says: When the assembly hears a report read or given orally, it receives the report. Receiving a report doesn’t mean adopting it.

q0863.answer: It hears the report as read.

sources.says: When a report contains recommendations, the reporting member usually moves to implement them at the end of the presentation, if a member of the assembly.
A motion by the reporting member to implement a committee’s recommendations requires no second, since it is made on behalf of the committee.

Adopting an entire report endorses every word of it, including the facts and reasoning, as the assembly’s own statement. That motion should be made by someone other than the reporting member and needs a second.

q0866.answer: It endorses every word of the report.

sources.says: If a motion “to accept” a report is adopted and given its proper meaning, it implies the assembly has endorsed the complete report.
Adopt, accept, and agree to are all equivalent.
A committee report should always be worded in the third person, not “I report…” or “We recommend…”.
A written committee report usually isn’t addressed or dated.
All committee reports should be submitted in writing, with limited exceptions.

q0868.answer: The false statement is that reports should be in the first person.

sources.says: A report should begin by identifying the committee. For a standing committee: “The Committee on… reports that…” or “submits the following report.”
A committee may authorize its chairman to sign a report alone, in which case the chairman adds the word “Chairman” after the signature, certifying the committee adopted it.

If no provision is made for committee reports, the reporting member seeks the floor and says a report is ready. If the chair thinks the assembly wants it, the chair has the member proceed, but if anyone objects, the chair puts the question to the assembly.

q0871.answer: Put the question to the assembly.

sources.says: When a report contains recommendations, the reporting member usually makes the motion to implement them, such as moving adoption of the proposed resolution, at the end of the presentation.

q0872.answer: The reporting member moves its adoption.

sources.says: When a committee recommends several amendments, normally the first is reread, opened to debate and secondary amendment, and voted on, then the next is read, and so on.

q0873.answer: Vote on each recommendation after it is read and debated.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The organization of a convention is carried out by three committees: the Credentials Committee, the Committee on Standing Rules, and the Program Committee.

q0874.answer: The Credentials Committee, Committee on Standing Rules, and Program Committee.

sources.says: A “minority report” is the formal presentation of views from committee members who don’t concur with the committee report. The assembly usually allows it when asked.
The report adopted by a majority vote in the committee should always be called “the committee report,” never “the majority report.”
Formally presenting a minority report is a privilege the assembly may grant, not a matter of right, since the assembly is primarily interested in the majority’s findings.

q0877.answer: It is a privilege the assembly may grant.

sources.says: If the committee report ends with a proposed resolution, the minority can recommend rejecting it, amending it, or adopting some other suitable motion to dispose of it.
The chair calls for the minority presentation unless someone objects, in which case the chair puts the question on receiving it. It needs a majority and is undebatable.

q0879.answer: Have the assembly vote on receiving it, without debate.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: In a committee of the whole, quasi committee of the whole, or informal consideration, any member can speak on the main question or any amendment, for the usual length of time, as often as they can get the floor.

q0880.answer: As often as they can obtain the floor.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: In quasi committee of the whole, the presiding officer of the assembly doesn’t appoint a chairman but remains in the chair throughout.

q0881.answer: The quasi committee of the whole.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: A committee of the whole is suited to large assemblies, quasi committee of the whole to medium-size meetings, and informal consideration to small meetings of ordinary societies.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: In a committee of the whole, votes are recommendations rather than final decisions, and a chairman is appointed while the regular presiding officer leaves the chair.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: In quasi committee of the whole, the presiding officer remains in the chair throughout.

q0884.answer: The quasi committee of the whole.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: Quasi committee of the whole may be convenient in meetings of medium size, about 50 to 100 members. Its votes are reported to the assembly for final consideration, and the presiding officer stays in the chair.

q0885.answer: It suits groups of about 50 to 100 members.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: Informal consideration is suited to small meetings of ordinary societies. It removes the limit on the number of speeches, and its votes are final decisions of the assembly.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: In ordinary societies whose meetings aren’t large, a much simpler alternative to a committee of the whole is to consider a question informally, which only suspends the limit on how many times a member may speak on the main question and its amendments.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: Once informal consideration is adopted, there is no limit to how many times a member can speak on the question or on any amendment.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: Only the number of speeches is informal. All votes are formal, any other motion follows the regular rules of debate, and the proceedings are recorded in the minutes as usual.

q0887.answer: The false statement is that members can debate amendments only once. They can speak on amendments as often as they like. The rest are true: nothing changes except the limit on speeches, so the regular presiding officer stays in the chair.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The “informal” aspect applies only to the number of speeches allowed in debate on the main question and its amendments. All votes are formal, and other motions follow the regular rules of debate.

q0888.answer: It removes the limit on how many times members can speak.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The motion to go into a committee of the whole is a form of the motion to Commit. A member obtains the floor and says “I move to go into a committee of the whole to consider the pending question.”

q0889.answer: Move to go into a committee of the whole.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: When referral to a committee of the whole is adopted, the presiding officer immediately calls another member to the chair, frequently but not necessarily the vice-president.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The committee of the whole’s secretary keeps a temporary memorandum, but its proceedings are not entered in the assembly’s minutes.

q0891.answer: They are not entered in the minutes.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The assembly’s minutes record the referral to the committee of the whole, the committee’s report, and the assembly’s action on the report, as for an ordinary committee.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: Like ordinary committees, a committee of the whole can’t alter the text of a resolution referred to it, but can propose amendments and report them as recommendations to the assembly.

q0893.answer: It proposes amendments and reports them as recommendations.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The only motions in order in a committee of the whole are to adopt, to amend, and to rise, plus a few incidental motions. Adjourn and Recess aren’t among them.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: A committee of the whole can’t close or limit debate itself, but must rise and ask the assembly. It can’t order a roll-call or ballot vote.

q0894.answer: The false statement is that a motion to close debate may be made anytime.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The quorum of a committee of the whole is the same as the assembly’s, unless the bylaws provide or the assembly establishes a different one.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: If a committee of the whole finds itself without a quorum, it must rise and report that fact to the assembly.

q0896.answer: It must rise and report the fact to the assembly.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The motion to consider a resolution in quasi committee of the whole must be seconded, and it is debatable as to the desirability of doing so, like any other motion to Commit.

q0897.answer: Ask for a second, allow debate, then vote.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: In quasi committee of the whole, the main question and amendments are open to debate as in a real committee of the whole, with each member allowed to speak an unlimited number of times.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: Considering a question informally in effect suspends only the rule limiting how many times a member can speak on the main question and its amendments.

q0899.answer: There’s no limit on the number of times members can speak.

sources.says: When a question is considered informally, the same information is recorded in the minutes as under the regular rules, since only the debate is informal.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: As soon as the main question is disposed of, temporarily or permanently, informal consideration automatically ends without any motion or vote.

A mass meeting is a meeting of an unorganized group announced, in a call, as convened to take appropriate action on a particular problem or purpose stated by its sponsors, and as open to everyone interested (or everyone in a specified group).

q0902.answer: An unorganized group called to act on a specific problem.

sources.says: A mass meeting is a meeting of an unorganized group.
A series of meetings held to organize a society are in the nature of mass meetings only until the society has been formed.

q0903.answer: A mass meeting, since it is by definition a meeting of an unorganized group.

sources.says: A mass meeting is an unorganized group’s meeting, called to take appropriate action on a particular problem or purpose stated by its sponsors.

q0904.answer: It is called to act on a specific problem.

sources.says: Sponsors of a mass meeting may limit the right of attendance, or at least participation, to people in general sympathy with the announced purpose. That is how it differs from a town meeting or public forum.

q0905.answer: The sponsors may limit the right of attendance.

sources.says: It may be wise for a mass meeting to adopt a standard parliamentary authority, which can be done by majority vote on a member’s motion, usually made right after the secretary is elected.

q0906.answer: By majority vote on a member’s motion.

sources.says: A chairman and a secretary are in general the only officers a mass meeting requires, elected right after the meeting is called to order.
Once the chairman is elected and takes the chair, they may say a few words and then announce “Nominations are now in order for secretary of this meeting.”

q0908.answer: Conduct the election of a secretary.

sources.says: At a mass meeting, any motion within the purpose announced in the call is in order, but any motion outside or contrary to that purpose is not. A meeting called to oppose an airport can’t take up a motion to support it.

q0909.answer: Rule the motion out of order as contrary to the meeting’s purpose.

sources.says: At a mass meeting with no other rule, members need the assembly’s permission to speak longer than ten minutes at a time.

q0910.answer: No longer than ten minutes at a time.

sources.says: In a mass meeting it is usually advisable to have all committees appointed by the chair, assuming the chairman was well chosen.
In a mass meeting, unless a time for another meeting has been set, a motion to adjourn is not in order while business is pending.

q0912.answer: It is not in order while business is pending.

sources.says: Unless a time has been set for another meeting, adopting a motion to adjourn a mass meeting dissolves the assembly.
When a group needs more than one meeting, as when forming a permanent society, the officers elected at the first meeting are designated chairman pro tem and secretary pro tem.
At the first meeting to organize a society, the first business is electing a chairman pro tem, and then a secretary.

q0915.answer: Elect a chairman pro tem and then a secretary.

sources.says: After the resolution to form the society is adopted, the next steps are generally a motion that the chair appoint a committee to draft bylaws, then a motion fixing the date, hour, and place of the next meeting.

q0916.answer: A motion that the chair appoint a committee to draft bylaws.

sources.says: A committee of a specified number is appointed by the chair to draft bylaws for the new society, consulting an attorney where incorporation may be needed.
At the second organizational meeting, the first item of business is reading and approving the minutes of the first meeting.

q0918.answer: Reading and approval of the first meeting’s minutes.

sources.says: After the bylaws are adopted, people join by signing a permanent record sheet filed with the organization’s original papers, agreeing to the bylaws and to pay dues. Those who sign become “charter members.”

sources.section: §55 Merger, Consolidation, and Dissolution of Societies
sources.says: In a merger, one organization continues and the other loses its identity and ceases to exist. In a consolidation, all the organizations end and a new entity is formed.

q0920.answer: In a merger, one continues and the other ceases to exist.

sources.section: §55 Merger, Consolidation, and Dissolution of Societies
sources.says: In either a merger or a consolidation, the resulting organization may be given a new name.

q0921.answer: It may be given a new name.

sources.section: §55 Merger, Consolidation, and Dissolution of Societies
sources.says: To dissolve an unincorporated society, a resolution such as “Resolved, That the X Society be dissolved as of…” is adopted. It is in effect a motion to rescind the bylaws.

q0922.answer: Adopt a resolution that in effect rescinds its bylaws.

sources.section: §55 Merger, Consolidation, and Dissolution of Societies
sources.says: Because a resolution dissolving an unincorporated society is in effect a motion to rescind the bylaws, it requires the same notice and vote as amending them.

q0923.answer: The same notice and vote needed to amend the bylaws.

sources.says: A committee to draw up proposed bylaws should generally be large, including the most judicious people, those interested in the rules, and those likely to spend a lot of time debating them later.
In bylaws, every punctuation mark matters and clear meaning outranks readability. Each sentence should be written so it can’t be quoted out of context.

q0925.answer: So it can’t be quoted out of context.

sources.says: Unlike amending existing bylaws, adopting the bylaws that bring a society into being requires only a majority vote.
Article I of an unincorporated society’s bylaws gives the society’s full, exact, properly punctuated name.
The object should be concisely expressed in a single sentence and should be general, since it sets the boundaries of business that can be introduced at meetings.
The article on members usually covers classes of members, qualifications and admission procedures, and fees and dues with due dates. It doesn’t list members’ names.
Article IV should specify the officers required and how they are elected or appointed, listed in order of rank.
A method of nominating officers may be prescribed in a section of this article.

The length of terms should be prescribed, and unless terms begin the moment the chair declares each officer elected, the time they begin must be specified, such as “at the close of the annual meeting.”

q0930.answer: Dunbar’s key says the specific date new officers take over isn’t included.
q0930.conflict: RONR 12th ed. 56:27 says the bylaws must specify when terms begin unless they start at the moment of election. That is usually tied to an event like the close of the annual meeting rather than a calendar date. The key holds only if “specific date” means a fixed calendar date.

sources.says: Officers rank in the order listed in the bylaws, so the president should be named first, then the vice-president, and so on.

q0931.answer: The president should be listed first among the officers.

sources.says: A method of nominating officers may be prescribed in a section of the article on officers.
For term-limit purposes, an officer who has served more than half a term is considered to have served a full term.
The article on meetings should establish the day of regular meetings, such as “the first Friday of each month.”
The hour and place of regular meetings should be fixed by a standing rule, not the bylaws.
The quorum for all meetings should be established in this article.

q0934.answer: Regular meeting days should be established there.

sources.says: If there is an executive board, this article should specify its composition, delineate its powers, and provide for its meetings.

The article on committees provides for each known standing committee, with a section giving its name, composition, manner of selection, and duties. Special committees are created as needed, not listed.

q0936.answer: The names of special committees aren’t included.

sources.says: The sample bylaws list standing committees such as a Finance Committee, Program Committee, and Auditing Committee, and allow other standing or special committees to be created as needed.
A committee formed for one specific task is a special committee, not a standing one.

q0937.answer: A committee formed at a meeting to pick a picnic location is a special committee, not a standing committee in the bylaws.

sources.says: If the president is ex officio a member of all committees except the Nominating Committee, the president has the right, but not the duty, to participate in their work.
As an ex-officio committee member, the president has the same rights as other members but isn’t obligated to attend.

q0938.answer: The president may debate at committee meetings.

sources.says: When a particular work is adopted as parliamentary authority, what any other book says in conflict with it carries no authority.

q0939.answer: Robert’s Rules of Order Newly Revised.

sources.says: If the bylaws contain no provision for amending them, they can be amended by a two-thirds vote with previous notice, or by a majority of the entire membership.
Bylaws articles are commonly designated with Roman numerals and their sections with Arabic numerals.

Each society decides the meaning of its own bylaws. Where a bylaw is ambiguous, a majority vote can decide the interpretation. Where the meaning is clear, even a unanimous vote can’t change it except by amending the bylaws.

q0942.answer: Changing a bylaw’s wording takes an amendment by the members. An unclear meaning can also be interpreted by majority vote.

sources.says: The bylaws should provide for their own amendment, requiring at least advance notice in a specified manner and a two-thirds vote.
A revision is open to amendment as fully as if the society were adopting bylaws for the first time, and can be perfected by first-degree and second-degree amendments.

q0944.answer: By first- and second-degree amendments. Third-degree amendments are never allowed.

sources.says: When noticed amendments conflict so that all can’t take effect, the chair arranges them in a logical order, generally taking the least inclusive first and the most inclusive last.

q0945.answer: The least inclusive amendment is voted on first.

sources.says: Notice of a bylaw amendment given at a meeting is usually given under new business, though it can be given at any time before the chair declares the meeting adjourned.
Any member may give notice of a bylaw amendment, usually under new business at a meeting, or it can be sent with the call of the meeting where it will be considered.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Matters made general orders for the present meeting are taken up under Unfinished Business and General Orders.

q0947.answer: Dunbar’s key treats a noticed bylaw amendment as a general order for the meeting where it is to be considered.
q0947.conflict: We couldn’t find this rule stated directly in RONR 12th ed. The book covers how notice is given (57:14) and how general orders are taken up (41:23), but doesn’t say that notice alone makes the amendment a general order. Treat this as Dunbar’s reading.

sources.says: A bylaw amendment goes into effect immediately upon adoption, unless the motion or an earlier vote sets a different time.
Amendments to a proposed bylaw amendment can be made in the first and second degrees and adopted by a majority vote without notice, within limits on the scope of change.
A proviso delaying when a bylaw amendment takes effect can be added to its enacting words, or adopted as a separate incidental motion. Either method requires only a majority vote.
Corrections of article or section numbers or cross-references that can’t change the meaning can be delegated to the secretary or, in more involved cases, to a committee.
A convention is an assembly of delegates chosen, normally for one session only, as representatives of constituent units.
A convention is an assembly of delegates, usually chosen specially for each session as representatives of the constituent units within a larger group.
In some societies, “house of delegates” or “house of representatives” describes delegates elected for a fixed term, during which they hold sessions from time to time as the bylaws prescribe.

q0954.answer: Delegates elected for a fixed term who hold sessions periodically.

sources.says: In an established society with constituent units, the parent body’s bylaws should prescribe delegates’ qualifications, the basis for their number, and how they are elected.

q0955.answer: By the bylaws of the parent organization.

sources.says: The parent body’s bylaws should authorize a periodic convention, define its powers, fix its quorum, specify its voting members, and cover delegates and the call.
The parent body’s bylaws should prescribe the qualifications of delegates and alternates, the basis for determining their number, and the method of electing them.
To avoid a change of officers during a convention, the bylaws should provide that newly elected officers take up their duties at the close of the convention.

q0958.answer: At the close of the convention.

sources.says: For an alternate to replace a registered delegate, proof of the delegate’s withdrawal must be presented to the Credentials Committee, and the alternate must be reregistered as the new delegate before sitting or voting.

Unless the body’s rules provide otherwise, no alternate can substitute for a delegate who remains registered. A delegate’s temporary absence doesn’t let an alternate make motions, debate, or vote, even with the delegate’s authorization.

q0960.answer: No, unless the organization’s rules provide for it.

sources.says: When members of a delegation meet as a group, before or during a convention, to decide how to act on matters coming before it, the meeting is usually called a caucus.

Unless instructed otherwise, a caucus is governed by the rules for committees, since the delegation is in effect a committee of its unit, unless it is so large that rules for assemblies are more appropriate.

q0962.answer: It follows committee procedure unless it is large.

sources.says: Delegates are free to vote as they see fit except where their unit has given an instruction, which is binding, such as a position on a measure or a vote for certain candidates.

q0963.answer: The delegate must vote as instructed.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The parliamentary functions most directly connected with organizing a convention are performed by the Credentials Committee, the Committee on Standing Rules, and the Program Committee.

q0964.answer: The Credentials, Standing Rules, and Program Committees.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The Credentials Committee prepares and certifies to the convention the list of officers, delegates, and alternates it has registered after finding them entitled to accreditation.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The parliamentarian advises at convention meetings, seated next to the presiding officer, but the most important work may well be performed before the convention opens.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Before a convention can transact business, it must officially form itself into a single voting body at its first business meeting. Preliminary ceremonies aren’t business.

q0967.answer: Officially form itself into a single voting body.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: A convention is organized by adopting the reports of the Credentials Committee, the Committee on Standing Rules, and the Program Committee, in that order.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The reports of the Credentials Committee, the Committee on Standing Rules, and the Program Committee are considered and adopted separately, in that order.

q0969.answer: Credentials, Standing Rules, and Program Committees.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The Credentials Committee sends each constituent body, well in advance, information on its authorized number of representatives and alternates, eligibility requirements, and how and when to elect them, along with credentials forms.

q0970.answer: Send each constituent body information about its number of representatives and eligibility.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: If a delegate is found ineligible, for instance for nonpayment of dues, the Credentials Committee advises the unit of its right to designate one of its elected alternates in that delegate’s place.

q0971.answer: Advise the chapter it may designate an alternate instead.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Registration normally involves the member submitting evidence of entitlement, the committee verifying the credentials, recording the member as registered on paying any fee and signing the list, and issuing the proper badge and program.

q0972.answer: Sending the secretary a list of members who haven’t paid dues isn’t a registration step.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Before the Credentials Committee report is adopted, the only motions in order are those related to its consideration or the conduct of the meeting, and those allowed without a quorum. Even a motion about the validity of holding the convention isn’t in order.
Even without a quorum, the assembly may recess, adjourn, or fix the time to which to adjourn.

q0973.answer: A motion to Recess is in order.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The Credentials Committee report states the total number of convention members entitled to vote and the number of registered alternates. The list of names is normally not read unless requested.

q0974.answer: The total number of voting members and the number of registered alternates.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Unless there is debate or a proposed amendment, the chair, before voting on the report, asks “Are there any questions on the report?”

q0975.answer: The chair asks if there are questions on the report.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: When the Credentials Committee report is adopted, it is ratified as the official roll of voting members of the convention, subject to later reports.

q0976.answer: The roll of voting members of the convention.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: A voting member who registers after the first report assumes full status as soon as they register, if their status isn’t questioned.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: If the bylaws or convention standing rules don’t set a quorum, it is a majority of the voting members who have registered as attending, whether or not some have left.

q0978.answer: A majority of the registered delegates, including any who have left.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The standing rules of a convention apply to that one convention only. They can’t conflict with the bylaws but may modify rules in the parliamentary authority, and they usually include both parliamentary rules about conducting business and nonparliamentary rules.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: A convention is organized by adopting the reports of the Credentials Committee, the Committee on Standing Rules, and the Program Committee. The credentials and program reports need a majority vote; the standing rules report normally needs two-thirds.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: A set of proposed standing rules needs a two-thirds vote whenever it includes any rule that would need two-thirds if voted on by itself. Because convention standing rules nearly always include such provisions, adopting them as a package normally takes two-thirds.

q0979.answer: Convention standing rules contain both parliamentary and nonparliamentary rules. They aren’t presented by the Credentials Committee (they come from the Committee on Standing Rules), which also rules out “All of the above.”
q0979.conflict: Going by 59:34, the “package” statement is normally true as well, since a package of convention standing rules almost always needs two-thirds. Dunbar keys the first choice because that one isn’t guaranteed in every case, so expect it to be marked correct.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: “The Standing Rules of the Convention” apply to that one convention only. They can’t conflict with the bylaws but can modify rules in the parliamentary authority.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Convention standing rules that would need two-thirds individually are those that would need two-thirds in an ordinary assembly, such as a rule limiting debate time. Rules about badges or report format need only a majority.

q0981.answer: Limiting speeches to two minutes would need two-thirds.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: A convention standing rule is individually adoptable by majority vote if it could be an ordinary standing rule, such as rules on wearing badges or the format of written reports.

q0982.answer: A rule on the format of written reports.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Amending or rescinding a convention standing rule normally takes two-thirds or a majority of registered voting members, but a rule adoptable by majority can be amended by majority after notice on at least the preceding day.

q0983.answer: A majority after notice on at least the preceding day.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Any convention standing rule, except one prescribing the parliamentary authority, can be suspended for a specified purpose by a majority vote.

q0984.answer: The one prescribing the parliamentary authority.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: When the convention adopts the program, it becomes the order of business for the entire convention session.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: When the invocation, national anthem, and Pledge of Allegiance are all in the opening ceremonies, they should be in that order: invocation first and pledge last.

q0986.answer: The Pledge of Allegiance is last.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: At a convention, officers report in the order listed in the bylaws, and action on the auditors’ report should immediately follow the treasurer’s report.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Business unfinished at the end of a convention day is normally taken up after the reading of the minutes (or after opening, if minutes aren’t read) when business resumes the next day.

q0988.answer: After the reading of the minutes.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Nominations and elections of officers should take place relatively early in the convention if possible, so there is time for further balloting if needed.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The reports of the Credentials Committee and the Program Committee are adopted by a majority vote. The standing rules normally need two-thirds.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Changing the program after adoption requires two-thirds, a majority of registered voting members, or unanimous consent, which is usually easy to get when a departure is justified.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Voting members should always be seated in a separate section if other people are assigned seats on the convention floor.

q0992.answer: Seat the voting members in a separate section.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: The Resolutions Committee, also called the Reference Committee or sometimes the Platform Committee, screens all original main motions not screened by another committee.

q0993.answer: The Resolutions, Reference, or Platform Committee.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Depending on its authority, the Resolutions Committee may put resolutions in proper form, eliminate duplication, arrange related resolutions in logical sequence, and, in some cases, make substantive changes with the sponsor’s consent. It recommends action; the convention decides.

q0994.answer: Adopting resolutions for the convention isn’t within its power.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Unless the rules say otherwise, the Resolutions Committee must report all resolutions referred to it, though it may report one with “no recommendation.”

q0995.answer: It must report all resolutions referred to it.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: In a platform with a preamble, each paragraph begins with a participle, such as “Believing in the…”, instead of “Whereas.”

sources.section: §60 Conventions Not of a Permanent Society
sources.says: A convention called for a specific purpose not involving a permanent organization is like a mass meeting in that it has no bylaws or officers when called to order, and without bylaws it may be harder to determine the properly appointed delegates.

sources.section: §60 Conventions Not of a Permanent Society
sources.says: Someone designated by the sponsoring group, sometimes the chairman of the Convention Arrangements Committee, calls the meeting to order and presides until a temporary chairman is elected.

q0998.answer: The chairman of the Convention Arrangements Committee.

sources.section: §60 Conventions Not of a Permanent Society
sources.says: After the elected temporary chairman takes the chair, a temporary secretary is elected.

sources.section: §60 Conventions Not of a Permanent Society
sources.says: After temporary officers are elected, the Credentials, Rules, and Program Committees are appointed or their prior selection ratified. Until the Credentials report is adopted, no other business may be considered.

q1000.answer: Authorizing or ratifying the appointment of the Credentials, Rules, and Program Committees.

sources.section: §60 Conventions Not of a Permanent Society
sources.says: If a convention is called to form a permanent organization, permanent officers aren’t elected until after the bylaws are adopted, though a resolution declaring the intent to form the organization is adopted early.
Punishments a society can impose generally include censure, fine (if authorized in the bylaws), suspension, or expulsion. The extreme penalty is expulsion.
Formal disciplinary procedures should generally be regarded as a drastic step reserved for serious situations. It is usually best to first try to resolve the matter quietly and informally.

q1003.answer: A drastic step reserved for serious situations.

sources.says: Nonmembers can be excluded from part or all of a meeting by a ruling of the chair in cases of disorder, by adopting a rule on the subject, or by an appropriate motion, which is a question of privilege.
All persons present at a meeting are obliged to obey the legitimate orders of the presiding officer, though members can appeal, move to suspend the rules, or move to reconsider.

q1005.answer: Obey the presiding officer’s legitimate orders.

sources.says: For a slight breach of order, such as once straying from the merits of the pending question, the chair simply raps lightly, points out the fault, and advises the member to avoid it.

q1006.answer: Rap lightly, point out the fault, and advise the member to stay on topic.

sources.says: For a more serious breach, the chair or any other member can call the member to order.
A member who notices a harmful breach of order rises and, without waiting for recognition, addresses the chair.

q1007.answer: The member doesn’t need to be recognized by the chair.

sources.says: In cases of obstinate or grave breach of order, the chair can, after repeated warnings, “name” the offender, which amounts to preferring charges and should be used only in extreme circumstances.
The chair can’t impose a penalty, but the assembly can.

q1008.answer: The member committed a serious breach, the chair is preferring charges, and the assembly may impose a penalty.

sources.says: For an offense against the assembly during a meeting, no formal trial is needed if any penalty is imposed promptly, since the witnesses are all present and form the body deciding the penalty.

q1009.answer: No formal trial with witnesses is needed.

sources.says: The chair has no authority to impose a penalty or order an offending member removed from the hall, but the assembly has that power.

q1010.answer: By a vote of the assembly.

sources.says: On the demand of a single member (other than the named offender), the vote on imposing a penalty must be taken by ballot, unless the penalty is only an apology or censure.

q1011.answer: One member can require the vote on a penalty to be by ballot.

sources.says: The chair alone can require nonmembers to leave or order their removal at any time, and nonmembers have no right to appeal that order.
If someone refuses to leave, the chair can have a committee or the sergeant-at-arms escort them out.

sources.section: §62 Removal from Office and Other Remedies for Dereliction of
sources.says: If the chair ignores a properly made, nondilatory motion or violates any other rule, any member may immediately raise a Point of Order.

sources.section: §62 Removal from Office and Other Remedies for Dereliction of
sources.says: If the chair ignores a point of order three times, the member can put it to a vote. If the point was that the chair improperly ignored a motion, the maker may instead put that motion to a vote from the floor.

q1014.answer: The maker of the motion can put it to a vote from the floor.

sources.section: §62 Removal from Office and Other Remedies for Dereliction of
sources.says: If the chair ignores a properly made and seconded appeal, the member can repeat it, and if it is ignored a third time after being seconded, the member can, standing in place, put the appeal to a vote without debate.

q1015.answer: The member can put the appeal to a vote without debate.

sources.section: §62 Removal from Office and Other Remedies for Dereliction of
sources.says: If the offending occupant of the chair is an appointed or elected chairman pro tem, a motion can be made to “declare the chair vacant and proceed to elect a new chairman.” It is a question of privilege affecting the assembly.

q1016.answer: Move to declare the chair vacant and elect a new chairman.

sources.says: A society may investigate its members, but information obtained may not be made public, so a trial must always be held in executive session, as must the resolutions leading up to it.
A society’s trial cannot legally establish guilt as a court would. It can only establish guilt as it affects the society’s judgment of the person’s fitness for membership or office.

q1018.answer: It establishes guilt only as to fitness for membership.

sources.says: The basic steps of fair disciplinary process are: confidential investigation by a committee; the committee’s report and preferral of charges if warranted; formal notification of the accused; trial; and assembly review of a trial committee’s findings.

q1019.answer: An outside investigation by police, auditors, or detectives isn’t one of the steps.

sources.says: A committee selected for integrity and good judgment conducts a confidential investigation, including trying to interview the accused, to decide whether further action such as charges is warranted.

q1020.answer: A confidential investigation by a select committee.

sources.says: The trial is a formal hearing on the validity of the charges. The accused has the right to be represented by counsel, to speak, and to produce witnesses in their own defense.

q1021.answer: The false statement is that the accused can’t call witnesses.

sources.says: If the accused fails to appear for trial at the appointed time as directed, the trial proceeds without them.

q1022.answer: The trial proceeds without the accused.

sources.says: In calling the trial meeting to order, the chair should point out that the meeting is in executive session and that the obligation of secrecy applies.

q1023.answer: Remind everyone the meeting is in executive session and secret.

sources.says: After the preliminary steps, the trial proceeds: first, the chair directs the secretary to read the charge and specifications; then the chair asks the accused how they plead.

q1024.answer: The chair directs the secretary to read the charges.

sources.says: The secretary reads the charges, the accused pleads, and if the plea is not guilty the trial begins with opening statements by both sides, managers first, followed by witnesses.
After closing arguments the accused leaves the room, and each specification and then the charge is read, opened to debate, and voted on separately, though the votes can be taken on a single ballot.

q1026.answer: Each charge is opened to debate and voted on separately.

sources.says: A trial committee reports its findings to the assembly in executive session, with resolutions recommending a penalty if it finds guilt.
After the accused may respond, the assembly acts on the committee’s resolutions.

q1027.answer: The assembly votes on the committee’s resolutions.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: The privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn takes precedence over all other motions.

q1028.answer: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: The main motion, which takes precedence over nothing, ranks lowest in the order of precedence.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The privileged motions in ascending rank are: Call for the Orders of the Day, Raise a Question of Privilege, Recess, Adjourn, and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q1030.answer: Call for the Orders of the Day.

sources.says: When Amend is applied to a motion other than a main motion, it takes precedence over the motion it proposes to amend.
Recess takes precedence over the main motion and all subsidiary and incidental motions, and yields to a motion to Amend applied to it.

q1031.answer: An amendment to the motion to Recess outranks the Recess itself, and therefore everything else listed.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The subsidiary motions are listed in ascending rank: Postpone Indefinitely, Amend, Commit, Postpone to a Certain Time, Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, Previous Question, and Lay on the Table.
The privileged motions are all undebatable, because their high privilege would let debate interfere with business.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day is not debatable.
For the two lowest-ranking privileged motions, it is the “calling” or “raising” that is undebatable.

q1034.answer: Call for the Orders of the Day.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely is debatable, and debate can go fully into the merits of the main question.
The privileged motions, including raising a question of privilege and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn, are undebatable.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: All subsidiary motions can be amended except Postpone Indefinitely, the Previous Question, and Lay on the Table.
Motions to Amend can be applied to the motion to Commit.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: All subsidiary motions can be amended except Postpone Indefinitely, the Previous Question, and Lay on the Table.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: The main motion ranks lowest, the subsidiary motions (including Amend) rank above it, and the privileged motions (including Adjourn) rank above all subsidiary motions.
Recess outranks the main motion and all subsidiary motions, but yields to Adjourn and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: The main motion, which takes precedence over nothing, ranks lowest of all.
The privileged motion to Adjourn takes precedence over all motions except Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q1040.answer: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.says: Motions to Amend, to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, and for the Previous Question can be applied to Commit without affecting the main question.
A main motion yields to all subsidiary motions (such as Amend and the Previous Question), all privileged motions (such as Adjourn), and applicable incidental motions.

q1042.answer: All of those can be made while a main motion is pending.

sources.says: Motions to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate and for the Previous Question can be applied to a pending primary or secondary amendment.
Postpone Indefinitely can be made only while the main question is immediately pending.

q1043.answer: Limit Debate can be moved with an amendment pending. A new main motion or Postpone Indefinitely can’t.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely can be made only while a main question is immediately pending, since it ranks below Amend.

q1044.answer: Postpone Indefinitely is out of order while an amendment is pending.

sources.says: The Previous Question takes precedence over all debatable or amendable motions it applies to and over Limit or Extend Limits of Debate.
The privileged motion to Recess takes precedence over the main motion and all subsidiary and incidental motions.

q1045.answer: A recess for five minutes is in order. The other motions rank below the pending Previous Question.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: When several motions are pending, the one most recently stated by the chair is the immediately pending question.
An amendment applied to another motion, such as Recess, takes precedence over the motion it amends.

q1046.answer: The amendment to the motion to Recess is immediately pending, as it outranks all the others.

sources.says: Recess takes precedence over the main motion and all subsidiary motions, including Commit and Postpone to a Certain Time.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: The highest-ranking motion made most recently is the immediately pending question.
Ordering the Previous Question prevents other subsidiary motions except Lay on the Table, but doesn’t prevent privileged or incidental motions.

q1048.answer: Refer is out of order. Recess, Adjourn, and a Parliamentary Inquiry are still allowed.

sources.says: No subsidiary motion can be applied to the motion to Lay on the Table.
Lay on the Table takes precedence over the main motion, all other subsidiary motions, and pending incidental motions, and yields to all privileged motions.
Postpone Indefinitely takes precedence over nothing but the main question, so it can’t be made while an amendment is pending.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: Pending motions are voted on beginning with the immediately pending one, the most recently stated, highest-ranking motion.
The Previous Question outranks Limit Debate, Postpone Indefinitely, and the main motion.

q1052.answer: The Previous Question is voted on first.

sources.says: Raising a Question of Privilege yields only to the higher-ranking privileged motions: Recess, Adjourn, and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q1053.answer: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.says: A main motion requires a second, is out of order when another has the floor, is debatable and amendable, and normally needs a majority vote.

q1054.answer: It must be seconded. It need not be debated and needs only a majority.

sources.says: A motion to adjourn that isn’t privileged is treated like any other incidental main motion.
A main motion must be seconded, is debatable and amendable, and requires a majority vote.

q1055.answer: As a main motion, adjournment is debatable and amendable.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: A standing rule can be adopted by a majority vote without previous notice, as long as it doesn’t conflict with an existing rule.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: A convention standing rule needs two-thirds individually if, in an ordinary society, it would need two-thirds, such as a rule limiting debate. These are “parliamentary standing rules.” Others can be adopted by majority, like ordinary standing rules.

q1057.answer: Parliamentary standing rules in a convention require a two-thirds vote, while ordinary standing rules need only a majority.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The subsidiary motions are Postpone Indefinitely, Amend, Commit, Postpone to a Certain Time, Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, Previous Question, and Lay on the Table.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Appeal and Consideration by Paragraph are incidental motions, and Adjourn is privileged.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day doesn’t require a second.
The privileged motion to Adjourn must be seconded, as must Postpone Indefinitely and Rescind.

q1059.answer: Call for the Orders of the Day.

sources.says: Amend is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, is debatable only when the motion it applies to is, is itself amendable, and requires a majority vote, with no notice.

q1060.answer: The false statement is that it requires notice. It needs only a majority vote.

sources.says: The subsidiary motion to Amend, whether primary or secondary, must be seconded and requires a majority vote, regardless of the vote needed for the motion being amended.

q1061.answer: All three are true of both.

sources.says: Rescind and Amend Something Previously Adopted are incidental main motions that must be seconded and are debatable, with debate going into the merits of what they would change.
The subsidiary motion to Amend is debatable only when the motion it applies to is debatable.

q1062.answer: Amend Something Previously Adopted is always debatable, while an amendment to a pending motion isn’t always.

sources.says: Rescind and Amend Something Previously Adopted are two forms of one incidental main motion.

q1063.answer: It is an incidental main motion.

sources.section: §59 Organization of a Convention of an Established Society
sources.says: Amending or rescinding a convention standing rule requires a two-thirds vote or a majority of all registered voting members, with an exception for rules adoptable by majority.

q1064.answer: Two-thirds, or a majority of the registered voting members.

sources.says: An Appeal is in order when another has the floor and must be seconded. It is undebatable when it relates to the priority of business.

q1065.answer: It may interrupt a member speaking.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: An Objection to the Consideration of a Question doesn’t require a second and is neither debatable nor amendable.

q1066.answer: Objection to the Consideration of a Question.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The motion to consider a question informally is a variation of the motion to Commit.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists “Consider informally” as a subsidiary motion.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists “Consider informally” as requiring a majority vote for adoption.

q1068.answer: A majority of those present and voting.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The motion to consider a question informally must be seconded, and is debatable only as to whether to consider the question informally.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists “Consider informally” as out of order when another has the floor, requiring a second, debatable, amendable, and needing a majority vote.

q1069.answer: Dunbar’s key says it is unamendable.
q1069.conflict: RONR 12th ed.’s Table of Rules Relating to Motions lists “Consider informally” as amendable. The other choices are clearly wrong (it needs a second, is debatable, and can’t interrupt a speaker), so the key likely reflects an older reading.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, isn’t debatable, is amendable, and requires a two-thirds vote.

q1070.answer: The false statement is that a member may interrupt a speaker to propose it.

sources.says: Division of a Question is an incidental motion. It takes precedence over the main motion and over Postpone Indefinitely.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Commit (Refer) is a subsidiary motion. Reconsider and Take from the Table are among the motions that bring a question again before the assembly.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: A Point of Order is listed among the incidental motions, raised when a member believes the chair is failing to enforce the rules.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely, Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, and the Previous Question are subsidiary motions.

q1072.answer: Point of Order is never a subsidiary motion.

sources.says: The motion to Commit is debatable, but debate is limited to whether it’s desirable to commit the main question and to the details of the motion to Commit. It doesn’t extend to the merits of the main question.

q1073.answer: Debate must stay on the motion to Commit itself, not the main question.

sources.says: Discharging a committee requires a two-thirds vote, a majority vote with previous notice, or a majority of the entire membership.

q1074.answer: Any of the three votes will do.

sources.says: A Division of the Assembly is in order when another has the floor, doesn’t require a second, isn’t debatable, and isn’t amendable.

q1075.answer: It allows no debate, no amendment, and needs no second.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists Division of the Assembly as an incidental motion that is not debatable, needs no second, and is in order when another has the floor.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table lists Division of a Question as an incidental motion that is not debatable, must be seconded, is amendable, needs a majority, and is out of order when another has the floor.

sources.section: §30 Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
sources.says: Motions about methods of voting are out of order when another has the floor, though a member can claim preference in recognition to make one right after a vote. They must be seconded, aren’t debatable, are amendable, and require a majority.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says motions relating to voting (other than closing or reopening the polls) can be reconsidered.

q1077.answer: Dunbar’s key says the maker may interrupt a speaker to propose a counted vote.
q1077.conflict: Under RONR 12th ed., a motion for a counted vote can’t interrupt a speaker. It gets only preference in recognition right after a vote. It is undebatable and needs a majority, and it can be reconsidered, which makes that choice the better fit under the 12th edition.

sources.says: The incidental motion for Division of a Question must be seconded, isn’t debatable, is amendable, and requires a majority vote.

q1078.answer: All three are true: majority vote, needs a second, and amendable.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Among the incidental motions, a member who doubts the chair’s announcement of a voice vote can demand a Division of the Assembly, forcing a rising vote.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Lay on the Table is a subsidiary motion, while Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn and Call for the Orders of the Day are privileged motions.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says Division of a Question must be seconded.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table says the Previous Question must be seconded.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table says Discharge a Committee must be seconded.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn, when moved while a question is pending, as a privileged motion requiring a majority vote.

q1081.answer: A majority of those present and voting.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists a Request for Information as needing no second, undebatable, unamendable, and not voted on.

q1082.answer: None, because a Point of Information is not voted on.

sources.says: Lay on the Table is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, isn’t debatable, isn’t amendable, and needs a majority. An affirmative vote on it can’t be reconsidered, since the question can simply be taken from the table.

q1083.answer: It can’t interrupt another member who has the floor.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: A formal motion to approve the minutes isn’t necessary, though it isn’t out of order. The chair asks for corrections, which are usually handled by unanimous consent.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When no more corrections are offered, the chair declares the minutes approved. They’re approved without a formal vote, even if a motion to approve was made.

q1084.answer: Dunbar’s key says the motion is adopted by a majority vote.
q1084.conflict: RONR 12th ed. says minutes are approved without a formal vote even when a motion to approve is made (41:11), and Table II says such a motion “is not voted on.” The other choices are still wrong: the motion needs a second, is debatable, and can’t interrupt a speaker.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists a motion to dispense with the reading of the minutes as an incidental motion that must be seconded, isn’t debatable or amendable, and requires a majority vote.

q1085.answer: A majority of the members present and voting.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says Lay on the Table must be seconded, isn’t debatable, and isn’t amendable.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table says Take from the Table must be seconded, isn’t debatable, and isn’t amendable.

q1086.answer: All three are true of both.

sources.says: A Point of Order is ruled on by the chair without a vote in the normal case. It is in order when another has the floor and needs no second.
Requests and inquiries are in order when another has the floor if they need immediate attention, and a Parliamentary Inquiry needs no second.

q1087.answer: Both may be made when another member has the floor.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: An Objection to the Consideration of a Question doesn’t require a second and is neither debatable nor amendable.

q1088.answer: It is not seconded, debated, or amended.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day, if in order at the time, can be made when another has the floor, even interrupting a speaker. It doesn’t need a second, isn’t debatable, and isn’t amendable.

q1089.answer: None of the statements are true.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: When a single member calls for the orders of the day, they must be enforced. The assembly can set them aside only by a two-thirds vote.

q1090.answer: No vote is needed to adopt it, because a single member’s call requires the orders to be followed.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules describes the Previous Question as a motion to close debate immediately and to stop the making of subsidiary motions except Lay on the Table. It needs a two-thirds vote.

q1091.answer: Debate ends on the motions it applies to, and the assembly moves to a vote.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists Postpone Indefinitely as a subsidiary motion that must be seconded, is debatable, isn’t amendable, and needs a majority.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table lists Postpone to a Certain Time as a subsidiary motion that must be seconded, is debatable and amendable, and needs a majority unless it makes a special order.

Debate on Commit and Postpone to a Certain Time is quite limited, because the main question will be open to debate again later. Debate is confined to whether and how to postpone or commit, not the merits of the main question.

q1093.answer: The chair should politely remind the member that debate is limited to the motion to postpone.

sources.says: A main motion that becomes pending after being admitted as a question of privilege can be amended, like other main motions.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists a question of privilege in the form of a main motion as a main motion, so it must be seconded and is debatable and amendable.

The privileged motion to Recess is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, isn’t debatable, is amendable only as to the length of the recess, needs a majority, and can’t be reconsidered.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says a motion to recess made while business is pending is privileged, not debatable, amendable, and needs a majority.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table says a motion to recess made while no question is pending is a main motion, debatable and amendable, and needs a majority.

q1096.answer: The main motion to recess is debatable, and the privileged one is not.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Recess, Adjourn, and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn each have a corresponding incidental main motion of the same name.
A motion to recess made when no question is pending is a main motion, and the characteristics of the privileged motion don’t apply to it.

q1097.answer: It is an incidental main motion.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says a motion to recess made while no question is pending must be seconded, is debatable and amendable, and needs a majority.

q1098.answer: It still needs to be seconded.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists Reconsider as a motion that brings a question again before the assembly. It must be seconded, isn’t amendable, needs a majority vote, and can’t itself be reconsidered.
Rescind and Amend Something Previously Adopted are two forms of one incidental main motion. Rescind is also known as Repeal or Annul.

q1100.answer: Annul, Repeal, and Rescind are all names for the same incidental main motion.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Take from the Table and Reconsider are classed only as motions that bring a question again before the assembly and don’t fit well in any other class.

q1101.answer: It is a motion that brings a question again before the assembly.

sources.says: Rescind requires a majority vote with previous notice, a two-thirds vote, or a majority of the entire membership.
Without previous notice, the motion to rescind requires a two-thirds vote or a majority of the entire membership.

q1102.answer: Any of the three votes will do.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says a motion to suspend ordinary standing rules must be seconded, isn’t debatable or amendable, and requires a majority vote.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: By contrast, suspending rules of order generally takes a two-thirds vote.

q1103.answer: A majority of the members present and voting.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says Take from the Table must be seconded, isn’t debatable or amendable, and requires a majority vote.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says a motion to grant permission to withdraw or modify a motion, after the chair has stated it, needs a second if the person asking permission makes it, but not if another member does.

q1105.answer: It needs a second when made by the member requesting permission.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says a motion relating to voting made while no question is pending is a main motion. It is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, is debatable and amendable, and needs a majority.
Forms for a motion to adjourn include “I move to adjourn” or “I move that the meeting adjourn.”
When words go at the end of a passage, the motion is made as one to add, such as “I move to amend by adding the words….” Inserting is used for placing words elsewhere.

sources.section: §62 Removal from Office and Other Remedies for Dereliction of
sources.says: A member who disagrees with a ruling rises right away and, without waiting for recognition, says “I appeal from the decision of the chair.”

q1109.answer: “I appeal from the decision of the chair.”

sources.says: A member can move that a blank be created, as in a motion “to create a blank by striking out” a sum from the pending resolution.

q1110.answer: “I move to create a blank by striking out ‘$500.’”

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: To consider a question informally, a member moves “that the question be considered informally.” It is a variation of the motion to Commit.
The variations of Commit let the full assembly consider a question with the freedom of debate allowed in committees, meaning no limit on the number of times a member can speak.

q1111.answer: “I move that the question be considered informally.”

sources.says: Any member, without a second, can demand that a voice vote be retaken as a rising vote. Without obtaining the floor, the member calls out “Division!”
When a Division is demanded, the chair retakes the vote by rising and may count it. A member who wants the division counted must make a motion to that effect.
No single member can force a count. A member who thinks one is desirable should move that the vote be counted, and the motion needs a second and a majority.

q1113.answer: Any of these forms asking that the vote be counted will do.

sources.says: A member may say “I have a request for information” or “A point of information, please,” and the chair asks them to state the question.
If the information is wanted from a member who is speaking, the inquirer may instead ask whether the member will yield for a question.

q1114.answer: Any of the three forms is correct.

sources.says: The forms are “I move to lay the question on the table” or “I move that the resolution be laid on the table.” Moving “to table” or “that the motion be tabled” is better avoided.

q1115.answer: “I move that the motion be laid on the table.”

sources.says: If the assembly doesn’t want to read and approve the minutes at the regular time, it can “dispense with the reading of the minutes” by majority vote without debate. The minutes can then be taken up later in the meeting while no business is pending.

q1116.answer: “I move that the reading of the minutes be dispensed with.”

sources.says: A member who notices a breach of order rises and, without waiting for recognition, says “I rise to a point of order” or “Point of order!”
If the point concerns a breach of the rules of debate, the member may say “I call the gentleman to order.”

q1117.answer: “Order, order!” is not a correct form.

sources.says: The form is “I move the previous question.” Members calling out “Question!” from their seats aren’t moving the Previous Question, and it’s disorderly if another member is speaking or seeking recognition.
One usual form of this motion is “I move to suspend the rules and take up….”

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says taking up a question out of its proper order is done by suspending the rules.

q1119.answer: “I move to suspend the rules and take up….”

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says a Request for Information is in order when another has the floor and needs no second.
