Raising a question of privilege is in order when another has the floor if the urgency of the situation calls for it.
When the question of privilege has been handled, business resumes where it was interrupted, and a member who had the floor gets it back.

sources.section: List IV, Motions and Parliamentary Steps by Floor and Second
sources.says: RONR’s list of motions by floor and second places Appeal among those in order when another has the floor but that must be seconded.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: An Objection to the Consideration of a Question is in order when another has the floor only until consideration of the question has begun. It doesn’t require a second and isn’t debatable.

q1123.answer: Objection to the Consideration of a Question.

sources.section: List IV, Motions and Parliamentary Steps by Floor and Second
sources.says: RONR’s list of motions by floor and second lists making Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes as in order when another has been assigned the floor but hasn’t begun to speak. Calling up a motion to Reconsider is listed as out of order when another has the floor and needs no second.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says the motion to Reconsider itself must be seconded.

q1124.answer: Dunbar’s key says Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes.
q1124.conflict: In RONR 12th ed., making Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes can be done after another member is assigned the floor (before they speak) and must be seconded. The step that is out of order when another has the floor and needs no second is calling up a motion to reconsider.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says Commit or Refer is debatable and amendable, while the Previous Question, Suspend the Rules, and Take from the Table are none of those.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists Take from the Table as neither debatable nor amendable.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table lists Consider by Paragraph or Seriatim as not debatable but amendable.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate isn’t debatable but is amendable, and any amendment to it is also undebatable. It requires a two-thirds vote.

q1127.answer: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate.

sources.says: Postpone Indefinitely is debatable, and debate can go fully into the merits of the main question, but it isn’t amendable.

sources.section: List V, Motions and Parliamentary Steps by Debate and Amendment
sources.says: RONR’s list of motions on which debate can go into the merits of the main question includes Amend Something Previously Adopted, Discharge a Committee, Postpone Indefinitely, Ratify, Reconsider a debatable motion, and Rescind.

q1129.answer: All of the listed motions open the main question to debate.

sources.says: Without previous notice, Amend Something Previously Adopted requires a two-thirds vote or a majority of the entire membership.
An amendment to a pending motion needs only a majority, whatever vote the underlying motion needs.

q1130.answer: Amend Something Previously Adopted (when no notice was given).

sources.says: An amendment, primary or secondary, requires a majority vote regardless of the vote needed for the question being amended.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A two-thirds vote is required for motions that suspend a rule of order or close, limit, or extend debate.

q1131.answer: A secondary amendment needs only a majority.

sources.says: Raising a question of privilege is ruled on by the chair, and no vote on its admissibility is taken unless the ruling is appealed.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says closing nominations requires a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §30 Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
sources.says: A motion to close the polls requires a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn can be reconsidered.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table says a privileged motion to recess can’t be reconsidered, and neither can Division of a Question or Suspend the Rules.

q1133.answer: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says Take from the Table can’t be reconsidered.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says for Postpone Indefinitely, only an affirmative vote can be reconsidered.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says only a negative vote on Consider Informally can be reconsidered.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table says only a negative vote on Discharge a Committee can be reconsidered.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table says only a negative vote on Rescind can be reconsidered.

q1136.answer: All three allow reconsideration of a negative vote.

sources.says: A ballot is credited to the voter’s choice if its meaning is clear and the choice is valid. Unintelligible ballots are illegal votes, counted as cast but credited to no one.
Doubtful ballots can be treated as illegal if they can’t possibly affect the result.
Two or more filled-out ballots folded together count as one illegal vote and aren’t credited.

q1137.answer: Dunbar’s key says none of the three is credited.
q1137.conflict: Under RONR 12th ed., a clear ballot for one eligible candidate is credited to that candidate (45:32). Only the unclear ballot and the folded-together ballots go uncredited.

sources.says: Only ballots that indicate a preference count toward the votes cast. A blank ballot shows no preference, so it isn’t credited to any candidate.

q1138.answer: It is not credited to any candidate.

sources.says: The original author wrote that the majority should give the minority a full chance to make its case, and the minority, having lost, should accept the decision as the whole organization’s action and help carry it out until it can get it repealed.

q1139.answer: A member who disagrees is not withdrawn from the society.

sources.says: Previous notice means notice of the proposal, briefly describing it, must be announced at the preceding meeting or included in the call of the meeting where it will be considered.

q1140.answer: It must be included in the call of the meeting.

sources.says: Everyone who attends a mass meeting has the right to participate as a member, on the understanding that they generally support the meeting’s purpose as stated in the call.

q1141.answer: Everyone who attends and supports the meeting’s purpose.

sources.says: A large attendance isn’t an essential feature of a mass meeting, though it’s usually wanted.

q1142.answer: It doesn’t need a large attendance to function.

sources.says: The assembly of a local club or local branch of an organized permanent society is the type the average person is most likely to experience directly.

q1143.answer: A local branch of an organized permanent society.

sources.says: An ordinary convention rarely lasts more than a week, but in principle there’s no limit on the session’s length. A constitutional convention may go on for weeks or months.
When a society’s next convention meets a year or two later, it is a new assembly.

q1144.answer: The false statement is that a state society’s convention can’t last more than a week.

sources.says: A legislative body is made up of representatives elected for a fixed term. It usually has two houses, its sessions may last months, and members can be legally compelled to attend.

q1145.answer: It usually has two houses, and its sessions may last for months.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: The recommended practice is to combine these rules into a single document, usually called the “bylaws.” In this book, “bylaws” means that combined document, whatever the organization calls it.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Bylaws define the organization’s primary characteristics, prescribe how it functions, and include the rules it considers too important to change without notice and a larger vote.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Typical bylaw articles cover name, object, members, officers, meetings, board, committees, parliamentary authority, and amendment. The list covers offices, not the people holding them.

q1147.answer: The names of the current officers don’t belong in the bylaws.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: The articles found in the bylaws of a typical society cover, in order: the name of the organization, its object, members, officers, meetings, the executive board (if needed), committees, the parliamentary authority, and how the bylaws are amended.

q1148.answer: The first letters spell N-O-M-O-M-E-C-P-A, so the two M’s are Members and Meetings.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: A corporate charter sets out the society’s name and object.
The article on the object, like the one on the name, can be left out of the bylaws in incorporated societies.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: When an organization has both a constitution and bylaws as separate documents, the constitution is the higher of the two and supersedes the bylaws.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Special rules of order are adopted separately from the bylaws. They should be printed in the same booklet but under a separate heading.

q1151.answer: In the same booklet but under a separate heading.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Standing rules usually aren’t adopted when a society is organized. They’re adopted one at a time, if and when the need arises.

q1152.answer: Individually, if and when the need arises.

sources.says: Under the U.S. Constitution, the quorum in both houses of Congress is a majority of the members.
A quorum is the number of members who must be present for business to be validly transacted. It is based on members present.
Officers who are members of the assembly have the full rights of members.

q1154.answer: They are counted in deciding whether a quorum is present.

sources.says: A society’s president is addressed as “Mr. President” or “Madam President,” whether the woman is married or not.
By long usage, someone presiding who has no regular title, or whose position is only temporary, is addressed as “Mr. Chairman” or “Madam Chairman.”
The chair generally avoids using members’ names, but in ordinary lay assemblies it’s common to name members when assigning the floor, appointing committees, and similar occasions.
When the chair appoints a committee, the first member named is its chairman, and the chair should specifically say so.

q1157.answer: All three are occasions when naming a member is appropriate.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: The standard order of business is: minutes; reports of officers, boards, and standing committees; reports of special committees; special orders; unfinished business and general orders; new business.

q1158.answer: Reports of Officers, Boards, and Standing Committees.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Adopting an agenda or program for each session is customary in conventions and other sessions lasting several days.
The main motion is the basic form of motion, and the only one whose introduction brings business before the assembly.
A motion to receive a communication or committee report means only allowing the paper to be read. Such a motion isn’t customary.

q1161.answer: It means the report will be read to the assembly.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: The chair normally recognizes a member by announcing, as applicable, the member’s name, title, or the place or unit the member represents.
When the chair knows those seeking the floor hold opposite views, the chair alternates as far as possible between those for and against the measure.

q1163.answer: Members who want to speak for and against.

sources.says: If the chair assigns the floor to the wrong person, a Point of Order can call attention to it, and the chair must correct the error.
When a member thinks the assembly’s rules are being violated, a Point of Order calls on the chair for a ruling and enforcement.
A main motion outside the organization’s object as defined in its bylaws is out of order unless the assembly allows it by two-thirds vote.

q1164.answer: A Point of Order can be raised in all three situations.

sources.says: The first step is a member making the motion. The words move and offer also refer to this step.

q1165.answer: All three terms describe the first step.

sources.says: Once a motion that is in order has been made and seconded, the chair formally places it before the assembly by stating the question.
A resolution or long motion should be written out before it is offered, and the mover passes it to the chair as soon as it has been offered.

q1167.answer: It is given to the chair after being offered.

sources.says: If a motion wasn’t heard or isn’t clear, a member can ask that it be repeated. The chair can ask the maker or the secretary to repeat it, or do it personally.

q1168.answer: Any of them may repeat it.

sources.says: In large assemblies, the seconder stands and, without waiting for recognition, gives their name and says “Mr. President [or Chairman], I second the motion.”

q1169.answer: The member stands, gives their name without waiting for recognition, and says “Mr./Madam Chairman, I second the motion.”

sources.says: In some organizations, especially labor unions, members say “support” instead of “second.”
If no one seconds, the chair must be sure everyone heard the motion before moving on, and normally asks “Is there a second to the motion?” In a large hall, the chair may repeat the motion first.

q1171.answer: Repeat the motion and ask “Is there a second to the motion?”

sources.says: If there’s still no second, the chair says the motion is not seconded, then immediately announces the next item of business or asks whether there’s further business.
A motion made on behalf of a board or properly appointed committee needs no second from the floor, as long as that group has more than one person.

q1173.answer: A one-person committee’s motion needs a second.

sources.says: A point of order must be raised promptly when the breach happens. If the chair states a motion that wasn’t seconded, the time to raise the point is when the chair states it.

q1174.answer: Raise a point of order right away.

sources.says: The chair must state the question as soon as a motion is made and seconded, unless the motion is out of order or its wording is unclear.
After a motion is made but before the chair states it, no debate is in order, but a member may ask the maker to accept a modification.
When the maker accepts a modification suggested by another member, the suggester has in effect seconded the modified motion, so no other second is needed.

q1176.answer: The false statement is that the chair must ask for a second after the maker accepts a modification.

sources.says: Each member may speak twice on the same question on the same day. A member who has spoken twice has exhausted the right to debate that question for that day.
That member can still speak twice on each amendment or other debatable motion that comes up.

q1177.answer: The member has spoken twice and can’t speak a third time that day.

sources.says: Speakers must address their remarks to the chair, stay courteous, and avoid personal remarks. They must never attack members’ motives and should avoid using other members’ names.

q1178.answer: Address their remarks to the chair.

sources.says: Except in committees and small boards, the presiding officer doesn’t take part in debate on the merits and normally stays seated while members speak.
The presiding officer can’t close debate while any member who hasn’t used up their right to speak wants the floor. Only a two-thirds vote of the assembly can do that.
For a voice vote, the chair says “Those in favor of the motion, say aye,” pauses, then “Those opposed, say no.” “As many as are in favor” is an acceptable alternative.

q1180.answer: The chair left out the negative cue (“say no”).

sources.says: If the vote was counted, the chair gives the count first, then announces which side has it.
For a counted rising vote, the chair gives the affirmative count, then the negative count, then says “The affirmative has it and the motion is adopted.”

q1182.answer: “There are 20 in the affirmative and 10 in the negative. The affirmative has it and the motion is adopted….”

sources.says: When the affirmative leads by one without the chair’s vote, the chair can vote no to create a tie. A tie means the motion is lost, since a majority wasn’t reached.
If the chair is actually in doubt about a voice vote, the chair doesn’t announce a result but immediately retakes the vote, strictly speaking always as a rising vote, and counts it if it looks close.

q1184.answer: Retake the vote as a rising vote (a division).

sources.says: A vote retaken by rising at a member’s demand is called a Division of the Assembly, or simply “a division.”
The chair may say “If there is no objection…” or ask “Is there any objection…?”, pause, and then announce that since there is no objection the action is taken.

q1186.answer: “Is there any objection…?” (pause) “Since there is no objection, the motion that… is adopted.”

sources.says: When a speaker whose time has expired asks for two more minutes, the chair may ask whether there is any objection, pause, and then announce the time is extended since no one objects.

q1187.answer: “Is there any objection to the member’s time being extended two minutes?” (pause) “The chair hears no objection, and it is so ordered.”

sources.says: When unanimous consent is already apparent, the chair may assume it, such as letting a speaker who is almost done finish.
An action that requires a two-thirds vote can in principle be taken by unanimous consent. Unanimous consent requires a quorum, like any other way of doing business.

q1188.answer: All three statements are true, so none of them is false.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: Subsidiary, privileged, and incidental motions, the second, third, and fourth classes, are together called “secondary motions.”

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Main motions, the first class, are divided into original main motions and incidental main motions. Incidental main motions are separate from incidental motions, which are the fourth class.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: Subsidiary, privileged, and incidental motions together are called secondary motions. Main motions, including original main motions, are a separate class.

q1191.answer: Original main motions are not secondary motions.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: A secondary motion can be made and considered while a main motion is pending, without breaking the one-question-at-a-time principle.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: When a secondary motion is stated, it becomes the immediately pending question, and the main motion stays pending too.

q1192.answer: A secondary motion can be made while a main motion is pending.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: A main motion is the immediately pending question whenever it is pending with no secondary motion.

q1193.answer: When it is pending with no secondary motion.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: If motion B can be made while motion A is pending and, once stated, temporarily replaces A as the immediately pending question, B takes precedence over A, and A yields to B.

q1194.answer: Motion B takes precedence over motion A.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: A main motion takes precedence over nothing and yields to all applicable secondary motions.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: The main motion, seven subsidiary motions, and five privileged motions form an order of precedence. The main motion ranks lowest and the privileged motions rank highest.
Take from the Table can be made only when no question is pending.

q1196.answer: Privileged motions outrank subsidiary motions, main motions, and the motions that bring a question back, which come up only when nothing else is pending.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: Incidental motions have no rank among themselves, and none can be assigned a position in the order of precedence.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Subsidiary motions are applied to another motion while it is pending, and adopting one changes that motion’s status without adopting or rejecting it. They can be applied to any main motion and fit into an order of precedence.

q1198.answer: They fit into an order of precedence.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: When Amend is applied to another subsidiary motion, its rank changes so that it takes precedence over that motion, even if that motion normally ranks higher than Amend.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The four lowest-ranking subsidiary motions can be debated, except that Amend is undebatable when applied to an undebatable motion.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The three highest-ranking subsidiary motions can’t be debated, since debate would defeat their purpose.
No subsidiary motion can be applied to the motion to Lay on the Table.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The Previous Question can be applied to any of the five subsidiary motions that rank below it.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The five privileged motions fit into an order of precedence, and all of them take precedence over motions of every other class, with certain exceptions.
The privileged motion to Recess yields to motions to Amend or for the Previous Question applied to it.

q1203.answer: The false statement is that all subsidiary motions take precedence over privileged motions.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: The order of precedence ranks thirteen motions: the main motion, the seven subsidiary motions, and the five privileged motions.
A member who disagrees with the chair’s ruling can appeal from the decision, which takes the question from the chair and gives the final decision to the assembly.
While an election is pending, a member may move to decide how nominations are made (if the rules don’t say) and may move to close or reopen nominations.

q1206.answer: None of them. All three can be made while an election is pending.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: A Point of Order takes precedence over any pending question it arises from, however high-ranking, but only at the time the breach of order occurs.

q1207.answer: Only at the moment the breach of order happens.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: A point of order arising from a motion to Recess yields only to the two higher-ranking privileged motions, Adjourn and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.
Reconsider can be applied to a vote that either adopted or rejected a motion.
Rescind cancels or countermands an action or order previously adopted, so there must be an adopted measure to rescind.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: Reconsider can be applied to several subsidiary, privileged, or incidental motions. In certain cases, it takes on the character of a secondary motion that can be made and considered while other motions are pending.
A session is a meeting or series of connected meetings devoted to a single order of business, program, agenda, or announced purpose.

q1211.answer: It is usually devoted to a single order of business.

sources.says: Calling the interval between regular sessions a “recess,” as in Congress’s summer recess, is a colloquialism unrelated to the term’s parliamentary meaning.

q1212.answer: It has no connection to the parliamentary meaning of the term.

sources.says: In a session lasting several days, the minutes are normally read at the beginning of the first meeting each day.

q1213.answer: Each day, at the beginning of the first meeting.

sources.says: The next meeting of the session may be set by a program adopted at the start of a convention, by adopting a motion to fix the time to which to adjourn, or by specifying it in a motion to adjourn.
Common expressions include “regular [or ‘stated’] meeting” and “special [or ‘called’] meeting.”
Notice of a special meeting’s time, place, and purpose, clearly describing the business to be brought up, must be sent to all members a reasonable number of days in advance.

q1216.answer: The time, place, and exact purpose.

sources.says: The bylaw provision authorizing special meetings should say who can call them and the number of days’ notice required.

q1217.answer: The number of days’ notice required.

sources.says: In any society, certain disciplinary matters, such as trials, must be handled only in executive session.

q1218.answer: Discipline, especially when a trial is involved.

sources.says: A main motion brings business before the assembly and can be made only while no other motion is pending.

q1219.answer: While no other motion is pending.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says a main motion to limit or extend limits of debate for the duration of a meeting requires a two-thirds vote.

Motions to “reaffirm” a position already adopted are not in order. The original motion is still in effect, amending the reaffirmation would conflict with other rules, and a failed reaffirmation would create confusion.

q1221.answer: A motion to reaffirm a position previously taken.

sources.says: A member may speak in debate on the main motion and finish by offering a secondary motion.
This follows the principle that a member recognized for any legitimate purpose has the floor for all legitimate purposes.

q1222.answer: Any of these: an amendment, a motion to refer, or another secondary motion.

sources.says: When a main motion is referred, any pending amendments go to the committee with it and are reported back with it. A pending motion to Postpone Indefinitely is dropped.

q1223.answer: The amendment stays attached to the main motion and goes to the committee with it.

sources.says: Certain questions can come before the assembly as main motions after interrupting other business when brought up by one of the two lowest-ranking privileged motions: Call for the Orders of the Day and Raise a Question of Privilege.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: Of the privileged motions, Call for the Orders of the Day ranks lowest.

q1224.answer: To Call for the Orders of the Day.

sources.says: Ratification applies to actions taken without a quorum, actions at a special meeting outside the call, actions exceeding authority, local actions needing state or national approval, and state or national actions subject to approval by constituent units.

q1225.answer: All three are proper cases for ratification, so none is excluded.

sources.says: The motion to Postpone Indefinitely isn’t amendable.
An amendment is out of order if it would turn one parliamentary motion into another.

q1226.answer: Declare the amendment out of order.

sources.says: Postponing a main question indefinitely suppresses it for the rest of the session, so adopting the motion is in effect an indirect rejection of the main motion.

q1227.answer: It rejects the main motion indirectly.

sources.says: If a main motion is referred while Postpone Indefinitely is pending, that motion is ignored and doesn’t go to the committee, since referral shows the assembly doesn’t favor indefinite postponement.

q1228.answer: It does not go to the committee.

sources.says: Neither the member who offers an amendment nor the maker of the main motion “makes an amendment.” Only the assembly can do that.

When applied to a main motion, Amend takes precedence over the main motion and over Postpone Indefinitely. It yields to the higher subsidiary motions, all privileged motions, and applicable incidental motions.
A motion to divide the main question can’t be made while an amendment to it is pending, and the same is true of Consideration by Paragraph.

q1230.answer: It takes precedence over Postpone Indefinitely.

sources.says: Amend can be applied to a pending primary amendment, creating a secondary amendment (an “amendment to an amendment”), but it can’t be applied to a secondary amendment.

Commit, Postpone Definitely, or Lay on the Table can’t be applied to an amendment alone, but the main question can be committed, postponed, or tabled with its amendments. The motion to Amend can’t be postponed indefinitely.
Amend is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, and is debatable only when the motion it would amend is debatable.
An amendment requires a majority vote, whatever vote the question being amended needs.

The three processes of amendment are inserting (or adding) words, striking out words, and striking out and inserting words. Separate forms exist for inserting, striking out, or substituting whole paragraphs.

q1235.answer: Changing wording within a single sentence.

sources.says: “Amendment of the first degree” and “amendment to the main question” are correct, but “primary amendment” is the preferred term.
“Amendment of the second degree” and “amendment to the amendment” are correct, but “secondary amendment” is the preferred term.
Amendments of the first and second degree are correct expressions, but an amendment of the third degree is not permitted.
Only two degrees of amendment are possible. A primary amendment applies to the pending motion, and a secondary amendment applies to the pending primary amendment.
A third-degree amendment isn’t permitted. A member can say that if the pending secondary amendment is voted down, they will offer another one.

q1239.answer: One primary amendment and one secondary amendment.

sources.says: An amendment is out of order if it would turn one parliamentary motion into another, such as changing a motion to postpone to a certain time into Postpone Indefinitely.

q1240.answer: Rule the amendment out of order because it would change the motion into a different kind of motion.

sources.says: A primary amendment to substitute is open to debate while no secondary amendment is pending, and that debate may go fully into the merits of both the original text and the proposed substitute.

q1241.answer: Debate may go into the merits of the main motion.

sources.says: A motion to create a blank may look like an amendment to strike out and insert, but it is actually an incidental motion.
Each proposal for filling a blank is voted on in turn as a separate question. As soon as one receives a majority vote, the chair declares the blank filled.
When a blank exists, members can suggest names, places, numbers, dates, or amounts to fill it.

q1244.answer: All of these: names, amounts of money, and places, dates, and numbers.

sources.says: Proposals should be arranged so the one least likely to be accepted is voted on first.
For a measure to spend money, amounts are voted on from highest to lowest.
The vote that fills a blank doesn’t decide the motion containing it. Once the blank is filled, the chair states the question on adopting the completed motion, which stays pending.

q1246.answer: The false statement is that the vote filling the blank decides the main motion.

sources.says: Commit can’t be postponed definitely or tabled alone, though the main question can be, taking Commit with it. It is amendable, and it can’t be postponed indefinitely.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists Commit, Refer, or Recommit a pending question as requiring a majority vote.
If the main question is to go to a standing committee, the motion should name the committee.

When different committees are proposed, the chair votes on them in this order until one gets a majority: committee of the whole, quasi committee of the whole, consider informally, standing committees, then special committees, largest first.
A committee may include nonmembers, but if the chair appoints it, the names of all nonmembers must be submitted to the assembly for approval unless the rules or the motion authorize otherwise.
When the chair appoints a committee, the chair names the chairman first. That person automatically becomes chairman unless they immediately decline.
If the committee is named by some body other than the chair, such as the assembly, that body may designate the chairman when making the appointments. Otherwise, the committee elects its own chairman.

q1253.answer: The assembly that elected the committee members.

sources.says: The power to appoint a committee includes the power to fill any vacancy in it. Resignations go to the appointing power, which is responsible for filling the vacancy.

q1254.answer: The president, who appointed the committee.

sources.says: Typical forms include “I move to refer the motion to a committee” and “I move that the motion be referred to the Social Committee.”

q1255.answer: “I move to refer the motion to a committee.”

sources.says: Typical forms of the motion to Commit name what is referred and where, such as “I move that the motion be referred to the Social Committee.”

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: Going into a committee of the whole is a form of Commit, made as “I move that the assembly now resolve itself into a committee of the whole to consider….”

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The motion “that the question be considered informally” is a variation of Commit.

q1256.answer: “I move to commit or refer” is not a correct form.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: The motion is called Postpone to a Certain Time, Postpone Definitely, or simply Postpone. The expression “to defer” should be avoided because it is often used vaguely.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: A motion to postpone a matter that isn’t pending, such as hearing a committee report, is not the subsidiary motion to Postpone. It is an incidental main motion.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: The motion to Postpone can’t be laid on the table alone, though the main question can be tabled and take it along. It can’t be postponed indefinitely or committed.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Postpone to a Certain Time is amendable as to the time the main question is postponed to, and as to making it a special order.

q1260.answer: The time the main question is postponed to.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Neither the motion to Postpone to a Certain Time nor an amendment to it is in order if its effect would be the same as Postpone Indefinitely, killing the measure.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: When more than a quarterly time interval will pass between meetings, a question can’t be postponed beyond the end of the current session.

q1261.answer: The false statement is that it has the same effect as Postpone Indefinitely.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: Postponing to tomorrow a question about something happening tonight would kill it, so it can’t be treated as Postpone to a Certain Time. The chair must rule it out of order or treat it as a motion to Postpone Indefinitely.

q1262.answer: Rule the motion out of order.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: A whole class of business, such as officer or committee reports, can’t be postponed as a group. Each report can be postponed separately as it is announced or called for.

q1263.answer: Suggest a separate motion to postpone each report as it is called for.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: A matter the bylaws require at a particular session can be postponed to an adjourned meeting, after first adopting, if needed, a motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q1264.answer: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Where the order of business has no specific headings, special orders not set for a particular hour are taken up before unfinished business and general orders, and in any event before new business. General orders come after unfinished business.

q1265.answer: The false statement is that special orders are normally taken up after new business.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: General orders are taken up after any unfinished business.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Unfinished business includes questions set as general orders for the previous meeting (by postponement or otherwise) that weren’t reached before it adjourned.

q1267.answer: It becomes unfinished business at the next regular meeting.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: When a question is taken up on a different day from the one it was postponed on, members’ right to debate starts over, so each member can again speak twice on each debatable question.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: To make sure a question comes up at the next meeting and isn’t crowded out, the form is “I move that the question be postponed to the next meeting and be made a special order.”

q1269.answer: “I move that the question be postponed to the next meeting and be made a special order.”

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: To have a question come up at exactly a certain hour, even interrupting pending business, the form is “I move that the resolution be postponed and be made a special order for [the time].” It needs a two-thirds vote.

q1270.answer: “I move that the motion be postponed and be made a special order for 3 p.m. tomorrow.”

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate and the Previous Question are the two motions for special control over debate. Neither is allowed in committees.

q1271.answer: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate and the Previous Question.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: This motion can limit the number or length of speeches, set a later time for closing debate, or allow more and longer speeches. It can’t close debate immediately, which requires the Previous Question.

q1272.answer: It can’t force an immediate close of debate.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: When an order limiting or extending debate stops applying to all the motions it affected, the order is said to be “exhausted.”

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: A motion changing the limits of debate made while no question is pending is an incidental main motion, not the subsidiary motion.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says such a main motion, for the duration of a meeting, requires a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, and isn’t debatable. It is amendable, but any amendment is also undebatable.

q1275.answer: The false statement is that an amendment to it is debatable.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: The motion can apply to the immediately pending question, a consecutive part of the series, or the whole series. If it doesn’t say which, only the immediately pending question is affected.

The Previous Question takes precedence over Limit or Extend Limits of Debate. If adopted, it overrides an unexhausted order limiting or extending debate for the motions it applies to. It isn’t debatable and needs two-thirds.
Once the motion is seconded and members object to closing debate, the chair must immediately take a vote on it.

q1277.answer: Take a vote on the Previous Question once it is seconded.

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: The order is exhausted when all the questions it applied to have been voted on, when the remaining ones are referred or postponed indefinitely, or at the end of the session, whichever comes first.

q1278.answer: All three (the meeting ending counts when it ends the session).

sources.section: §15 Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
sources.says: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate yields to the Previous Question and Lay on the Table, and to all privileged and applicable incidental motions.

q1279.answer: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate.

sources.says: The Previous Question can be applied to an immediately pending debatable or amendable motion, to a whole series of them, or to any consecutive part of the series starting with the immediately pending question.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The Previous Question can close amendment on motions that are amendable but not debatable.
Ordering the Previous Question closes debate on and stops amendment of the questions it applies to.

The Previous Question isn’t amendable. But when it is immediately pending on a series of questions, it can be moved again to include more or fewer of the pending questions, which works much like an amendment.

q1282.answer: It can be moved again to include more or fewer pending questions.

sources.says: The Previous Question requires a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A two-thirds vote means at least two-thirds of the votes cast by those entitled to vote, not counting blanks or abstentions.
The rules of the U.S. House of Representatives allow the Previous Question to be ordered by a majority vote, but conditions there differ from those in ordinary organizations.
Forms like “I call for [or call] the question,” “I move to close debate,” or “I move we vote now” are simply the Previous Question in nonstandard form and follow all its rules.
“I move we vote now” is a motion for the Previous Question in nonstandard form and is subject to all the same rules.

q1286.answer: A motion for the Previous Question.

sources.says: “I move the previous question,” without more, applies only to the immediately pending question.

Adopting Lay on the Table lets a majority stop consideration of a question immediately without debate. In ordinary assemblies, it’s out of order if the evident intent is to kill or avoid dealing with a measure.

q1288.answer: The false statement is that it may be used to avoid dealing with a motion.

sources.says: Lay on the Table applies only to a question actually pending. A group of questions, such as orders of the day, unfinished business, or committee reports, can’t be laid on the table as a unit.
An essential feature of Lay on the Table is that it can’t be qualified in any way. While the question stays on the table, when or whether it is taken up is left open.

q1290.answer: It cannot be qualified in any way.

sources.says: An affirmative vote on Lay on the Table can’t be reconsidered, because it’s easier and more direct to move to take the question from the table.

q1291.answer: Rule that the vote to lay on the table cannot be reconsidered.

sources.says: At a special meeting, a question can be taken from the table only if it was laid there earlier in the same session, or if the call of the meeting names the question or its subject.

q1292.answer: Only if the call of the meeting gives notice of it.

sources.says: A motion the same day to lay the same question on the table is in order only after material progress in business or debate, or when an unforeseen urgent matter needs immediate attention.
Lay on the Table is often wrongly used to kill a question without a direct vote or to suppress it without debate.
Its proper use is to set the pending question aside temporarily when something of immediate urgency has come up.
At a special meeting, it’s dilatory and out of order to move to lay on the table the matter the meeting was called for.

q1295.answer: To lay on the table the matter the meeting was called for.

sources.says: To dispose of a question without a direct vote, the suitable motion is Postpone Indefinitely. It can be followed by the Previous Question to avoid more debate.
When moving to lay on the table, a member can mention the intended purpose or a time they plan to move to take it from the table, but can’t attach a condition like “until 2 P.M.”

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day takes precedence over all motions except other privileged motions and a motion to Suspend the Rules relating to the priority of business.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: Recess is a privileged motion ranking above Call for the Orders of the Day.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: A Call for the Orders of the Day lets a member require the assembly to follow its agenda or order of business, or to take up a general or special order that is due, unless two-thirds wish otherwise.

q1299.answer: To take up a general order that is due but not being considered.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: When no special order is involved and a member starts a motion that departs from the correct order of business, the call must be made before the chair states the motion.

q1300.answer: Before the chair states the motion.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: The chair can put the question on proceeding to the orders of the day. It takes a two-thirds vote in the negative to refuse to take them up.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: Once the assembly has refused to proceed to the orders of the day, they can’t be called for again until the pending business is disposed of.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: To call for the orders of the day, a member rises and addresses the chair without waiting for recognition.

sources.section: §18 Call for the Orders of the Day
sources.says: The member rises and, without waiting for recognition, says “Mr. President, I call for the orders of the day” or “I demand the regular order.”

q1304.answer: “Mr. President, I call for the orders of the day.”

sources.says: When a member rises to a question of privilege, the chair immediately directs the member to state it, then rules whether it is a question of privilege and whether it is urgent enough to interrupt.

q1305.answer: Direct the member to state the question of privilege.

sources.says: A recess is a short break that doesn’t close the meeting. Afterward, business resumes at exactly the point where it was interrupted.

q1306.answer: Afterward, the meeting continues exactly where it left off.

sources.says: In ordinary cases, a motion simply “to adjourn,” even when made with no question pending, is not debatable or amendable and follows the rules of the privileged motion.
The privileged motion to Adjourn isn’t in order while the assembly is voting or verifying a vote, or before the chair announces the result (with an exception for ballot votes).
The privileged motion to Adjourn can’t be applied to any other motion. It takes precedence over pending motions without being applied to them.
The privileged motion to Adjourn must be seconded, isn’t debatable or amendable, and requires a majority vote.
When a special committee has finished its assigned business, it “rises” and reports, which is equivalent to the main motion to adjourn sine die (without day).

q1311.answer: The main motion to adjourn (sine die).

sources.says: While the privileged motion to Adjourn is pending, a member may still give notice of a motion to be made at the next meeting, among other steps.
The motion to Adjourn isn’t debatable or amendable and needs only a majority.

q1312.answer: Give notice of a motion to be made at the next meeting.

sources.says: However the vote to adjourn was taken, the meeting isn’t closed until the chair declares it “is adjourned,” and members shouldn’t leave their seats before then.
If a member who hasn’t properly obtained the floor calls out “I move to adjourn,” it can be entertained as a motion only by unanimous consent.
When a scheduled adjournment hour arrives in a convention or multi-meeting session, no motion is needed. The chair announces the fact and declares the meeting adjourned.

q1315.answer: Announce the fact and declare the meeting adjourned.

sources.says: When a motion to adjourn is made and seconded with no other business, and the chair senses a general desire to adjourn, the chair may say “If there is no objection, the meeting will now adjourn,” pause, then declare it adjourned.

q1316.answer: “If there is no objection, the meeting will now adjourn.” (pause) “Since there is no objection, the meeting is adjourned.”

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: A motion to fix the time to which to adjourn made while no question is pending is in order, is debatable, and follows all the other rules for main motions.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: The privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn takes precedence over all other motions. It yields only to Amend or the Previous Question applied to it, and to applicable incidental motions that arise.
Recess ranks below Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: The motion is amendable as to the date, hour, or place, and such amendments are undebatable.

q1319.answer: All three: date, hour, and place.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Amend can be applied to this motion, and amendments as to date, hour, or place are undebatable.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Amendment as to time and place is possible, but no debate is in order.

q1320.answer: Take a vote on the amendment without debate.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: The privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn takes precedence over all other motions and requires a majority vote.
An adjourned meeting picks up where the previous meeting left off, except that the minutes of the preceding meeting are read first.

sources.section: §22 Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
sources.says: Adopting this motion doesn’t adjourn the current meeting or set a time for its adjournment. It is very different from a motion to fix the time at which to adjourn.
A Point of Order is in order when another has the floor, even interrupting a person speaking or reading a report, if the point truly needs attention right then.
A Point of Order is normally ruled on by the chair. No vote is taken unless the chair is in doubt or the ruling is appealed.

q1325.answer: It isn’t voted on unless the chair is in doubt or the ruling is appealed.

sources.says: If the chair notices a breach, the chair corrects it immediately. Otherwise, any member can raise a Point of Order.

A member unsure whether there’s a breach can make a parliamentary inquiry. In ordinary meetings, raising points of order on minor technical irregularities is undesirable when no one’s rights are harmed.
Any two members can appeal the chair’s ruling, one moving and one seconding.

q1326.answer: The false statement is that points of order should be raised on every trivial technical irregularity.

sources.says: A point of order must generally be raised promptly, at the time the breach occurs.

q1327.answer: As soon as the breach occurs.

sources.says: After a member rises to a point of order, the chair asks the member to state the point of order.

q1328.answer: Ask the member to state the point.

sources.says: When a member rises to a point of order, anyone who is speaking takes their seat.
After stating the point of order, the member sits down, and the chair then rules on it.
The chair rules whether “the point of order is well taken” or “is not well taken,” briefly stating the reasons, which go in the minutes.

q1331.answer: Rule whether the point of order is (or is not) well taken and give the reason.

sources.says: Before ruling, the chair can consult the parliamentarian, if there is one, and may ask experienced members for advice.
When a point of order submitted to a vote is debatable, as with an appeal, no member can speak more than once, except the chair.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: In that debate, the chair may speak once before any other member and again at the close of debate.

q1333.answer: The chair, who can speak first and last.

sources.says: An appeal must be made at the time of the chair’s ruling. If any debate or business has intervened, it’s too late to appeal.

q1334.answer: Rule that the appeal is too late.

sources.says: When an appeal is debatable, no member may speak more than once except the presiding officer, who doesn’t leave the chair to speak but should stand.

q1335.answer: The chair may join the debate without leaving the chair.

sources.says: A member who disagrees with the chair’s ruling on a substantial question should not hesitate to appeal.

sources.section: §62 Removal from Office and Other Remedies for Dereliction of
sources.says: The member rises immediately after the ruling and says “I appeal from the decision of the chair.”

q1336.answer: Appeal the decision of the chair.

sources.says: Rules can’t be suspended in a way that conflicts with the bylaws, applicable law, or a fundamental principle of parliamentary law.
Rules protecting absentees can’t be suspended, even by unanimous consent, because the absentees haven’t consented.

q1337.answer: None of them can be suspended.

sources.says: If a motion to suspend the rules fails, it can’t be renewed for the same purpose at the same meeting without unanimous consent. It can be renewed after an adjournment, even the same day.
Rules protecting absentees, including the requirement of previous notice for a bylaw amendment, can’t be suspended, even by unanimous consent or a unanimous vote, when any member is absent.

sources.section: §2 Rules of an Assembly or Organization
sources.says: Standing rules deal with administrative details, such as the hour meetings begin, and can be adopted or changed like any ordinary act of the society.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says suspending ordinary standing rules requires only a majority vote, while suspending rules of order generally takes two-thirds.

q1340.answer: The standing rule setting the time meetings begin.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: An Objection to the Consideration of a Question lets the assembly avoid an original main motion entirely when it finds the question irrelevant, unprofitable, or contentious.

sources.section: §26 Objection to the Consideration of a Question
sources.says: If the objection is sustained, the main motion is dismissed for that session and can’t be renewed during it except by unanimous consent or reconsideration.

q1341.answer: The pending motion is not considered during that meeting.

sources.says: When a motion has two or more parts that could each stand as separate questions, the assembly can vote to divide it so the parts are considered and voted on separately.

q1342.answer: The pending motion is divided into separate parts for action.

sources.says: Division of a Question is out of order when another has the floor, must be seconded, isn’t debatable, is amendable, needs a majority, and can’t be reconsidered.
Division of a Question can be applied to main motions and to their amendments, if they can be divided.
A motion can’t be divided unless each part would be a proper question on its own even if the other parts aren’t adopted.

q1345.answer: Rule the motion to divide out of order, since the second part can’t stand alone.

sources.says: A Division of the Assembly needs no second, isn’t debatable or amendable, and no subsidiary motion can be applied to it.
When retaking the vote, the chair can count it or order it counted if it looks close.

q1346.answer: The false statement is that debate is allowed on it.

sources.says: A Division of the Assembly is in order when another has the floor, is called for without obtaining the floor, and may be demanded until the result is announced or immediately afterward.
When a Division is demanded, the chair retakes the vote, first having the affirmative rise, then the negative.

sources.section: §30 Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
sources.says: Motions relating to methods of voting take precedence over the motion being voted on or to be voted on, and yield to privileged motions.

q1349.answer: It takes precedence over the motion being voted on.

sources.says: Incidental motions relating to nominations yield to privileged motions and Lay on the Table, must be seconded, and can generally be reconsidered, except as to closing nominations.
Motions relating to nominations need a majority vote, except that closing nominations requires two-thirds, since it takes away the right to nominate.

q1351.answer: A majority, except that closing nominations needs two-thirds.

sources.says: When different nominating methods are treated as filling blanks, they are voted on in this order: by the chair, from the floor, by a committee, by ballot, by mail, then by electronic means.

sources.section: §32 Request to Be Excused from a Duty
sources.says: A motion to grant a Request to Be Excused from a Duty is debatable and amendable, and needs a majority unless settled by unanimous consent.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules lists a Parliamentary Inquiry as neither debatable nor amendable. The same is true of a Request for Information.

q1353.answer: A Request to Be Excused from a Duty.

sources.says: Before the chair states the question, the maker has the right to modify the motion or withdraw it entirely.
Another member can ask whether the maker will accept a change, and the maker can accept or reject it.
If the maker accepts a modification suggested by another member, the suggester has in effect seconded the modified motion, so no other second is needed.

q1355.answer: The member who suggested the change has in effect seconded it.

sources.says: When a paper is laid before the assembly for action, every member has the right to have it read once, and read again before the vote if there was debate or amendment. Otherwise, reading requires the assembly’s permission.
Members are usually allowed to read short, relevant printed extracts in debate, as long as they don’t abuse the privilege.

q1356.answer: A paper laid before the assembly for action can be read once.

sources.says: Take from the Table takes precedence over no pending motion, so it can’t be moved while any other question is pending.

q1357.answer: It takes precedence over no pending motion.

sources.says: Rescind must be seconded, is debatable, with debate going into the merits of what it would rescind, and is amendable.

sources.section: Table II, Table of Rules Relating to Motions
sources.says: The table of rules says an Objection to Consideration needs no second and isn’t debatable or amendable.
Discharge a Committee is debatable, and debate can go into the merits of the question in the committee’s hands.

q1359.answer: It can go into the merits of the question referred to the committee.

sources.says: When a committee is discharged, a standing committee continues to exist, but a special committee appointed to take up that matter ceases to exist.
For a special committee, a member who has obtained the floor may say, “I move that the committee to which was referred the resolution relating to… be discharged.”

q1361.answer: After obtaining the floor: “I move that the committee to which was referred the motion related to… be discharged.”

sources.says: The purpose of reconsidering a vote is to correct hasty, ill-advised, or erroneous action, or to account for new information or a changed situation.
Reconsider can’t be applied to a motion that can be renewed, to an affirmative contract vote after the other party has been notified, or to a vote on a motion to Reconsider, among other exceptions.
The motion to Reconsider can be made only by a member who voted with the prevailing side. The restriction applies to the maker.
The motion to Reconsider is seconded by another member, with no requirement about how the seconder voted.

q1364.answer: The seconder may have voted on either side.

sources.says: To call up the motion to Reconsider, a member obtains the floor and calls it up. No second is needed, because it was seconded when it was made.
If reconsideration happens on a different day from the original vote, every member’s right to debate starts over, regardless of earlier speeches.

q1366.answer: Every member may debate twice again.

sources.says: Debate on a motion to reconsider an amendment to the pending main question can go into the merits of the amendment, but not the main question apart from the amendment.

q1367.answer: The merits of the amendment may be debated.

sources.says: In standing and special committees, a motion to reconsider can be made and taken up no matter how much time has passed since the vote, and a question can be reconsidered any number of times.

q1368.answer: At any time after the vote.

sources.says: If the maker of the motion to Reconsider doesn’t say which side they voted on, the chair, before anything else, directs the member to do so.

q1369.answer: Immediately tell the member to state it.

sources.says: If the motion was adopted by unanimous consent, the chair asks whether the member was present at the time.

q1370.answer: Ask whether the member was present at the time.

sources.says: Adopting the motion to Reconsider puts the question back before the assembly in the exact position it held just before the original vote.
After adoption of the motion to Reconsider, and after any debate, the vote on the reconsidered question is taken again.

q1371.answer: State the question on the main motion again, open to debate.

sources.says: Subsidiary motions like Commit, a Call for the Orders of the Day, and Take from the Table can be renewed after progress in business or debate.

An assembly can’t be asked to decide the same or substantially the same question twice in one session, except through Reconsider, Rescind, or amending something already adopted. That limits renewal of a rejected main motion.
Except for Rescind or Amend Something Previously Adopted, a motion is out of order if it conflicts with a motion previously adopted and still in force. If adopted anyway, it is null and void.
A quorum is the number of members who must be present to transact business. It refers to members present, not the number voting on a question.
The number constituting a quorum varies by organization. In many churches without effective dues or reliable rolls, the quorum is whoever attends.

q1374.answer: The false statement is that a quorum is the number of members voting on a motion.

sources.says: Depending on the organization and the provision it adopts, the number of members constituting a quorum may vary.
In organizations with no required dues and no reliable membership list, such as many churches, the quorum at a properly called meeting is those who attend.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: The quorum of a committee of the whole is the same as the assembly’s unless the bylaws provide otherwise or the assembly sets a different one.

q1377.answer: The same as in the assembly.

sources.says: If the chair notices a quorum is missing, the chair must declare that fact, at least before taking any vote or stating any new motion.

q1378.answer: Declare that there is no quorum.

sources.says: Any member who notices the apparent absence of a quorum can raise a point of order at any time, as long as they don’t interrupt a person speaking.

q1379.answer: As long as the member doesn’t interrupt someone who is speaking.

sources.says: Debate on a pending question can be allowed to continue after a quorum is gone, until a member raises the point. A member may not interrupt a speaker to do so.
When a Call of the House is ordered, the clerk first calls the roll of all members, then calls the absentees’ names again. After that, no member may leave.
A Call of the House isn’t applicable in voluntary societies.
After a Call of the House is ordered, only motions relating to the call are in order.

q1381.answer: The false statement is that the clerk calls the absentees’ names first.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When no one responds to “Are there any corrections to the minutes?”, the chair says that, there being no corrections, the minutes stand approved.

q1382.answer: “If there are no corrections, the minutes stand approved.”

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Business that relates to the reports of officers, boards, and standing committees and is on the table can be taken from the table under that heading.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Business relating to special committee reports that is on the table can be taken from the table under that heading.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Any business on the table can be taken from the table under Unfinished Business and General Orders when no question is pending.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Standing committees listed in the bylaws are called on in the order they are listed.

q1384.answer: In the order they are listed in the bylaws.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: The standard order of business includes a heading called Unfinished Business and General Orders.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: The chair shouldn’t ask “Is there any unfinished business?” but should state the question on the first item due to come up under that heading.

q1386.answer: State the question on the first item under that heading.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Under Good of the Order, General Good and Welfare, or Open Forum, members who get the floor are commonly allowed to offer informal observations about the organization’s work, unlike the usual rule that discussion needs a pending motion.

q1387.answer: Offer informal observations about the organization’s work.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: The chair can’t depart from the prescribed order of business. Only the assembly can, by at least a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §14 Postpone to a Certain Time (or Definitely)
sources.says: A whole class of business can’t be postponed, but each item can be postponed separately.

q1388.answer: The false statement is that the chair can depart from the order of business without the assembly’s permission.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: To get unanimous consent, the chair may say “If there is no objection, the chair proposes at this time to proceed to take up….”

q1389.answer: “If there is no objection, the chair proposes at this time to proceed to take up….”

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: An order of the day can’t be taken up before its set time except by reconsidering the vote that set it, or by suspending the rules by a two-thirds vote.

q1390.answer: By suspending the rules with a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: A special order suspends rules that would interfere with it, except rules relating to adjournment or recess, questions of privilege, earlier special orders, and a few other cases.

q1391.answer: All three can interfere with it.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: A pending question can be made an order of the day by postponing it to a specified time by majority vote (a general order), or by two-thirds as a special order.

q1392.answer: By postponing it to a specified time by majority vote.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: Even when its hour has come, a general order is taken up only if no other business is pending, no special order interferes, and no motion to Reconsider interferes.

q1393.answer: All three conditions must be met.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: When an entire meeting is devoted to one subject as the special order for the meeting, it is taken up as soon as the minutes have been approved.

q1394.answer: After the minutes have been approved.

sources.section: §41 Order of Business; Orders of the Day; Agenda or Program
sources.says: After an agenda has been adopted, it can be changed only by a two-thirds vote, a majority of the entire membership, or unanimous consent.

q1395.answer: A two-thirds vote, unanimous consent, or a majority of the entire membership.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: When the floor can be granted only for limited purposes, such as while an undebatable question is pending, and the chair isn’t sure the member knows this, the chair asks “For what purpose does the member rise?”

q1396.answer: Ask, “For what purpose does the member rise?”

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: A member who rises before the floor is yielded isn’t entitled to it if another member rises afterward and addresses the chair.

q1397.answer: Give the floor to member B.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: When the floor is assigned to a claimant who wasn’t the first to rise and address the chair, that member is said to be entitled to “preference in being recognized.”

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: When an undebatable question is immediately pending, the floor can be granted only for limited purposes.

sources.section: §5 Basic Classifications; Order of Precedence of Motions
sources.says: A motion that takes precedence over the pending question can be made while it is pending and temporarily replaces it.

q1399.answer: A motion that takes precedence over the immediately pending question.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: When a motion is voted down at the urging of a member who said in debate they would then offer a different motion on the subject, that member is entitled to preference in recognition to introduce it.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: When no question is pending and someone seeks the floor for a main motion, another member has preference if rising to move to reconsider, to call up a motion to reconsider, to give previous notice, and for a few other purposes.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: Except in a mass meeting, any two members can appeal the chair’s decision in assigning the floor, one making the appeal and one seconding.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: In a large hall, members may line up at numbered microphones and be recognized in numerical order, or someone may list them for the chair.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: A member presenting a report who hands it to the secretary to read doesn’t yield the floor, and has it again when the reading is finished.

q1404.answer: The member has the floor again when the reading is finished.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: When a member has risen to claim or has been assigned the floor, it is out of order for others to call out motions to adjourn or to table, or to call “Question!” The chair must restore order and protect the member’s rights.

q1405.answer: All three are out of order.

sources.says: A matter can’t be debated until it has been brought before the assembly as a motion proposing a specific action.
There is no such thing as “gaveling through” a measure. The chair can’t cut off debate or secondary motions by putting a question to a vote so quickly that no member can get the floor.

q1407.answer: The chair puts a question to a vote so fast that members can’t get the floor.

sources.says: When a vote is retaken for verification, as when a Division is demanded, debate can’t resume except by unanimous consent.
Debate rights aren’t transferable. A member who yields the floor before using the full ten minutes is presumed to have waived the rest of the time, and can’t give it to someone else or save it.

sources.section: §42 Rules Governing Assignment of the Floor
sources.says: In debate on an appeal, the chair may speak once before any other member and again at the close. Other members are limited to one speech.
Merely asking a question or making a brief suggestion doesn’t count as speaking in debate.

q1411.answer: They are not counted as speaking in debate.

sources.says: A member who has spoken twice on the main motion can still speak twice on each amendment the same day, since each debatable motion is a separate question.
While a debatable question is pending, the length or number of speeches can be reduced or increased for that question by Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, adopted by a two-thirds vote.
Limits of debate on a pending question can be reduced or increased by Limit or Extend Limits of Debate. The Previous Question closes debate immediately.

sources.section: §52 Committee of the Whole and Its Alternate Forms
sources.says: Informal consideration removes limits on the number of speeches on the main question and its amendments. Other motions follow the regular rules.
Speeches made in committee of the whole, quasi committee, or informal consideration don’t count against a member’s right to debate the question again under the regular rules the same day.

q1415.answer: Dunbar’s key says a total of two times on the same question on the same day.
q1415.conflict: That is right only once the assembly returns to its regular rules: the informal speeches don’t count, so the member gets two speeches that day. While the question is still being considered informally, RONR 12th ed. puts no limit on the number of speeches.

sources.says: As soon as the chair hears words like “fraud,” “liar,” or “lie” used about a member in debate, the chair must act immediately and firmly to correct it and prevent it from happening again.

q1416.answer: Correct the matter at once and prevent it from happening again.

sources.says: There’s no need to refer to oneself in the third person, like “this member.” The first person is quite acceptable in debate.
In debate on an appeal, or a point of order the chair has put to the assembly, the presiding officer doesn’t leave the chair, since that participation relates to presiding.
Debate on Commit is confined to whether to refer, the choice of committee members, and the committee’s instructions.

sources.section: §6 Description of Classes and Individual Motions
sources.says: The three highest-ranking subsidiary motions, Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, the Previous Question, and Lay on the Table, can’t be debated, since that would defeat their purpose.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A majority means more than half of the votes cast by those entitled to vote, not counting blanks or abstentions.

q1421.answer: 11, since more than half of 21 is 11.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A two-thirds vote means at least two-thirds of the votes cast by those entitled to vote, not counting blanks or abstentions. For example, 30 votes cast need 20, and 32 votes cast need 22.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A two-thirds vote is required for any motion that suspends or modifies a rule of order, prevents the introduction of a question, closes or limits debate, limits nominating or voting, or takes away membership.

q1423.answer: A motion that takes away membership or office.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: RONR works an example: with 30 present and 25 voting, a majority is 13, a two-thirds vote is 17, and two-thirds of the members present is 20. Each basis uses its own base number.

q1424.answer: The false statement is that two-thirds of the 60 members present is 41. It is 40.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: In a board fixed at 12 members, if 2 seats are vacant, a majority of the entire membership is based on the 10 actual members. A majority of the fixed membership would still be based on 12.

q1425.answer: 6, a majority of the 10 remaining members.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
sources.says: A presiding officer who is a member may vote whenever it will affect the result: to break or cause a tie, or to cause or block a two-thirds vote.

sources.section: §44 Bases for Determining a Voting Result
